title: A Course in Differential Privacy
text:
Preface
This book is a course in differential privacy. It starts from the failures that motivate the subject, builds the definition and its basic algorithms, and goes on to answering many queries, private statistics and machine learning, lower bounds, and deployments.
Each chapter takes one topic. The text is short, and the mathematics is complete. Definitions, theorems and proofs are set apart and numbered, and every proof is given in full or, where it is long and standard, cited with what it needs. The prose between them says why each result comes next and what it means.
The reader should know discrete probability, including expectation, variance, independence and the inequalities of Markov, Chebyshev and Hoeffding, and basic linear algebra and calculus. Results from probability that the course needs beyond these are stated and proved where they are first used.
Notation. A dataset is \(D = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathcal X^n\), a list of \(n\) records from a universe \(\mathcal X\). Two datasets are neighbours, \(D \sim D'\), when they differ in one record, which is the replace-one relation. A mechanism \(M\) maps a dataset to a random output in a set \(\mathcal Y\). The privacy parameters are \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0,1]\). The natural logarithm is written \(\ln\), and the logarithm to base 2 is written \(\log_2\).

title: Privacy Failures
text:
Privacy is easy to promise and hard to deliver, so this part shows what goes wrong without a definition before the course gives one. The first chapter looks at real releases that their owners protected with pseudonyms, removed names, summary statistics or a trained model. An attacker defeated each one by combining the release with information from another source. The second chapter turns these cases into theorems: answers to counting queries that are too accurate let an analyst rebuild almost every secret bit. Together the chapters set the requirements for a definition of privacy. It must hold against any side information and apply to any kind of output. It must degrade gracefully as more data comes out, and it must allow the error that the attacks show to be necessary.



Table 1: The chapters of this part.





Chapter
Question it answers




Attempts at Data Privacy
Why do pseudonyms, removing identifiers, releasing models or statistics, and \(k\)-anonymity fail to protect people?


Reconstruction Attacks
How much error must answers to counting queries have before an analyst cannot rebuild the data?

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.1 Pseudonyms: the taxi trips
This chapter looks at five releases of sensitive data whose owners believed them safe. An attacker undid each one by combining the release with information from another source. Each protection came from intuition, and nobody could say what it guaranteed or against whom. The last section shows that \(k\)-anonymity, the first formal answer to these attacks, fails in the same way.
In 2014, a public-records request obtained the record of every New York City taxi trip of 2013. Each record holds the times and places of the pickup and drop-off, the fare, the cab’s medallion number and the driver’s licence number. The two numbers would show where each driver worked and how much they earned, so the regulator replaced each one by a string of 32 hexadecimal digits. This step is called pseudonymization, and the attack below uses its one essential property: the same identifier always gets the same code.
An analyst saw that one licence pseudonym earned far more per day than any driver could. It was the MD5 hash of the string 0, a placeholder for a missing licence, so the function \(h\) was MD5 with no secret key. A hash function is hard to invert when its inputs come from a huge set. But the identifier formats allowed only about 22 million strings: about 3 million licence numbers and 19 million medallion numbers. With so few inputs, anyone can hash all of them and look up each pseudonym.
A licence number is not yet a name, so the attacker joined the decoded table with a public list of licensed drivers. That list gives the name for each licence number, so every driver’s trips and income became public. This join with a second table that names people turns every attack in this chapter into a disclosure.
Random pseudonyms would stop the dictionary attack, but not linkage. A passenger knows the time and place of their own pickup and can read the driver’s licence number in the cab, so that one row gives the driver’s pseudonym, which then points to every other trip by the same driver. Passengers are exposed too, because the time and place of a pickup identify the trip, and its drop-off point is often a home.

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
Definition 1.1 (Pseudonymization) Let \(\mathcal U\) be a set of identifiers, such as licence numbers. A pseudonymization replaces each identifier \(u \in \mathcal U\) in a table by \(h(u)\), where \(h\) is a fixed injective function, so that the same person gets the same pseudonym in every row.



Proposition 1.1 (Dictionary attack) Let the set of identifiers \(\mathcal U\) be finite, and let the pseudonymization function \(h\) be injective and computable by anyone. Then \(|\mathcal U|\) evaluations of \(h\) recover the identifier behind every pseudonym in the table.


Proof. 

Compute \(h(u)\) for every \(u \in \mathcal U\) and store the pairs \((h(u), u)\) in a table sorted by \(h(u)\). This takes \(|\mathcal U|\) evaluations of \(h\).
For each pseudonym \(v\) in the released table, look up \(v\). Since \(h\) is injective, exactly one stored pair has first entry \(v\), and its second entry is the identifier.




Definition 1.2 (Linkage attack) Let \(T\) be a released table and \(T'\) an auxiliary table that names people, and let \(Q\) be a set of attributes that both tables contain. A linkage attack joins \(T\) and \(T'\) on \(Q\). A row of \(T\) is re-identified when its values on \(Q\) match exactly one row of \(T'\) and no other row of \(T\).

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.2 Rich records: the Netflix Prize
In 2006, Netflix released about 100 million film ratings from about 480,000 subscribers for a contest. Each rating was a user pseudonym, a film, a score and a date. Such histories are sensitive, because they can hint at a person’s politics or sexuality.
Narayanan and Shmatikov showed in 2008 that the pseudonyms protected little, because many subscribers also post reviews on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb) under their name or a stable handle. A linkage attack in the sense of Definition 1.2, with \(Q\) the films, scores and dates, matches the two sources. The match need not be exact. The authors scored each candidate pair of users by how many films both rated with similar scores on nearby dates, and they gave rarely rated films more weight. They reported that 8 ratings, 2 of which may be wrong, with dates known only to within 14 days, single out 99% of the records.
So in a sparse table with many columns, almost every record is unique, and no attribute is harmless. A handful of a person’s ratings is enough to identify them.

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.3 Releasing a model: memorization
A trained model seems safer to release than a table. Carlini and coauthors tested this in 2019 on language models. Such a model predicts each word from the words before it, with a vector of parameters \(\theta\) learned from a corpus of text. To test whether a model has memorized a string, the authors measured how surprised the model is by it, in bits, so a string the model finds likely gets a small score.

Definition 1.3 (Log-perplexity) Write \(\Pr_\theta\) for the probability that the model with parameters \(\theta\) assigns to a sequence of words, or to the next word given the words before it. The log-perplexity of a sequence \(x_1, \dots, x_\ell\) of \(\ell\) words under this model is
\[
P_\theta(x_1, \dots, x_\ell) = -\log_2 \Pr_\theta[x_1, \dots, x_\ell] = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} -\log_2 \Pr_\theta\left[x_i \mid x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}\right].
\tag{1.1}\]

The second form follows from the chain rule of probability. A model of English gives “the cat sat on the mat” a low score and a string of unrelated words a high one. The question is whether a rare string in the training text, such as a password or an identity number, gets a much lower score than it would otherwise. If it does, the model memorized it, and anyone who can query the model may find it.
To measure this, the authors put a canary into the training text: a sentence of a fixed format with a random secret, such as “my identity number is 314-15-9265”. They then compared its score with those of all other sentences of that format. Exposure is large when the model ranks the true canary above most of them.

Definition 1.4 (Exposure) Let \(\mathcal R\) be the finite set of candidate secrets, all sentences of the canary’s format, and let \(N = |\mathcal R|\). Sort \(\mathcal R\) by increasing log-perplexity under the model, and let \(\operatorname{rank}(r) \in \{1, \dots, N\}\) be the position of \(r\), so that rank \(1\) is the most likely candidate. The exposure of \(r\) is
\[
\operatorname{exposure}(r) = \log_2 N - \log_2 \operatorname{rank}(r).
\tag{1.2}\]

Exposure goes from \(0\), for the least likely candidate, to \(\log_2 N\), for the most likely one, and an attacker can read a canary at the top off the model by trying the candidates in order. To know what a large exposure is, you need the exposure of a canary that the model never saw, which the next result bounds.

Proposition 1.2 (Exposure without memorization) Suppose the canary \(r\) is drawn uniformly from \(\mathcal R\), independently of the model, and the ranking breaks ties in a fixed way. Then for every \(t \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr[\operatorname{exposure}(r) \ge t] \le 2^{-t}, \qquad \mathbb E[\operatorname{exposure}(r)] < \frac{1}{\ln 2} \approx 1.443 .
\tag{1.3}\]


Proof. 

The ranking depends only on the model, and \(r\) is uniform and independent of it. So \(\operatorname{rank}(r)\) is uniform on \(\{1, \dots, N\}\).
The exposure is at least \(t\) exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}(r) \le N 2^{-t}\). By step 1 this has probability \(\lfloor N 2^{-t} \rfloor / N \le 2^{-t}\).
By step 1, the average exposure is \(\log_2 N - \frac1N\sum_{k=1}^N \log_2 k = \frac{1}{N\ln 2}\left(N\ln N - \ln N!\right)\).
Since \(\ln\) is increasing, \(\ln k\) is at least the integral of \(\ln x\) over \([k-1, k]\) for \(k \ge 2\). Summing over \(k\) gives

\[
\ln N! \ge \int_1^N \ln x\,\mathrm d x = N\ln N - N + 1.
\tag{1.4}\]

Steps 3 and 4 give \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{exposure}(r)] \le \frac{N-1}{N\ln 2} < \frac{1}{\ln 2}\).


So if the model never saw the canary, an exposure of \(t\) bits is as surprising as an event of probability \(2^{-t}\). With nine-digit secrets, \(N = 10^9\), and the largest possible exposure is \(\log_2 10^9 \approx 29.9\).
The experiments found both outcomes. A translation model trained on about 100,000 pairs of sentences got a canary with a nine-digit identity number, and after four insertions the canary reached the largest possible exposure. Gmail’s Smart Compose, trained on billions of word sequences, got canaries with \(N\) of order \(10^{12}\), and even after \(10{,}000\) insertions their exposure reached only about \(10\) of a possible \(39.9\). Standard defences against overfitting, such as dropout and regularization, did not reduce exposure. Training with differential privacy, the subject of the next part, was the only method the authors found that did.

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.4 Releasing statistics: genomic studies
Medical studies must publish their findings, and aggregate statistics seemed a safe middle ground. But suppose a study enrols only people with a stigmatized disease. Then the fact that a person took part reveals their diagnosis, and a test that decides membership from the published statistics is an attack.
Homer and coauthors showed in 2008 that such a test exists for genetic data. It compares a person’s genotype with the published allele frequencies of the study group and of a reference population. Under conditions on the number of genetic markers and the size of the group, it tells whether the person’s DNA was in the group. In practice the test makes more false positives than this analysis suggests, because its threshold depends on how well the reference population matches the study group. Even so, the National Institutes of Health in the United States moved aggregate genomic statistics behind an approval process.

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.5 Removing identifiers: \(k\)-anonymity
In the mid-1990s, the Group Insurance Commission of Massachusetts gave researchers the hospital records of every state employee, with names and social security numbers removed. Each record still held the patient’s ZIP code, date of birth, sex and diagnosis. Latanya Sweeney bought the voter roll of Cambridge, Massachusetts, which lists every voter’s name, ZIP code, date of birth and sex. A linkage attack (Definition 1.2) on these three attributes found the governor’s hospital records. The attack works at scale, because Sweeney later estimated that 87% of the population of the United States is the only person with their five-digit ZIP code, sex and date of birth.
Her answer, with Samarati, sorts the attributes of a table into three kinds. The release removes identifiers, such as names, and keeps sensitive attributes, such as the diagnosis, because they are what the release is for. In between are quasi-identifiers, such as ZIP code, age and sex, which are harmless alone but identify people in combination. So the release coarsens them, for example a ZIP code to three digits. It stops when each person hides among at least \(k\) rows that look the same.

Definition 1.5 (\(k\)-anonymity) Let \(k \ge 1\) be an integer. A table is \(k\)-anonymous with respect to a set of quasi-identifiers if every combination of quasi-identifier values that appears in the table appears in at least \(k\) rows. The rows that share a combination form an equivalence class.

A \(k\)-anonymous table stops the attack on the governor, because a linkage on the quasi-identifiers matches every person to at least \(k\) rows. But the definition says nothing about the sensitive values in a class, or about other releases. Two examples show what goes wrong, with tables from two hospitals in the same town.

The first example shows that a class whose rows all share one sensitive value hides nothing.

Example 1.1 (Homogeneity) A neighbour aged 35, living in ZIP code 02139, was a patient of hospital A. In Table 1.1, the neighbour must be in the class with ZIP code 021** and age 30–39. All three of its rows say hepatitis, so the attacker learns the diagnosis without knowing which row is the neighbour’s.

The second example has varied diagnoses in each class, but combines the two releases.

Example 1.2 (Intersection) A colleague aged 27, living in ZIP code 02139, was treated at both hospitals for the same condition. In Table 1.1 the colleague’s class allows influenza, asthma or diabetes. In Table 1.2 the class with age 25–34 allows diabetes, migraine or fracture. Only diabetes is in both lists, so the two releases together reveal the diagnosis, although each is \(3\)-anonymous.

The second example is a failure of composition: each hospital checked its own table and could not know what the other released. Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith showed in 2008 that such attacks succeed in practice, also against refinements of \(k\)-anonymity.
The five cases give three requirements for a definition of privacy. It must hold whatever side information an attacker has, because every attack above used some. It must apply to any output, such as a table, a model or a statistic. And it must degrade gracefully when several releases are combined. Differential privacy, defined in the chapter on randomized response, meets all three.

title: 1  Attempts at Data Privacy
text:
1.7 References

Vijay Pandurangan, “On Taxis and Rainbows”, 2014. Inverts the hashed medallion and licence numbers.
Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov, “Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets”, 2008. Links the Netflix Prize data with public reviews.
Nicholas Carlini, Chang Liu, Úlfar Erlingsson, Jernej Kos and Dawn Song, “The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks”, 2019. Defines canaries and exposure and measures them on real models.
Nils Homer and coauthors, “Resolving Individuals Contributing Trace Amounts of DNA to Highly Complex Mixtures Using High-Density SNP Genotyping Microarrays”, 2008. Gives the membership test on aggregate genetic statistics.
Rosemary Braun, William Rowe, Carl Schaefer, Jinghui Zhang and Kenneth Buetow, “Needles in the Haystack: Identifying Individuals Present in Pooled Genomic Data”, 2009. Shows that the test’s false-positive rate depends on the reference population.
Latanya Sweeney, “Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely”, 2000. Estimates how often ZIP code, sex and date of birth identify a person.
Pierangela Samarati and Latanya Sweeney, “Generalizing Data to Provide Anonymity when Disclosing Information”, 1998. Defines \(k\)-anonymity.
Srivatsava Ranjit Ganta, Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan and Adam Smith, “Composition Attacks and Auxiliary Information in Data Privacy”, 2008. Gives intersection attacks on independently anonymized releases.

title: 2  Reconstruction Attacks
text:
2.1 Subset queries and blatant non-privacy
This chapter asks when answers to counting questions about a dataset, each only slightly wrong, let an attacker rebuild almost the whole dataset. It does not yet define privacy. Instead it defines a failure so flagrant that nobody would call it private, and shows that a wide class of algorithms fails in this way. If a curator answers every possible counting query, it must make errors of order \(n\), the number of people, to stop the attack. If it answers only about \(n\) random queries, errors of order \(\sqrt n\) are needed. ## Reconstruction from exact statistics {#sec-rec-census}
Exact statistics give the data away. A census collects microdata, one record per person with fields such as age, sex and race. It publishes tables of counts, medians and means for each small area, such as a city block. It suppresses cells about fewer than three people, but suppression alone protects nobody, because tables overlap. If three of a group’s four residents are women, a published median age for its men is the age of its one man.
Every published number is a constraint on the unknown microdata, and enough constraints leave only one possibility. The next example counts the age combinations that one line of a census table leaves for three people.
So one line of the table cuts the possibilities by a factor of almost \(10{,}000\). The other lines group the same people differently and cut them further. A reconstruction attack searches for microdata that satisfies every constraint. This search is an integer program, which is hard in the worst case, but solvers handle such instances quickly. For a fictional block of seven people, Garfinkel, Abowd and Martindale found that the constraints of its full table have exactly one solution, which a solver finds in a fraction of a second.
The attack scales. The United States Census Bureau ran it on its 2010 tables, and the rebuilt records matched the confidential ones exactly for 46% of the population. They matched for 71% if ages could be off by one year. A link of these records with commercial databases then gave the names of more than 50 million people. So the Bureau adopted differential privacy for the 2020 census.
To analyse such attacks, strip the setting to its core. There are \(n\) people. Each has public attributes that identify them, such as a name, and one secret bit, such as whether they have a disease. The secret bits form the vector \(d = (d_1, \dots, d_n) \in \{0,1\}^n\). An analyst asks how many people who satisfy a condition on the identifiers have secret bit \(1\). A condition such as “the name is Alice, Bob or Eve” can single out any set of people, so a query is a subset \(S \subseteq [n] = \{1, \dots, n\}\). We identify it with its indicator vector \(S \in \{0,1\}^n\), whose entry \(i\) is \(1\) when person \(i\) is in the set and \(0\) otherwise.
A curator holds the secret bits and answers the queries. The definition assumes only a bound \(E\) on how far each answer may be from the truth.
The error need not be random. The curator may pick the most misleading answer in the allowed range, so every attack below also works against random noise. Some error is necessary, because the exact answer to the query \(S = \{i\}\) is the secret bit of person \(i\).
To measure how much an attacker learns, count the bits it gets wrong. The attacker outputs a guess \(c \in \{0,1\}^n\) of the secret vector \(d\), and the Hamming distance \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) = |\{i : c_i \ne d_i\}|\) is the number of positions where the guess is wrong. The next definition names the clearest failure of privacy: for every secret vector, some attacker gets all but a vanishing fraction of the bits right, except with a vanishing probability.
Such an attacker, with \(o(n)\) wrong bits (a vanishing fraction of \(n\)), learns the secret of almost everyone. Whatever privacy means, this violates it.

title: 2  Reconstruction Attacks
text:
Definition 2.1 (Subset queries and a curator with error \(E\)) Let \(d \in \{0,1\}^n\) be the vector of secret bits. The true answer to a subset query \(S \in \{0,1\}^n\) is the number of people in \(S\) whose bit is \(1\),
\[
a(S) = \sum_{i \in S} d_i = \langle S, d \rangle ,
\tag{2.1}\]
where \(\langle S, d \rangle = \sum_i S_i d_i\) is the inner product of the indicator vector \(S\) with \(d\).
A curator with error \(E\) answers each query \(S\) with a response \(r(S)\), a number within \(E\) of the truth, \(|r(S) - a(S)| \le E\). Within that bound, the curator may choose its answers in any way, depending on \(d\) and on all the queries.




Definition 2.2 (Blatant non-privacy) Consider a family of curators, one for each number of people \(n\). The family is blatantly non-private if three things exist. The first is an attacker that interacts with the curator and outputs a guess \(c \in \{0,1\}^n\). The second is a bound \(g(n)\) on the number of wrong bits, with \(g(n)/n \to 0\). The third is a failure probability \(\beta(n)\), with \(\beta(n) \to 0\). They must satisfy, for every \(n\) and every secret vector \(d \in \{0,1\}^n\),
\[
\Pr\left[\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le g(n)\right] \ge 1 - \beta(n).
\tag{2.2}\]

title: 2  Reconstruction Attacks
text:
2.2 Asking every query
The first attack ignores cost. It asks all \(2^n\) subset queries and outputs any candidate that agrees with every answer.

Theorem 2.1 (Reconstruction from all subset queries) Let \(E \ge 0\), and let a curator with error \(E\) answer all \(2^n\) subset queries, giving the answer \(r(S)\) to the query \(S\). An attacker that outputs any \(c \in \{0,1\}^n\) satisfying
\[
\left|\langle S, c \rangle - r(S)\right| \le E \quad \text{for every } S \subseteq [n]
\tag{2.3}\]
finds such a \(c\), and every such \(c\) differs from the secret vector \(d\) in at most \(4E\) positions, \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 4E\).


Proof. 

The true vector \(d\) satisfies Equation 2.3 by Definition 2.1, so a candidate exists.
Let \(I_0 = \{i : d_i = 0\}\). The attacker asked the query \(I_0\), so Equation 2.3 gives \(\langle I_0, c\rangle \le r(I_0) + E\). The curator’s bound gives \(r(I_0) \le \langle I_0, d\rangle + E = E\). Hence \(\langle I_0, c \rangle \le 2E\). This sum counts the positions of \(I_0\) where \(c_i = 1 \ne d_i\), so \(c\) and \(d\) differ in at most \(2E\) positions of \(I_0\).
Let \(I_1 = \{i : d_i = 1\}\). In the same way, \(\langle I_1, c \rangle \ge r(I_1) - E \ge \langle I_1, d \rangle - 2E = |I_1| - 2E\). The number of positions of \(I_1\) where \(c_i = 0\) is \(|I_1| - \langle I_1, c\rangle \le 2E\).
The sets \(I_0\) and \(I_1\) partition \([n]\), so \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 4E\).


The attacker does not know \(I_0\) and \(I_1\), which is why it asks every query. With errors that are a vanishing fraction of \(n\), the bound meets Definition 2.2.

Corollary 2.1 If \(E = n/401\), the attacker of Theorem 2.1 recovers more than 99% of the bits. If \(E = E(n)\) with \(E(n)/n \to 0\), the curator is blatantly non-private, with \(g(n) = 4E(n)\) and \(\beta(n) = 0\).


Proof. For the first claim, \(4n/401 < n/100\), since \(4 \times 100 < 401\). The second claim is Theorem 2.1 with Definition 2.2, because the attacker never fails.

Errors of order \(n\) are the most a counting query can bear, since every answer lies between \(0\) and \(n\). The next result shows that error \(E\) always hides about \(E/2\) bits, however many queries the attacker asks.

Proposition 2.1 (Error \(E\) hides \(E/2\) bits) Let \(E \ge 1\) and \(k = \min(\lfloor E \rfloor, n)\). For every attacker, which may ask any queries in any adaptive order, there are a vector \(d \in \{0,1\}^n\) and a curator with error \(E\) for which \(\Pr[\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \ge k/2] \ge 1/2\).


Proof. 

Let \(d\) be all zeros, and let \(d'\) have ones in its first \(k\) positions and zeros elsewhere, so \(\operatorname{dist}(d, d') = k\).
On the data \(d'\), let the curator answer every query exactly, \(r(S) = \langle S, d' \rangle\). On the data \(d\), let it give the same answers. Their error is \(|\langle S, d' - d\rangle| \le k \le E\), so both are curators with error \(E\).
The answers to every query are the same on \(d\) and on \(d'\). So the attacker’s output \(c\) has the same distribution in the two cases.
For every \(c\), the triangle inequality gives \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) + \operatorname{dist}(c, d') \ge k\), so at least one of the two distances is at least \(k/2\). Hence \(\Pr[\operatorname{dist}(c,d) \ge k/2] + \Pr[\operatorname{dist}(c,d') \ge k/2] \ge 1\), and one of the two probabilities is at least \(1/2\).


So for the attacker who asks everything, safety needs error of order \(n\), and Theorem 2.1 is tight up to a factor of \(8\). But an attack with \(2^n\) queries is not a practical threat once \(n\) is more than a few dozen.

title: 2  Reconstruction Attacks
text:
2.3 Random queries
The second attack asks about \(n\) queries, each a uniformly random subset of the people. It defeats errors of order \(\sqrt n\), much smaller than the first attack can handle but still large next to the error a useful statistic can tolerate.
The idea is to fix a wrong candidate \(c\) and show that a random query is likely to expose it. If \(c\) differs from \(d\) in \(k\) positions, the answers \(\langle S, c \rangle\) and \(\langle S, d \rangle\) differ by a sum of about \(k/2\) random signs, which is typically of size \(\sqrt k\). A curator with error \(E\) can hide a difference of at most \(2E\), so when \(\sqrt k\) is much larger than \(E\), a random query rules \(c\) out with constant probability. To make “typically” precise, the proof needs a lower bound on the size of a random sum, the opposite of a concentration inequality.

Lemma 2.1 (A random subset sees a fixed vector) Let \(w \in \mathbb R^n\), with Euclidean length \(\|w\|_2 = (\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). Let \(S\) be a uniformly random subset of \([n]\), so that each \(i\) is in \(S\) independently with probability \(1/2\). Then the sum \(\langle S, w\rangle\) of the entries of \(w\) in \(S\) satisfies
\[
\Pr\left[\,|\langle S, w \rangle| \ge \tfrac14 \|w\|_2\,\right] \ge \frac{3}{32}.
\tag{2.4}\]


Proof. 

If \(w = 0\) the event always holds, so let \(w \ne 0\). Write \(S_i = (1 + \xi_i)/2\), where the signs \(\xi_i \in \{-1, +1\}\) are independent and uniform. Then \(\langle S, w\rangle = \tfrac12(a + Z)\), with the constant \(a = \sum_i w_i\) and the random sum \(Z = \sum_i \xi_i w_i\).
Moments of \(Z\). Expand the powers and use independence. A product of the \(\xi_i\) has mean \(0\) unless each index appears an even number of times. So \(\mathbb E[Z^2] = \sum_i w_i^2 = \|w\|_2^2\), and

\[
\mathbb E[Z^4] = \sum_i w_i^4 + 3\sum_{i \ne j} w_i^2 w_j^2 = 3\|w\|_2^4 - 2\sum_i w_i^4 \le 3\|w\|_2^4 .
\tag{2.5}\]

Paley–Zygmund inequality. Let \(Y \ge 0\) have \(\mathbb E[Y] > 0\), and let \(s \in [0,1]\). Split \(\mathbb E[Y]\) according to whether \(Y > s\,\mathbb E[Y]\), and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the second part:

\[
\mathbb E[Y] \le s\,\mathbb E[Y] + \mathbb E\left[Y \mathbf 1[Y > s\,\mathbb E[Y]]\right] \le s\,\mathbb E[Y] + \sqrt{\mathbb E[Y^2]\,\Pr[Y > s\,\mathbb E[Y]]}.
\tag{2.6}\]
Rearranging gives \(\Pr[Y > s\,\mathbb E[Y]] \ge (1-s)^2\,\mathbb E[Y]^2/\mathbb E[Y^2]\).

Apply step 3 to \(Y = Z^2\) with \(s = 1/4\), using step 2. The event \(|Z| > \|w\|_2/2\) has probability at least \((3/4)^2/3 = 3/16\).
Removing the constant \(a\). For every \(z\), \(|a + z| + |a - z| \ge 2|z|\), so \(|a + Z| \ge |Z|\) or \(|a - Z| \ge |Z|\). Flipping all signs maps \(Z\) to \(-Z\) and preserves the distribution and the event of step 4. Hence the events \(\{|Z| > \|w\|_2/2,\ |a+Z| \ge |Z|\}\) and \(\{|Z| > \|w\|_2/2,\ |a-Z| \ge |Z|\}\) have the same probability. Together they cover the event of step 4, so each has probability at least \(3/32\).
On the first of these events, \(|\langle S, w\rangle| = \tfrac12|a + Z| \ge \tfrac12|Z| > \tfrac14\|w\|_2\).


The lemma rules out one wrong candidate with constant probability per query. A union bound over the \(2^n\) candidates in \(\{0,1\}^n\) then shows that about \(n\) queries rule out all the wrong ones at once.

Theorem 2.2 (Reconstruction from random queries) Let \(E \ge 0\) and \(\beta \in (0, 1)\), and let
\[
m \ge \frac{32}{3}\left(n \ln 2 + \ln\frac1\beta\right).
\tag{2.7}\]
The attacker draws \(m\) independent, uniformly random subsets \(S_1, \dots, S_m\) of \([n]\) before seeing any answer. A curator with error \(E\) answers them with \(r_1, \dots, r_m\). The attacker outputs any \(c \in \{0,1\}^n\) with \(|\langle S_j, c\rangle - r_j| \le E\) for all \(j\). Then such a \(c\) exists and, with probability at least \(1-\beta\) over the queries, every such \(c\) has
\[
\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 64E^2 .
\tag{2.8}\]


Proof. 

The true vector \(d\) satisfies all \(m\) constraints by Definition 2.1, so a candidate exists.
One far candidate. Fix \(c\) with \(k = \operatorname{dist}(c, d) > 64E^2\), and let \(w = c - d\). Its entries are in \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\) and exactly \(k\) are nonzero, so \(\|w\|_2 = \sqrt k > 8E\). By Lemma 2.1, each query has \(|\langle S_j, w\rangle| \ge \sqrt k/4 > 2E\) with probability at least \(3/32\). The queries are independent, so the probability that \(|\langle S_j, w\rangle| \le 2E\) for every \(j\) is at most \((1 - 3/32)^m \le e^{-3m/32}\).
All far candidates. There are at most \(2^n\) candidates. By the union bound, the event \(B\) that some candidate with \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) > 64E^2\) has \(|\langle S_j, c - d\rangle| \le 2E\) for every \(j\) has probability at most \(2^n e^{-3m/32}\), which is at most \(\beta\) by the choice of \(m\).
Consistent candidates are close. Suppose \(B\) does not occur. If \(c\) is consistent with the answers, the triangle inequality gives \(|\langle S_j, c - d\rangle| \le |\langle S_j, c\rangle - r_j| + |r_j - \langle S_j, d \rangle| \le 2E\) for every \(j\). So \(c\) is not far, which is Equation 2.8. The event \(B\) depends only on the queries, so this holds whatever answers the curator chose.


The number of queries is about \(7.4n\): for \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(\beta = 0.01\) the theorem asks for \(m = 7{,}443\). Setting \(\beta = 2^{-n}\) gives the asymptotic statement.

Corollary 2.2 If \(E = E(n)\) with \(E(n)/\sqrt n \to 0\), the curator is blatantly non-private against \(15n\) random queries, with \(g(n) = 64E(n)^2\) and \(\beta(n) = 2^{-n}\). If \(E = \alpha\sqrt n\), the same attacker gets at most \(64\alpha^2 n\) bits wrong with probability at least \(1 - 2^{-n}\).


Proof. With \(\beta = 2^{-n}\), the bound on \(m\) in Theorem 2.2 is \(\frac{32}{3}\cdot 2n\ln 2 \approx 14.79\,n \le 15n\). Then \(g(n) = 64E(n)^2 = 64 n\,(E(n)/\sqrt n)^2\), and \(g(n)/n \to 0\).


2.3.1 An efficient attack
The attacker of Theorem 2.2 asks few queries but searches \(2^n\) candidates. A search over fractional vectors is a linear program, so this attack is called linear programming (LP) decoding. It looks for \(x \in [0,1]^n\) with \(|\langle S_j, x\rangle - r_j| \le E\) for all \(j\), which takes time polynomial in \(n\) and \(m\), and rounds \(x\) to the nearest bit vector. The analysis is the same as before with one extra step: a fractional candidate is not one of \(2^n\) points, so a fine grid replaces the set of candidates.

Theorem 2.3 (Reconstruction by linear programming) Let \(E > 0\), \(\beta \in (0,1)\), \(K = \lceil n/(2E) \rceil\), and
\[
m \ge \frac{32}{3}\left(n \ln(2K+1) + \ln\frac1\beta\right).
\tag{2.9}\]
The attacker draws \(m\) random subsets and receives answers from a curator with error \(E\), as in Theorem 2.2. It finds any \(x \in [0,1]^n\) with \(|\langle S_j, x\rangle - r_j| \le E\) for all \(j\), and it outputs \(c_i = 1\) if \(x_i \ge 1/2\) and \(c_i = 0\) otherwise. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\) over the queries,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 676E^2 .
\tag{2.10}\]


Proof. 

The vector \(d\) is feasible, so the linear program has a solution \(x\). Let \(z = x - d \in [-1, 1]^n\). As in step 4 of Theorem 2.2, \(|\langle S_j, z\rangle| \le 2E\) for every \(j\).
Rounding errors. If \(c_i \ne d_i\), then either \(d_i = 0\) and \(x_i \ge 1/2\), or \(d_i = 1\) and \(x_i < 1/2\). In both cases \(|z_i| \ge 1/2\), so \((2z_i)^2 \ge 1\). Summing over \(i\) gives \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 4\|z\|_2^2\).
The grid. Let \(h = 1/K \le 2E/n\), and let \(G\) be the set of vectors whose entries are multiples of \(h\) in \([-1, 1]\). It has \((2K+1)^n\) points. Round each entry of \(z\) to the nearest multiple of \(h\) to get \(z' \in G\), with \(|z_i - z'_i| \le h/2 \le E/n\). Then \(|\langle S_j, z - z'\rangle| \le \sum_i |z_i - z'_i| \le E\), so \(|\langle S_j, z'\rangle| \le 3E\) for every \(j\). Also \(\|z - z'\|_2 \le \sqrt n \cdot E/n \le E\).
Far grid points are ruled out. Fix \(g \in G\) with \(\|g\|_2 > 12E\). By Lemma 2.1, each query has \(|\langle S_j, g\rangle| \ge \|g\|_2/4 > 3E\) with probability at least \(3/32\). As in Theorem 2.2, the probability that \(|\langle S_j, g\rangle| \le 3E\) for every \(j\) is at most \(e^{-3m/32}\). A union bound over the \((2K+1)^n\) grid points bounds the probability that this happens for some far grid point by \((2K+1)^n e^{-3m/32} \le \beta\).
Outside that event, step 3 shows that \(z'\) is not far, so \(\|z'\|_2 \le 12E\) and \(\|z\|_2 \le 13E\). Step 2 gives \(\operatorname{dist}(c,d) \le 4 \cdot 169 E^2 = 676E^2\).


For \(1 \le E \le n\), the factor \(\ln(2K+1)\) is at most \(\ln(n+3)\), so the attack runs in polynomial time with \(O(n \log n)\) queries and gets at most \(676E^2\) bits wrong. So error \(o(\sqrt n)\) again lets an attacker recover all but a vanishing fraction of the bits. The constants \(64\) and \(676\) are far from the truth, as Figure 2.1 shows: on simulated data the attack recovers almost every bit at errors the theorem cannot handle.






Figure 2.1: The linear-programming attack on simulated data, with \(m = 8n\) random subset queries and an error drawn uniformly from \([-E, E]\) for each answer. The attacker finds a point of the feasible set of Theorem 2.3, up to a violation of at most \(0.01\), by projected gradient descent and rounds it. Each point averages \(1600/n\) runs. The curves for different \(n\) nearly coincide, so the error the attack tolerates grows like \(\sqrt n\). For \(n = 400\), a single run gets none of the bits wrong at \(E = \sqrt n/2\) and 17% of them at \(E = 2\sqrt n\).



Bounds on random matrices, which this course does not develop, show that \(O(n)\) queries suffice for the linear program (Dwork and Roth, 2014, Section 8.1). They also show that a linear program that minimizes the total error tolerates a constant fraction of arbitrary answers (Dwork, McSherry and Talwar, 2007). The argument above gives an inefficient version of that tolerance.

Proposition 2.2 (Tolerating some arbitrary answers) Let \(E \ge 0\), let \(\beta \in (0,1)\) be a failure probability, let \(\rho \in [0, 3/128)\) be the fraction of answers that may be arbitrary, and let
\[
m \ge \frac{2048}{9}\left(n\ln 2 + \ln\frac1\beta\right).
\tag{2.11}\]
The attacker draws \(m\) random subsets as in Theorem 2.2. The curator answers at least \((1-\rho)m\) of them with error at most \(E\) and the others arbitrarily, choosing which after seeing the queries. The attacker outputs any \(c \in \{0,1\}^n\) with \(|\langle S_j, c\rangle - r_j| \le E\) for at least \((1-\rho)m\) of the queries. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every such \(c\) has \(\operatorname{dist}(c, d) \le 64E^2\).


Proof. 

The true vector \(d\) meets the condition, so a candidate exists.
Fix \(c\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(c,d) > 64E^2\) and let \(V_j = \mathbf 1[|\langle S_j, c - d\rangle| > 2E]\) indicate that query \(j\) exposes \(c\). As in step 2 of Theorem 2.2, the \(V_j\) are independent with mean at least \(3/32\). Hoeffding’s inequality gives \(\Pr\left[\sum_j V_j < 3m/64\right] \le \exp(-2m(3/64)^2) = e^{-9m/2048}\).
A union bound over at most \(2^n\) candidates shows that, with probability at least \(1 - 2^n e^{-9m/2048} \ge 1-\beta\), every far candidate has \(\sum_j V_j \ge 3m/64\).
Suppose this holds, and let \(c\) be an output. The queries where \(c\) is consistent and those answered with error at most \(E\) each number at least \((1-\rho)m\), so at least \((1-2\rho)m\) queries are of both kinds. On each of them, the triangle inequality gives \(|\langle S_j, c - d\rangle| \le 2E\), so \(V_j = 0\). Hence \(\sum_j V_j \le 2\rho m < 3m/64\), and \(c\) is not far.


These attacks are nearly tight. The chapters on approximate differential privacy and advanced composition show that a curator can answer \(m\) subset queries with error of order \(\sqrt m\) and still meet the definition of differential privacy, up to logarithmic factors and factors that depend on the privacy parameters. So for \(n\) queries, the line between blatant non-privacy and a formal guarantee runs at error \(\sqrt n\).

title: 2  Reconstruction Attacks
text:
2.4 Reconstruction in practice
The random-query attack seems theoretical, because it asks about arbitrary sets of people, but it broke a deployed system. The company Aircloak built Diffix, an interface that let analysts ask an unlimited number of counting queries on sensitive data. It promised privacy with less error than differential privacy adds.
Diffix had defences against the attacks above. Each condition in a query added its own Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(1\), so the error grew with the number of conditions. The interface also rejected conditions joined by OR, suppressed small counts and altered extreme values. A random subset of \(n\) people needs about \(n/2\) conditions joined by OR to describe person by person, so both defences block that route.
Cohen and Nissim reversed the order of the attack. Instead of a random set that they then had to describe, they drew a random single condition from a family whose sets look random. Each condition tests a digit of a power of each person’s numeric identifier. One query they sent kept a row when
\[
\left\lfloor 100\,(2\cdot\text{identifier})^{0.7} + 0.5 \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor 100\,(2\cdot\text{identifier})^{0.7} \right\rfloor ,
\tag{2.12}\]
which holds exactly when the third decimal digit of \((2\cdot\text{identifier})^{0.7}\) is at most \(4\). Of the \(1{,}001\) identifiers from \(2000\) to \(3000\), it keeps \(501\), about half, as a random subset would.
Each such query has few conditions, so its error does not grow with the number of rows. Diffix added noise of standard deviation \(4\) to it. Cohen and Nissim targeted four ranges of identifiers with \(73\) to \(142\) rows each and asked \(3{,}500\) queries about each range. Gaussian noise is not bounded, so they used the linear program that minimizes the total error, which tolerates a few large errors as Proposition 2.2 does. It recovered the secret attribute of every row in all four ranges.
The theorems of this chapter do not apply to these queries as stated, because a fixed formula is not a random subset. But the proofs use the randomness of the queries only through Lemma 2.1, by which each query exposes a fixed wrong candidate with constant probability. The digit tests behave that way on real identifiers, as an empirical fact and not a theorem.

title: The Basics of Differential Privacy
text:
The first part showed that statistics about people can expose them. This part gives the answer that the rest of the course builds on, the definition of differential privacy (DP). Under DP, a change to one person’s data changes the probability of any outcome by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), for a small privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\). The part then builds the first private algorithms and the rules that combine them. Every later part uses these results, so each chapter gives exact constants and full proofs.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




Randomized response and the definition
How can one collect a sensitive bit from each person, and what does it mean for an algorithm to be private?


The Laplace mechanism
How much noise makes a numeric statistic private, and how do private algorithms combine?


Approximate differential privacy
What does a small additive slack \(\delta\) allow, how small must it be, and what does the Gaussian mechanism gain?


Advanced composition
Why does the privacy cost of \(k\) analyses grow only like \(\sqrt k\)?


The exponential mechanism
How can one privately choose the best object from a set?

title: 3  Randomized Response and the Definition
text:
3.1 Randomized response
A group of people each hold one sensitive bit, and an analyst wants the fraction of ones without learning anyone’s bit. This chapter solves the problem with a biased coin, the oldest private algorithm. It then turns the idea behind the coin, plausible deniability, into the definition of differential privacy (DP), on which the rest of the course builds.
Write \(n\) for the number of people. Person number \(i\) holds a bit \(x_i \in \{0,1\}\), for instance whether they cheated on an exam, and the analyst wants the fraction of ones,
\[
p = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i .
\tag{3.1}\]
Each person sends the analyst one message \(Y_i\), which may depend on \(x_i\) and on coins that only person \(i\) sees. At one extreme, if \(Y_i = x_i\), the analyst computes \(p\) exactly but sees every bit. At the other, if \(Y_i\) is a fair coin independent of \(x_i\), the analyst learns nothing about anyone. But the analyst also learns nothing about \(p\), because the average of the reports has the distribution \(\frac1n\mathrm{Bin}(n, \frac12)\) whatever the data. Randomized response goes between the two.
The value \(\kappa = 1/2\) gives the honest protocol and \(\kappa = 0\) the fair coin. In between, say at \(\kappa = 1/4\), a person who reports \(Y_i = 1\) can claim that their bit was \(0\) and the coin flipped it, which happens with probability \(1/4\). That plausible deniability is the privacy, and it grows as \(\kappa\) gets smaller.
The reports lean towards the truth, so their average is not \(p\). But the analyst knows the bias and can undo it, because the average of one report,
\[
\mathbb E[Y_i] = \left(\tfrac12+\kappa\right)x_i + \left(\tfrac12-\kappa\right)(1-x_i) = 2\kappa x_i + \tfrac12 - \kappa ,
\tag{3.3}\]
is linear in \(x_i\). Solving for \(x_i\) gives an unbiased estimate of each bit, and the average of those estimates is the estimator of \(p\).
The next theorem checks that the estimator is right on average and measures, through its variance, how far it typically strays.
By Chebyshev’s inequality, the error is at most two standard deviations, \(|\tilde p - p| \le 1/(2\kappa\sqrt n)\), with probability at least \(3/4\). For a small failure probability \(\beta\), Hoeffding’s inequality does better, because each \(Z_i\) takes only two values.
So the error is of order \(1/(\kappa\sqrt n)\) and goes to \(0\) as \(n\) grows. Read the other way, an error of at most \(\alpha\) with probability \(1-\beta\) needs
\[
n \ge \frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{8\kappa^2\alpha^2}
\tag{3.9}\]
people. A smaller \(\kappa\) hides each bit better and needs more people for the same accuracy. To say how much better it hides a bit, the next section gives a definition.

title: 3  Randomized Response and the Definition
text:
Definition 3.1 (Randomized response) For a bias \(\kappa \in [0, 1/2]\), which sets the probability \(\tfrac12 + \kappa\) of reporting the truth, person \(i\) reports
\[
Y_i = \begin{cases} x_i & \text{with probability } \tfrac12 + \kappa, \\ 1 - x_i & \text{with probability } \tfrac12 - \kappa, \end{cases}
\tag{3.2}\]
with fresh, independent coins for each person.






Definition 3.2 (Debiased estimator) For \(\kappa > 0\), the analyst outputs
\[
\tilde p = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{Y_i - \tfrac12 + \kappa}{2\kappa}.
\tag{3.4}\]



Theorem 3.1 For every \(\kappa \in (0, 1/2]\) and every input \(D \in \{0,1\}^n\), the estimator is unbiased, \(\mathbb E[\tilde p] = p\), and its variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde p) = \frac{1 - 4\kappa^2}{16\kappa^2 n} \le \frac{1}{16\kappa^2 n}.
\tag{3.5}\]


Proof. 

Each term \(Z_i = (Y_i - \tfrac12 + \kappa)/(2\kappa)\) has mean \(x_i\), by the formula for \(\mathbb E[Y_i]\) above. Averaging over \(i\) and using linearity of expectation gives \(\mathbb E[\tilde p] = p\).
The constants \(\tfrac12 - \kappa\) and \(2\kappa\) do not change the variance except through the scaling, so \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_i) = \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)/(4\kappa^2)\).
The report \(Y_i\) is a Bernoulli variable that equals \(1\) with probability \(\tfrac12 + \kappa\) or \(\tfrac12 - \kappa\), depending on \(x_i\). In both cases its variance is \((\tfrac12+\kappa)(\tfrac12-\kappa) = \tfrac14 - \kappa^2\).
The reports are independent because each person uses their own coins. So the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances, and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde p) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)}{4\kappa^2} = \frac{\tfrac14 - \kappa^2}{4\kappa^2 n} = \frac{1-4\kappa^2}{16\kappa^2 n}.
\tag{3.6}\]



Theorem 3.2 For every \(\kappa \in (0,1/2]\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1-\beta\) over the coins,
\[
|\tilde p - p| \le \frac{1}{2\kappa}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}} .
\tag{3.7}\]


Proof. 

The term \(Z_i\) takes the values \((\tfrac12+\kappa)/(2\kappa)\) and \(-(\tfrac12-\kappa)/(2\kappa)\), so it lies in an interval of length \(1/(2\kappa)\).
The \(Z_i\) are independent with mean \(x_i\). Hoeffding’s inequality for the average of \(n\) independent variables, each in an interval of length \(\ell\), gives

\[
\Pr\left[\,|\tilde p - p| \ge t\,\right] \le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2nt^2}{\ell^2}\right) = 2\exp\!\left(-8\kappa^2 n t^2\right).
\tag{3.8}\]

Setting the right-hand side equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) gives Equation 3.7.

title: 3  Randomized Response and the Definition
text:
3.2 Differential privacy
The setting is the central model. Each of \(n\) people sends their data point to a trusted curator, and they trust no one else. The curator runs an algorithm \(M\) on the dataset \(D = (x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathcal X^n\) and publishes the output, and anyone who sees the output may be an adversary. The guarantee is a property of the algorithm, called a mechanism in this field: no single person’s data has a large effect on the distribution of the output. To make “one person’s data” precise, compare two datasets that differ only in one person’s record.

Definition 3.3 (Neighbouring datasets) Two datasets \(D, D' \in \mathcal X^n\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), if they differ in exactly one record. This is the replace-one relation.

The definition asks that the distribution of the output barely change between neighbours. On every set of outputs, the probability may grow by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), where the privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\) sets how much change is allowed.

Definition 3.4 (Differential privacy) Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\). A randomized algorithm \(M \colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathcal Y\), which maps a dataset to an output in a set \(\mathcal Y\), is \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private (\(\varepsilon\)-DP) if for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all events \(S \subseteq \mathcal Y\),
\[
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\, \Pr[M(D') \in S] .
\tag{3.10}\]
The probability is over the coins of \(M\) only. The datasets are fixed.

Its other name is pure differential privacy, which sets it apart from the relaxation of a later chapter. Four of its features matter later.
First, the definition is quantitative. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the output distribution is the same on every dataset, which is perfect privacy and allows no accuracy. An algorithm that is not randomized is \(\infty\)-DP, which is no guarantee at all. Typical values of \(\varepsilon\) lie between about \(0.1\) and \(5\), and smaller is more private. Because the bound is \(e^\varepsilon\), privacy weakens quickly once \(\varepsilon\) is above \(1\).
Second, it is a worst-case guarantee: it holds for every pair of neighbours, however unlikely the data, with no distribution over datasets.
Third, it is symmetric. Swapping \(D\) and \(D'\) in Equation 3.10 gives the lower bound \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] \ge e^{-\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S]\).
Fourth, it bounds a ratio, not a difference. For small \(\varepsilon\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is close to \(1 + \varepsilon\). The exponential form makes factors multiply when guarantees are chained, \(e^{\varepsilon_1}e^{\varepsilon_2} = e^{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}\), which the next chapter uses for group privacy. An additive notion of closeness, such as a small total variation distance, sounds natural but gives no meaningful guarantee.
DP with these neighbours, which replace one record, has the name bounded DP. The add/remove relation, or unbounded DP, instead adds or removes one record. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition. So, by the chaining argument of the next chapter’s group privacy, \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove neighbours gives \(2\varepsilon\)-DP under replace-one neighbours. The converse can fail, because under add/remove neighbours the size \(n\) is itself private. The course uses replacement, which is more convenient mathematically, and you can compare two mechanisms only under the same relation.
For discrete outputs it is enough to check single outcomes, because the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its outcomes.

Lemma 3.1 Let \(\mathcal Y\) be countable. If \(\Pr[M(D) = y] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') = y]\) for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all outputs \(y \in \mathcal Y\), then \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. For an event \(S\), sum the pointwise inequality over the outputs \(y \in S\):
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] = \sum_{y \in S}\Pr[M(D) = y] \le e^{\varepsilon}\sum_{y\in S}\Pr[M(D') = y] = e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S].
\tag{3.11}\]

A first consequence of the definition is that privacy needs randomness.

Proposition 3.1 For \(\varepsilon < \infty\), a deterministic \(\varepsilon\)-DP algorithm is constant.


Proof. 

Let \(M\) be deterministic and \(D \sim D'\). Take the event \(S = \{M(D)\}\). The definition gives \(1 = \Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D') \in S]\), so \(\Pr[M(D') = M(D)] > 0\). Since \(M(D')\) is a single value, \(M(D') = M(D)\).
Any two datasets in \(\mathcal X^n\) are joined by a path of at most \(n\) neighbours, changing one record at a time. By step 1, \(M\) takes the same value at every step of the path, so it is constant.



3.2.1 Hypothesis testing
The definition has an operational meaning from the adversary’s side. Suppose an adversary knows that the dataset is one of two neighbours, \(D\) or \(D'\), and sees the output of \(M\). It must decide between the null hypothesis and the alternative,
\[
H_0\colon \text{the dataset is } D, \qquad H_1\colon \text{the dataset is } D' .
\tag{3.12}\]
A test is a function \(\phi\colon \mathcal Y \to [0,1]\), the probability of answering \(H_1\) given the output, so a test can be random. The test’s false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is the chance of answering \(H_1\) when \(H_0\) holds, and its false negative rate \(\mathrm{FNR}\) is the chance of answering \(H_0\) when \(H_1\) holds:
\[
\mathrm{FPR} = \mathbb E[\phi(M(D))], \qquad \mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathbb E[\phi(M(D'))].
\tag{3.13}\]
A test takes values in \([0,1]\), while the definition bounds only probabilities of events. The proof of the next theorem needs the bound for such functions, which the following lemma gives.

Lemma 3.2 Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP and let \(h\colon\mathcal Y \to [0,1]\). For all neighbours \(D \sim D'\),
\[
\mathbb E[h(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h(M(D'))] .
\tag{3.14}\]


Proof. 

A variable with values in \([0,1]\) has mean equal to the integral of its tail, so \(\mathbb E[h(M(D))] = \int_0^1\Pr[h(M(D)) > t]\,\mathrm d t\).
Each tail is the probability of the event \(\{y : h(y) > t\}\), which Equation 3.10 bounds by \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[h(M(D')) > t]\).
Integrating over \(t \in [0,1]\) gives \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h(M(D'))]\).


An adversary wants both error rates small. The next theorem says that differential privacy is exactly a limit on how small they can be together, for every test.

Theorem 3.3 A mechanism \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if, for every pair of neighbours and every test, the false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and the false negative rate \(\mathrm{FNR}\) satisfy
\[
\mathrm{FPR} + e^{\varepsilon}\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad e^{\varepsilon}\mathrm{FPR} + \mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 .
\tag{3.15}\]


Proof. 

DP extends from events to tests. Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP and let \(\phi\) take values in \([0,1]\). Then \(\mathbb E[\phi(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[\phi(M(D'))]\), and the same holds with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped. This is Lemma 3.2, applied to \(\phi\) in each direction.
DP implies the inequalities. Apply step 1 to \(\phi\), from \(D'\) to \(D\): \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} = \mathbb E[\phi(M(D'))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[\phi(M(D))] = e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR}\). This is the second inequality. Apply step 1 to \(1 - \phi\), from \(D\) to \(D'\): \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} = \mathbb E[1-\phi(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[1-\phi(M(D'))] = e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR}\). This is the first.
The inequalities imply DP. Take an event \(S\) and the test \(\phi(y) = \mathbf 1[y \in S]\), which answers \(H_1\) exactly when the output lands in \(S\). Its error rates are \(\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[M(D)\in S]\) and \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \Pr[M(D')\in S]\). The second inequality says \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D)\in S] + 1 - \Pr[M(D')\in S] \ge 1\), that is, \(\Pr[M(D')\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D)\in S]\). The pair of neighbours was arbitrary, so the same holds with the roles of \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped, which is Equation 3.10.


At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the two inequalities force \(\mathrm{FPR} + \mathrm{FNR} \ge 1\), which a test that ignores the output already achieves, such as a random guess (\(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathrm{FNR} = 1/2\)). As \(\varepsilon\) grows, the region of possible error pairs gets larger, and the adversary can beat a blind guess by more.


3.2.2 What the definition promises
In words, the probability of any event is about the same whether a given person’s data is in the dataset or is replaced by someone else’s. So a harm that comes from the output is not much more likely because the person took part. A linkage attack, for example, succeeds about as often without their record, whatever auxiliary data exists now or later. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the chance of any bad event grows by a factor of at most \(e^{0.1} \approx 1.105\). The guarantee holds against an adversary with unlimited computation and side information, so it is information theoretic, unlike most of cryptography.
The definition does not prevent inference from aggregate patterns. Suppose a study with differential privacy finds that smoking causes cancer, and an insurer then raises the premium of a smoker who took part. The study’s conclusion would be the same without that person’s record, so the harm comes from a fact about the population, not from their participation. Learning such facts is the purpose of statistics.

title: 3  Randomized Response and the Definition
text:
3.3 Randomized response revisited
Randomized response now gets a privacy guarantee. The theorem treats the whole vector of reports as the output, and the estimator Equation 3.4, a function of that vector, inherits the guarantee by post-processing, which the next chapter proves.

Theorem 3.4 Randomized response with bias \(\kappa \in [0,1/2)\), releasing \((Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\), is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for
\[
\varepsilon = \ln\frac{\tfrac12+\kappa}{\tfrac12-\kappa} .
\tag{3.16}\]
Equivalently, to obtain \(\varepsilon\)-DP, report the truth with probability \(\tfrac12 + \kappa = e^{\varepsilon}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon})\).


Proof. 

Fix an output \(y \in \{0,1\}^n\). The coins are independent across people, so \(\Pr[M(D) = y] = \prod_{i=1}^n \Pr[Y_i = y_i]\), where each factor depends only on \(x_i\).
Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ only in record \(j\), and write \(Y_j'\) for the report of person \(j\) on \(D'\). All factors with \(i \ne j\) are equal for the two datasets and cancel in the ratio:

\[
\frac{\Pr[M(D) = y]}{\Pr[M(D') = y]} = \frac{\Pr[Y_j = y_j]}{\Pr[Y_j' = y_j]} .
\tag{3.17}\]

Each probability on the right is \(\tfrac12+\kappa\) or \(\tfrac12-\kappa\), so the ratio is at most \((\tfrac12+\kappa)/(\tfrac12-\kappa) = e^\varepsilon\).
Lemma 3.1 turns this pointwise bound into the definition.
Solving \(e^\varepsilon = (\tfrac12+\kappa)/(\tfrac12-\kappa)\) for \(\tfrac12 + \kappa\) gives \(e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\).


For small \(\kappa\) the privacy parameter is \(\varepsilon = 4\kappa + O(\kappa^3)\), so a bias of order \(\varepsilon\) gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Exactly, the bias that gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP is
\[
2\kappa = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1} = \tanh\frac{\varepsilon}{2},
\tag{3.18}\]
so Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.1 become, with probability at least \(1-\beta\),
\[
|\tilde p - p| \le \coth\!\left(\frac\varepsilon2\right)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\tilde p) = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\, n}.
\tag{3.19}\]
Here \(p\) is again the fraction of ones and \(\tilde p\) its estimate. The factor \(\coth(\varepsilon/2)\) lies between \(2/\varepsilon\) and \(2/\varepsilon + \varepsilon/6\) for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), so the error is \(O\big(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\big)\) for \(\varepsilon \le 1\). Figure 3.1 compares this bound with simulation, and Example 3.1 gives the sizes at a typical privacy level.






Figure 3.1: Error of randomized response. For each \(\varepsilon\), the solid line is the 95th percentile of \(|\tilde p - p|\) over 2,000 simulated runs with \(p = 0.3\), and the dashed line is the bound of Equation 3.19 with \(\beta = 0.05\). Both fall as \(1/\sqrt n\). The bound is 1.4 to 2.2 times the simulated error, and it is loosest for large \(\varepsilon\), because Hoeffding’s inequality uses only the range of each term and not its smaller variance.




Example 3.1 With \(\varepsilon = 1\), each person tells the truth with probability \(e/(1+e) = 0.7311\). With \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\beta = 0.05\), the bound Equation 3.19 is \(\coth(0.5)\sqrt{\ln 40/20{,}000} = 2.1640 \times 0.01358 = 0.0294\). The standard deviation from Equation 3.19 is \(\sqrt{e/((e-1)^2 \cdot 10{,}000)} = 0.0096\).

Randomized response gives more than the definition asks for. Each person randomizes their own bit before sending it, so no one ever sees a true bit and the curator needs no trust. This is local differential privacy, the subject of a later chapter, and it implies the central guarantee proved here. The price is accuracy, because the \(\sqrt n\) in the error is not necessary under central privacy: the next chapter’s Laplace mechanism estimates \(p\) with error \(O(1/(\varepsilon n))\).

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.1 Sensitivity
Randomized response privatizes one bit per person. But most questions an analyst asks are numbers computed from the whole dataset, such as a count or a histogram. This chapter answers them with the Laplace mechanism, which computes the true answer and adds noise scaled to how much one person can change it. On the fraction of ones with privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\), its error is of order \(1/(\varepsilon n)\) rather than the \(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\) of randomized response. The chapter then proves three properties of differential privacy (DP) that let you build private algorithms from private parts: post-processing, group privacy and basic composition.
The output must hide the contribution of any one person, so the noise must be at least as large as the change that one person can cause in the answer. The sensitivity measures the largest such change. Recall from the randomized response chapter that two datasets are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ in exactly one record.
The \(\ell_1\) norm is what makes the privacy proof of Theorem 4.1 work. Other mechanisms use other norms, such as the \(\ell_2\) norm for the Gaussian mechanism of the next chapter. For \(d = 1\) all these norms are the absolute value, and for \(d > 1\) the \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) sensitivities can differ by a factor of up to \(\sqrt d\).
The running example of this chapter is the fraction of ones that randomized response estimates. Its sensitivity is small, because one person moves the fraction only a little.

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
Definition 4.1 (ℓ1 sensitivity) Let \(f\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^k\) map a dataset of \(n\) records to a vector of \(d\) numbers. The \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of \(f\) is the largest change in \(f\), measured by the sum of the absolute changes of its coordinates, between neighbours \(D \sim D'\):
\[
\Delta_1 f = \sup_{D \sim D'}\|f(D) - f(D')\|_1 ,
\tag{4.1}\]
where \(\|v\|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^d|v_j|\) for a vector \(v \in \mathbb R^d\).




Example 4.1 Let \(\mathcal X = \{0,1\}\) and let \(f(D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) be the fraction of ones. Changing one bit changes the sum by at most \(1\), so \(\Delta_1 f = 1/n\).

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.2 The Laplace distribution
The noise must hide a shift of the true answer by up to the sensitivity. A density that falls exponentially in the distance from zero does this, because a shift by a fixed amount changes its value by at most a fixed factor. The Laplace distribution is the simplest such density.

Definition 4.2 (Laplace distribution) The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b > 0\) has density
\[
\frac{1}{2b}\exp\!\left(-\frac{|x|}{b}\right), \qquad x \in \mathbb R.
\tag{4.2}\]

It is a two-sided exponential distribution: the exponential density, proportional to \(e^{-x/b}\) on \([0,\infty)\), reflected to the negative half-line. Its tails decay like \(e^{-|x|/b}\), more slowly than a Gaussian’s but still exponentially. The accuracy of the mechanism rests on three facts about this distribution: its mean, its variance and the exact size of its tails.

Lemma 4.1 Let \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z] = 0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) = 2b^2\), and for every \(t \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr[|Z| \ge tb] = e^{-t}.
\tag{4.3}\]


Proof. 

The density is symmetric about \(0\), so the mean is \(0\).
The absolute value \(|Z|\) has density \(\frac1b e^{-u/b}\) on \([0,\infty)\), the exponential distribution with mean \(b\). Its second moment is \(\int_0^\infty u^2\frac1be^{-u/b}\,\mathrm d u = 2b^2\), by integrating by parts twice. Since the mean of \(Z\) is \(0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \mathbb E[Z^2] = 2b^2\).
The tail of \(|Z|\) is \(\int_{tb}^\infty \frac1be^{-u/b}\,\mathrm d u = e^{-t}\).

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.3 The Laplace mechanism
The mechanism adds independent Laplace noise to each coordinate, with scale equal to the sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\).

Definition 4.3 (Laplace mechanism) For \(f\colon\mathcal X^n\to\mathbb R^d\) with \(0 < \Delta_1 f < \infty\) and for \(\varepsilon > 0\), the Laplace mechanism outputs
\[
M(D) = f(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_d),
\tag{4.4}\]
where \(Z_1, \dots, Z_d\) are independent with distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon)\).

Before the privacy proof, consider the accuracy of the mechanism on the running example. The mechanism is unbiased, and Lemma 4.1 gives its error.

Example 4.2 For \(f(D) = p\), the fraction of ones, Example 4.1 gives \(\Delta_1 f = 1/n\). The mechanism outputs \(\tilde p = p + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon n))\). So \(\mathbb E[\tilde p] = p\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde p) = 2/(\varepsilon n)^2\). By Equation 4.3 with \(t = \ln(1/\beta)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\),
\[
|\tilde p - p| \le \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{\varepsilon n}.
\tag{4.5}\]
With \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\beta = 0.05\), this is \(\ln(20)/10{,}000 = 3.0\times 10^{-4}\). Randomized response with the same \(\varepsilon\), \(n\) and \(\beta\) has the bound \(0.0294\), which is \(98\) times larger.

The gap grows with \(n\), because randomized response has error of order \(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\) and the Laplace mechanism of order \(1/(\varepsilon n)\). The price of the smaller error is a trusted curator who sees the true data, which randomized response does not need. It remains to prove that the mechanism is private.

Theorem 4.1 (Privacy of the Laplace mechanism) For every \(f\colon\mathcal X^n\to\mathbb R^d\) with \(0 < \Delta_1 f < \infty\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\), the Laplace mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\), and write \(p\) and \(q\) for the densities of \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) on \(\mathbb R^d\). In this proof \(p\) is a density, not the fraction of ones. Let \(b = \Delta_1 f/\varepsilon\). The coordinates are independent, so at a point \(y \in \mathbb R^d\),

\[
\frac{p(y)}{q(y)} = \prod_{j=1}^d \frac{\exp(-|f(D)_j - y_j|/b)}{\exp(-|f(D')_j - y_j|/b)} = \exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta_1 f}\sum_{j=1}^d\big(|f(D')_j - y_j| - |f(D)_j - y_j|\big)\right).
\tag{4.6}\]

By the triangle inequality, \(|f(D')_j - y_j| - |f(D)_j - y_j| \le |f(D')_j - f(D)_j|\) for each \(j\). Summing over \(j\) gives at most \(\|f(D) - f(D')\|_1\), which is at most \(\Delta_1 f\) by Definition 4.1. So \(p(y) \le e^\varepsilon q(y)\) for every \(y\).
For an event \(S \subseteq \mathbb R^d\), integrate the pointwise bound over \(S\): \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] = \int_S p \le e^\varepsilon\int_S q = e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D')\in S]\).


The proof shows why the Laplace distribution fits the definition. Its density falls exponentially in the distance from the true value, and the definition bounds a ratio by an exponential. So a shift of the centre by the sensitivity changes the density by a factor of at most \(e^\varepsilon\). Figure 4.1 shows the two densities for a one-dimensional statistic.






Figure 4.1: Left, the densities of the Laplace mechanism at \(\varepsilon = 1\) on two neighbours whose values differ by the sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f = 1\). Their ratio stays between \(e^{-1}\) and \(e\). Right, the 95th percentile of the error in estimating a fraction of ones, over 2,000 simulated runs with \(p = 0.3\). Randomized response falls as \(1/\sqrt n\) and the Laplace mechanism as \(1/n\). The dashed line is the exact 95th percentile \(\ln(20)/(\varepsilon n)\) from Equation 4.3.

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.4 Counting queries
A counting query asks how many people in the dataset have some property. It is given by a predicate \(\phi\colon\mathcal X \to \{0,1\}\) and has the value \(f(D) = \sum_{i=1}^n\phi(x_i)\). One record changes the count by at most \(1\), so \(\Delta_1 f = 1\), and the Laplace mechanism adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\). By Equation 4.3, its error is at most \(\ln(1/\beta)/\varepsilon\) with probability \(1-\beta\), whatever the size of the dataset.
Often an analyst asks many counting queries \(f = (f_1, \dots, f_k)\), with predicates \(\phi_1, \dots, \phi_k\), on the same data, such as whether a person smokes and whether their income is above a threshold. One person can then change all of the answers at once.

Proposition 4.1 The vector of \(k\) counting queries has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity at most \(k\), with equality when some record satisfies every predicate and another satisfies none. For every \(\beta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the Laplace mechanism answers all \(k\) queries with error at most
\[
\frac{k\ln(k/\beta)}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{4.7}\]


Proof. 

Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in one record, \(x\) in \(D\) and \(x'\) in \(D'\). In each query the other terms cancel, so \(\|f(D) - f(D')\|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^k|\phi_j(x) - \phi_j(x')| \le k\). The sum equals \(k\) when \(\phi_j(x) = 1\) and \(\phi_j(x') = 0\) for all \(j\).
The noise in each answer is \(\mathrm{Lap}(k/\varepsilon)\). By Equation 4.3 with \(t = \ln(k/\beta)\), each noise is at least \(k\ln(k/\beta)/\varepsilon\) in absolute value with probability \(\beta/k\).
The union bound over the \(k\) answers gives a failure probability of at most \(\beta\).


This analysis needs all \(k\) queries to be fixed in advance. The composition theorem of Section 4.6 gives the same privacy when each query is chosen after seeing the earlier answers.
Compare this error of order \(k/\varepsilon\) per query with the reconstruction chapter, where about \(n\) counting queries answered with error \(o(\sqrt n)\) let an attacker recover almost the whole dataset. Here, \(n\) counting queries get error of order \(n/\varepsilon\), up to a logarithm. The wide gap between \(\sqrt n\) and \(n\) is real slack: advanced composition, under a relaxation of the definition, lowers the error to about \(\sqrt{k}/\varepsilon\) per query, up to logarithmic factors.

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.5 Histograms
When the queries have structure, a sharper sensitivity bound is possible. In a histogram, each record falls into exactly one of \(k\) bins, such as an age in whole years, and the query counts the records in each bin: \(f_j(D) = |\{i : x_i \text{ is in bin } j\}|\).

Proposition 4.2 A histogram with \(k \ge 2\) bins has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(2\). For every \(\beta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1-\beta\), the Laplace mechanism, which adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) to each bin, answers every bin with error at most
\[
\frac{2\ln(k/\beta)}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{4.8}\]


Proof. 

Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in one record, which lies in bin \(a\) in \(D\) and in bin \(a'\) in \(D'\). If \(a = a'\) the histograms are equal. Otherwise count \(a\) drops by \(1\) and count \(a'\) rises by \(1\), so \(f(D) - f(D') = e_a - e_{a'}\), where \(e_j\) is the \(j\)-th unit vector, and \(\|e_a - e_{a'}\|_1 = 2\).
By Equation 4.3 with \(t = \ln(k/\beta)\), each of the \(k\) noises is at least \(2\ln(k/\beta)/\varepsilon\) in absolute value with probability \(\beta/k\). The union bound over the bins finishes the proof.


The sensitivity is \(2\) because a replacement moves a record from one bin to another. A single bin has error at most \(2\ln(1/\beta)/\varepsilon\) with probability \(1-\beta\), and the proposition pays only \(\ln k\) more to control all bins at once. So private histograms over very large domains are practical. For \(k = 100\) bins, \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\), the bound is \(2\ln(2000) = 15.20\), and in a simulation of 20,000 runs the 95th percentile of the largest error is \(15.17\). The same \(100\) bins treated as arbitrary counting queries would get the bound \(100\ln(2000) = 760.1\) from Proposition 4.1.

title: 4  The Laplace Mechanism
text:
4.6 Properties of differential privacy
Three properties let you reason about a private algorithm piece by piece.

4.6.1 Post-processing
No computation on a private output can undo its privacy, as long as the computation does not look at the data again. The randomized response chapter used this to turn the private reports into an estimate.

Theorem 4.2 (Post-processing) Let \(M\colon\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal Y\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and let \(F\colon\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\) be a randomized map whose coins are independent of those of \(M\). Then \(F\circ M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

A randomized map is a random choice of a deterministic one. Write \(F(y) = g_R(y)\), where \(R\) is the coins of \(F\) and each \(g_r\colon\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Z\) is deterministic.
Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an event \(S\subseteq\mathcal Z\). For fixed coins, \(g_R(M(D))\in S\) exactly when \(M(D) \in g_R^{-1}(S)\), so

\[
\Pr[F(M(D))\in S] = \mathbb E_R\Big[\Pr\big[M(D)\in g_R^{-1}(S)\big]\Big].
\tag{4.9}\]

Inside the expectation, apply the definition of \(\varepsilon\)-DP to the event \(g_R^{-1}(S)\), then undo step 2 for \(D'\):

\[
\mathbb E_R\Big[\Pr\big[M(D)\in g_R^{-1}(S)\big]\Big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_R\Big[\Pr\big[M(D')\in g_R^{-1}(S)\big]\Big] = e^\varepsilon\Pr[F(M(D'))\in S].
\tag{4.10}\]



4.6.2 Group privacy
The definition protects one record. Datasets that differ in several records, such as the records of one family, are still protected, with a guarantee that degrades in proportion to their number.

Theorem 4.3 (Group privacy) Let \(M\colon\mathcal X^n\to\mathcal Y\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and let \(D, D'\in\mathcal X^n\) differ in \(k\) records. For every event \(S\subseteq\mathcal Y\),
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S].
\tag{4.11}\]


Proof. 

The proof is a hybrid argument. Change the \(k\) differing records one at a time, from their values in \(D\) to their values in \(D'\). This gives datasets \(D = D^{(0)}, D^{(1)}, \dots, D^{(k)} = D'\) in which each consecutive pair are neighbours.
Apply the definition to each consecutive pair, from the first to the last:

\[
\Pr[M(D^{(0)})\in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D^{(1)})\in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D^{(2)})\in S] \le \dots \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D^{(k)})\in S].
\tag{4.12}\]

So a group of \(k\) people has the protection of \(k\varepsilon\)-DP, which means something only while \(k\varepsilon\) is small. The theorem also relates the two kinds of neighbours of the randomized response chapter. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition, so \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove neighbours gives \(2\varepsilon\)-DP under replace-one neighbours.


4.6.3 Basic composition
An analyst rarely runs one mechanism. Usually each mechanism is chosen in the light of the outputs of the earlier ones and runs on the same dataset.

Definition 4.4 (Adaptive composition) Let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) be mechanisms. For each \(i\) and each sequence of earlier outputs \(y_{<i} = (y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\), the mechanism \(M_i(\cdot\,; y_{<i})\) takes the dataset \(D\) and returns \(y_i\). Their adaptive composition \(M\) runs them in order on the same \(D\), each with fresh coins, and releases \((y_1,\dots,y_k)\).

Basic composition says that the privacy parameters add up, even though each mechanism may depend on the earlier outputs.

Theorem 4.4 (Basic composition) If each \(M_i(\cdot\,; y_{<i})\) is \(\varepsilon_i\)-DP for every \(y_{<i}\), then the adaptive composition of \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) is \(\big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i\big)\)-DP. In particular, \(k\) mechanisms that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP compose to a \(k\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.

The proof is simplest for countable outputs, where the probability of a sequence of outputs factors into conditional probabilities.

Proof. Countable outputs.

Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and outputs \(y = (y_1,\dots,y_k)\). Each \(M_i\) uses fresh coins, so the chain rule gives \(\Pr[M(D) = y] = \prod_{i=1}^k\Pr[M_i(D; y_{<i}) = y_i]\), and likewise for \(D'\).
Each factor for \(D\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon_i}\) times the matching factor for \(D'\), by the privacy of \(M_i(\cdot\,; y_{<i})\) applied to the event \(\{y_i\}\). Multiplying the \(k\) bounds gives

\[
\Pr[M(D) = y] = \prod_{i=1}^k\Pr[M_i(D; y_{<i}) = y_i] \le \prod_{i=1}^k e^{\varepsilon_i}\Pr[M_i(D'; y_{<i}) = y_i] = \exp\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i\Big)\Pr[M(D') = y].
\tag{4.13}\]

The pointwise lemma of the randomized response chapter turns this bound on single outcomes into the definition.


For outputs that are not countable, such as the real numbers that the Laplace mechanism releases, the same idea works with averages in place of products. It uses one fact about functions \(h\) with values in \([0,1]\): if \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then for all neighbours
\[
\mathbb E[h(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h(M(D'))].
\tag{4.14}\]
This is Lemma 3.2 of the randomized response chapter.

Proof. General outputs.

The composition of the first \(k-1\) mechanisms is itself a mechanism, so by induction on \(k\) it suffices to treat \(k = 2\).
Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an event \(S\) of pairs. For an output \(y_1\), write \(S_{y_1} = \{y_2 : (y_1,y_2)\in S\}\) and \(g_D(y_1) = \Pr[M_2(D; y_1)\in S_{y_1}]\), and define \(g_{D'}\) in the same way. Conditioning on the first output gives \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] = \mathbb E_{y_1\sim M_1(D)}[g_D(y_1)]\), and likewise for \(D'\).
By the privacy of \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\), \(g_D(y_1) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}g_{D'}(y_1)\) for every \(y_1\).
The function \(g_{D'}\) takes values in \([0,1]\), so the fact above, applied to \(M_1\), gives

\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_2}\,\mathbb E_{y_1\sim M_1(D)}[g_{D'}(y_1)] \le e^{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}\,\mathbb E_{y_1\sim M_1(D')}[g_{D'}(y_1)] = e^{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}\Pr[M(D')\in S].
\tag{4.15}\]

Basic composition recovers the analysis of Proposition 4.1. Each counting query with \(\mathrm{Lap}(k/\varepsilon)\) noise is \((\varepsilon/k)\)-DP, and \(k\) of them compose to \(\varepsilon\)-DP, now even when the analyst chooses the queries adaptively. So the cost of \(k\) analyses grows linearly in \(k\). It can grow like \(\sqrt k\) instead, but only under the relaxation of the definition that the next chapter introduces.
