title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
5.1 The definition
Pure differential privacy (DP) bounds the ratio of two output probabilities by \(e^\varepsilon\) on every event. This chapter adds a small additive slack \(\delta\) to that bound. The relaxed definition, \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, lets a mechanism fail with probability about \(\delta\), and the examples of the chapter show that \(\delta\) must be much smaller than \(1/n\). In exchange, the relaxation admits the Gaussian mechanism, which adds less noise than the Laplace mechanism to statistics with many coordinates, and the advanced composition of the next chapter.
An additive bound alone is the wrong notion of privacy. Suppose we asked only that, for all neighbours and all events,
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le \Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta .
\tag{5.1}\]
This allows no useful accuracy when \(\delta\) is small and allows harmful mechanisms when \(\delta\) is large (Vadhan, 2017, Section 1.6), as Section 5.3 shows. But together with the multiplicative bound of pure DP, an additive term gives the right definition. Recall that two datasets in \(\mathcal X^n\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ in exactly one record (the replace-one relation).
At \(\delta = 0\) this is the \(\varepsilon\)-DP of the randomized response chapter, which from now on is called pure DP. A definition with \(\delta > 0\) is called approximate DP.

title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
Definition 5.1 (Approximate differential privacy) Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0,1]\). A randomized algorithm \(M\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathcal Y\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-differentially private if for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all events \(S \subseteq \mathcal Y\),
\[
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta .
\tag{5.2}\]

title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
5.2 The privacy loss random variable
Definition 5.1 bounds probabilities of events, but it is easier to understand one outcome at a time. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\). An observer who sees an output \(y\) and asks whether the dataset was \(D\) or \(D'\) compares how likely \(y\) is under each. Write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distributions of \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\), and \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) for the likelihood of \(y\) under each: probabilities when \(\mathcal Y\) is countable, and densities when both outputs have densities. (In general, \(p\) and \(q\) are densities with respect to the measure \(P + Q\), which always exist.)
The privacy loss is the logarithm of the ratio \(p(y)/q(y)\). An outcome that can occur under \(D\) but never under \(D'\), with \(p(y) > 0\) and \(q(y) = 0\), rules \(D'\) out entirely, so its loss is \(+\infty\).

Definition 5.2 (Privacy loss) Let \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) be the probabilities, or densities, of an outcome \(y\) under \(M(D)\) and under \(M(D')\). The privacy loss of an outcome \(y\) with \(p(y) > 0\) is
\[
L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)},
\tag{5.3}\]
where \(L_{D,D'}(y) = +\infty\) if \(q(y) = 0\). Once the pair is fixed we write it \(L(y)\). The privacy loss random variable is \(L = L(Y)\) with \(Y = M(D)\): the privacy loss of the outcome the mechanism actually produces on \(D\).

The outcome \(M(D)\) has \(p(M(D)) > 0\) with probability \(1\), so \(L\) is always defined. A large value of \(L\) means that the outcome is much more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\), so it is evidence for \(D\). A negative value is evidence for \(D'\), and an infinite value means that the outcome is impossible under \(D'\).
The Laplace mechanism of the previous chapter gives a first example. For a function \(f\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R\) whose value changes by at most \(\Delta_1 f\) between neighbours, it releases \(f(D) + Z\), where \(Z\) has the Laplace density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\) with scale \(b = \Delta_1 f/\varepsilon\), and it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.

Example 5.1 Take neighbours with \(f(D) = a\) and \(f(D') = a - \Delta_1 f\), the largest gap allowed. The densities give
\[
L(y) = \frac{\varepsilon}{\Delta_1 f}\big(|y - a + \Delta_1 f| - |y - a|\big),
\tag{5.4}\]
which equals \(\varepsilon\) for \(y \ge a\), equals \(-\varepsilon\) for \(y \le a - \Delta_1 f\), and is linear in between.

The event \(y \ge a\) has probability \(\tfrac12\) under \(P\), because the noise is symmetric. So \(L\) has an atom of mass \(\tfrac12\) at \(\varepsilon\).
The event \(y \le a - \Delta_1 f\) needs noise below \(-\Delta_1 f = -\varepsilon b\), which has probability \(\tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon}\). So \(L\) has an atom of mass \(\tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon}\) at \(-\varepsilon\).
In between, write \(y = a - s\) with \(s \in (0, \Delta_1 f)\), so that \(L = \varepsilon - 2\varepsilon s/(\Delta_1 f)\). The variable \(s\) has density \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2\Delta_1 f}e^{-\varepsilon s/(\Delta_1 f)}\), and the change of variables gives \(L\) the density \(u \mapsto \tfrac14 e^{(u - \varepsilon)/2}\) on \((-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)\), of total mass \(\tfrac12(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\).

The three masses add up to \(1\). The privacy loss never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\), as Figure 5.1 shows on the left.







Figure 5.1: Privacy loss for two mechanisms on neighbours whose values differ by the full sensitivity. Left, the Laplace mechanism with \(\varepsilon = 1\), from Example 5.1: atoms of mass \(0.5\) at \(\varepsilon\) and \(0.184\) at \(-\varepsilon\), and a density in between. Right, the Gaussian mechanism with noise standard deviation \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\), from Lemma 5.4: the loss is Gaussian with mean \(1/2\) and variance \(1\), so it exceeds \(\varepsilon = 1\) with probability \(0.309\).



The example is an instance of a general fact. Pure DP says that the privacy loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) with probability \(1\), and approximate DP says, roughly, that it is at most \(\varepsilon\) except with probability \(\delta\). Both follow from one identity for the smallest \(\delta\) that works for a pair, which is the largest violation of the multiplicative bound over all events. The identity writes it as an average over the privacy loss, with the positive part \((z)_+ = \max(z, 0)\).

Lemma 5.1 For neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and \(\varepsilon \ge 0\),
\[
\sup_{S \subseteq \mathcal Y}\Big(\Pr[M(D)\in S] - e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D')\in S]\Big) = \mathbb E\Big[\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\big)_+\Big],
\tag{5.5}\]
where \(L\) is the privacy loss random variable of Definition 5.2 for this pair, \((z)_+ = \max(z, 0)\) is the positive part of \(z\), and \(e^{\varepsilon - L}\) is read as \(0\) when \(L = +\infty\). So \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP if and only if the right-hand side is at most \(\delta\) for every ordered pair of neighbours.


Proof. 

For an event \(S\), write the difference as an integral, \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] - e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D')\in S] = \int_S (p - e^\varepsilon q)\). The integrand is positive exactly on \(B = \{y : p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\}\), so the integral is largest for \(S = B\), where it equals \(\int (p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\).
Where \(p(y) = 0\), the integrand \((p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\) is \(0\). Where \(p(y) > 0\), it equals \(p(y)\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon}q(y)/p(y)\big)_+ = p(y)\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)}\big)_+\), which is also right when \(q(y) = 0\) and \(L(y) = \infty\).
Integrating \(p(y)\) times a function of \(y\) is taking the expectation under \(P\), so \(\int(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+ = \mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\).
Definition 5.1 asks that the left-hand side of Equation 5.5 be at most \(\delta\) for every ordered pair of neighbours, which proves the last sentence.


The right-hand side of Equation 5.5 is called the hockey-stick divergence of \(P\) from \(Q\), after the shape of the function \(z \mapsto (1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\). Its integrand is \(0\) when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and at most \(1\) otherwise. So the lemma ties \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP to how often \(L\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and the next theorem makes that tie precise in both directions.

Theorem 5.1 Let \(M\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathcal Y\) be a randomized algorithm, and let \(L\) be its privacy loss random variable for an ordered pair of neighbours \(D \sim D'\).

\(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if \(L \le \varepsilon\) with probability \(1\) for every ordered pair of neighbours. In that case \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) with probability \(1\).
If \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\) for every ordered pair of neighbours, then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.
If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, then for every \(t > 0\) and every ordered pair of neighbours,

\[
\Pr[L > \varepsilon + t] \le \frac{\delta}{1 - e^{-t}} .
\tag{5.6}\]


Proof. 

With \(\delta = 0\), Lemma 5.1 says that \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP exactly when \(\mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon-L})_+] = 0\) for every pair. The integrand is nonnegative, so this holds exactly when it is \(0\) with probability \(1\), that is, when \(L \le \varepsilon\) with probability \(1\). For the lower bound, apply the same fact to the pair \((D', D)\). It gives \(q \le e^\varepsilon p\) except on a set of \(Q\)-probability \(0\), and that set also has \(P\)-probability \(0\), because pure DP gives \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D')\in S]\). So \(L \ge -\varepsilon\) with probability \(1\) under \(P\).
The integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) is \(0\) when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and at most \(1\) when \(L > \varepsilon\). So its expectation is at most \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\), and Lemma 5.1 gives \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.
On the event \(L > \varepsilon + t\), the integrand is at least \(1 - e^{-t}\). So \((1 - e^{-t})\Pr[L > \varepsilon + t] \le \mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon-L})_+] \le \delta\), by Lemma 5.1.


The converse of part 2 fails with the same parameters, which is why part 3 pays in both \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). For example, the Gaussian mechanism on the right of Figure 5.1 has privacy loss above \(1\) with probability \(0.309\), yet Proposition 5.3 below shows that it is \((1, 0.127)\)-DP. With \(t = \varepsilon\), part 3 says that an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP mechanism has privacy loss above \(2\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta/(1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\). So, up to these constants, \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP says that the privacy loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) except with probability about \(\delta\), and it says nothing about what happens on that rare event.

title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
5.3 How small δ must be
On the event of probability \(\delta\), the privacy loss may be infinite. The first example shows this in its crudest form.

Example 5.2 Let \(\bot\) be a fixed symbol that carries no information about the data. The mechanism \(M(D)\) outputs \(\bot\) with probability \(1 - \delta\) and outputs the whole dataset \(D\) with probability \(\delta\). For neighbours \(D \ne D'\) and an event \(S\),
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le (1-\delta)\,\mathbf 1[\bot \in S] + \delta \le \Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta ,
\tag{5.7}\]
so \(M\) is \((0,\delta)\)-DP. With probability \(1 - \delta\) the privacy loss is \(\ln\frac{1-\delta}{1-\delta} = 0\), and with probability \(\delta\) it is infinite, because the output \(D\) is impossible under \(D'\).

This mechanism publishes everyone’s data with probability \(\delta\), so \(\delta\) must be small. The next example shows how small, because it publishes each record on its own.

Definition 5.3 (Name and shame) For \(\delta \in [0,1]\), the mechanism \(\mathrm{NS}_\delta\) draws independent coins \(c_1, \dots, c_n\), each equal to \(1\) with probability \(\delta\), and outputs the set of pairs \(\{(i, x_i) : c_i = 1\}\).

Each record, which might be a person’s medical file, is published in the clear with probability \(\delta\). Even so, the mechanism meets the definition with \(\varepsilon = 0\), because a person’s record affects the output only when that person’s coin comes up \(1\), which has probability \(\delta\).

Proposition 5.1 For every \(\delta \in [0,1]\), \(\mathrm{NS}_\delta\) is \((0,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ only in record \(i\), and run the mechanism on both datasets with the same coins. Let \(E\) be the event \(c_i = 1\), so \(\Pr[E] = \delta\).
On the complement \(\bar E\), record \(i\) is not published, and the output is a function of the coins and of the records \(j \ne i\), which the two datasets share. So on \(\bar E\) the two outputs are equal.
For an event \(S\), split on \(E\) and use step 2:

\[
\Pr[\mathrm{NS}_\delta(D) \in S] = \Pr[\mathrm{NS}_\delta(D) \in S,\ \bar E] + \Pr[\mathrm{NS}_\delta(D)\in S,\ E] \le \Pr[\mathrm{NS}_\delta(D') \in S,\ \bar E] + \Pr[E] .
\tag{5.8}\]

The first term is at most \(\Pr[\mathrm{NS}_\delta(D') \in S]\) and the second is \(\delta\), which is Equation 5.2 with \(\varepsilon = 0\).


So a mechanism that plainly harms people meets \((0,\delta)\)-DP. Its harm depends on the chance that it publishes at least one record, which the next proposition computes.

Proposition 5.2 The probability that \(\mathrm{NS}_\delta\) publishes at least one record is \(1 - (1-\delta)^n\), and
\[
n\delta - \frac{(n\delta)^2}{2} \le 1 - (1-\delta)^n \le n\delta .
\tag{5.9}\]


Proof. 

The coins are independent, so no record is published with probability \((1-\delta)^n\), and the complement gives the formula.
The upper bound is the union bound over the \(n\) records, each published with probability \(\delta\).
For the lower bound, \(1 - \delta \le e^{-\delta}\) gives \((1-\delta)^n \le e^{-n\delta}\). The inequality \(e^{-x} \le 1 - x + x^2/2\) for \(x \ge 0\) then gives \(1 - (1-\delta)^n \ge n\delta - (n\delta)^2/2\).


So the chance that someone is named is about \(n\delta\) when \(n\delta\) is small. At \(\delta = 1/n\), step 3 of the proof shows that some record is in the clear with probability at least \(1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632\). A guarantee that allows this is not privacy, so \(\delta\) must be well below \(1/n\). Even \(\delta = n^{-1.1}\) allows a chance of up to \(n\delta = n^{-0.1}\), which is \(0.25\) for a million records. Common choices are \(\delta \le 1/n^2\), or a cryptographically small \(\delta\), smaller than every inverse polynomial in \(n\).
In both examples the privacy loss is \(0\) or infinite, so the rare event is a catastrophe. Without more information about a mechanism, you must assume this worst case. But many mechanisms degrade gracefully. Their privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability about \(\delta\) but rarely exceeds it by much, so they meet a family of guarantees at once, such as \((1, 10^{-3})\)-DP and \((2, 10^{-6})\)-DP. The Gaussian mechanism of the next section is the main example, as Example 5.5 shows.
The definition must be stated for events, not single outcomes. For pure DP the two are equivalent on countable outputs, by the pointwise lemma of the randomized response chapter, but for approximate DP the pointwise version is much weaker.

Example 5.3 Let \(m = \lceil 1/\delta\rceil\) for some \(\delta \in (0,1)\). The mechanism \(M(D) = (D, U)\) outputs the whole dataset together with a number \(U\) drawn uniformly from \(\{1, \dots, m\}\). Every single outcome has probability at most \(1/m \le \delta\), so for all neighbours and all outcomes \(y\),
\[
\Pr[M(D) = y] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') = y] + \delta .
\tag{5.10}\]
Yet the event \(S = \{(D, u) : 1 \le u \le m\}\) has probability \(1\) under \(D\) and \(0\) under \(D'\), so \(M\) is not \((\varepsilon, \delta_0)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta_0 < 1\).

The privacy loss of this mechanism is infinite with probability \(1\). So Theorem 5.1, which looks at the privacy loss, catches the failure that the pointwise inequality misses.

title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
5.4 The Gaussian mechanism
The Laplace mechanism calibrates its noise to the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. The Gaussian mechanism adds Gaussian noise instead, calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller.

Definition 5.4 (ℓ2 sensitivity) The \(\ell_2\) sensitivity of a function \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) is
\[
\Delta_2 f = \sup_{D \sim D'} \|f(D) - f(D')\|_2 .
\tag{5.11}\]

The \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f\) of the previous chapter is the same supremum with the \(\ell_1\) norm. The two sensitivities are within a factor \(\sqrt d\) of each other, because the two norms are.

Lemma 5.2 For every \(v \in \mathbb R^d\), \(\|v\|_2 \le \|v\|_1 \le \sqrt d\,\|v\|_2\). Hence \(\Delta_2 f \le \Delta_1 f \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2 f\).


Proof. 

Expanding the square, \(\|v\|_1^2 = \sum_i v_i^2 + \sum_{i\ne j}|v_i||v_j| \ge \|v\|_2^2\).
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to \((|v_1|,\dots,|v_d|)\) and the all-ones vector gives \(\|v\|_1 = \sum_i |v_i|\cdot 1 \le \|v\|_2\sqrt d\).
Applying both inequalities to \(f(D) - f(D')\) and taking the supremum over neighbours gives the bounds on the sensitivities.


The Gaussian distribution \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) has density
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\tag{5.12}\]
Its tails fall like \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), faster than the \(e^{-|x|/b}\) of the Laplace distribution. Write \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) for the vector of \(d\) independent \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) coordinates. The Gaussian mechanism adds such a vector to the true answer.

Definition 5.5 (Gaussian mechanism) For \(f\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) and a noise level \(\sigma > 0\), the Gaussian mechanism outputs
\[
M(D) = f(D) + Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d).
\tag{5.13}\]

The theorem below says how large the noise level \(\sigma\) must be for a given \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\).

Theorem 5.2 (Privacy of the Gaussian mechanism) Let \(f\) have \(0 < \Delta_2 f < \infty\), and let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). The Gaussian mechanism with
\[
\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2 f}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon}
\tag{5.14}\]
is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


The proof is in Section 5.4.1. As \(\delta \to 0\), the noise level is \(\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2 f}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\,(1 + o(1))\). The Laplace mechanism has noise of scale \(\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon\) in each coordinate, so the Gaussian mechanism differs in two ways. It pays a factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) for only approximate DP, but it measures sensitivity in \(\ell_2\), which can save a factor \(\sqrt d\). The next example shows that the saving can be the larger effect.

Example 5.4 Each of \(n\) people answers \(d\) yes-or-no questions, so the dataset is \(D \in \{0,1\}^{n\times d}\) with rows \(x_i \in \{0,1\}^d\). The analyst wants the vector of averages \(f(D) = \frac1n\sum_i x_i\), with small error in \(\ell_2\) norm.

Replacing row \(x\) by row \(x'\) changes \(f\) by \((x - x')/n\). The largest change is from the all-ones row to the all-zeros row, so \(\Delta_1 f = d/n\) and \(\Delta_2 f = \sqrt d/n\).
The Laplace mechanism adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(d/(\varepsilon n))\) to each coordinate, and each coordinate has variance \(2d^2/(\varepsilon n)^2\). The root mean squared \(\ell_2\) error is

\[
\sqrt{\mathbb E\|Z\|_2^2} = \sqrt{d \cdot \frac{2d^2}{\varepsilon^2n^2}} = \frac{\sqrt2\, d^{3/2}}{\varepsilon n}.
\tag{5.15}\]

The Gaussian mechanism with Equation 5.14 adds \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) to each coordinate with \(\sigma = \frac{\sqrt d}{\varepsilon n}\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)+\varepsilon}\), so its root mean squared error is

\[
\sqrt d\,\sigma = \frac{d\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon n}.
\tag{5.16}\]

The ratio of the two errors is \(\sqrt{2d/(2\ln(1/\delta)+\varepsilon)}\). So the Gaussian mechanism is more accurate as soon as \(d > \ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon/2\), and its advantage grows like \(\sqrt d\).

With \(d = 100\) questions, \(n = 10{,}000\) people, \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the Laplace error is \(\sqrt2\cdot 1000/10{,}000 = 0.1414\) and the Gaussian error is \(100\sqrt{27.63+1}/10{,}000 = 0.0535\), smaller by a factor \(2.64\). A simulation of 20,000 runs of each mechanism gives \(0.1413\) and \(0.0535\).

So the choice is a trade-off: the Laplace mechanism gives the stronger guarantee of pure DP, and the Gaussian mechanism a weaker guarantee with less noise in high dimension.

5.4.1 Proof of privacy
The proof has two steps. First, the privacy loss of the Gaussian mechanism is itself Gaussian. Second, a Gaussian tail bound shows that it exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\), and part 2 of Theorem 5.1 concludes. The lemma below collects four facts about Gaussians: the first two give the distribution of the privacy loss, and the last two bound its tail.

Lemma 5.3 Let \(W \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\).

For constants \(\mu\) and \(a \ne 0\), \(\mu + aW \sim \mathcal N(\mu, a^2)\).
If \(V_1 \sim \mathcal N(0, a_1^2)\) and \(V_2 \sim \mathcal N(0, a_2^2)\) are independent, then \(V_1 + V_2 \sim \mathcal N(0, a_1^2 + a_2^2)\).
For every \(u \ge 0\), \(\Pr[W > u] \le e^{-u^2/2}\).
For every \(u > 0\), \(\Pr[W > u] \le e^{-u^2/2}/(u\sqrt{2\pi})\).



Proof. 

Completing the square in the density gives the moment generating function \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda W}] = e^{\lambda^2/2}\). A distribution is determined by its moment generating function when that function is finite near \(0\), as it is for all the variables here.
For part 1, \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda(\mu + aW)}] = e^{\lambda\mu + \lambda^2a^2/2}\), which is the moment generating function of \(\mathcal N(\mu, a^2)\).
For part 2, independence makes the moment generating function of the sum the product \(e^{\lambda^2a_1^2/2}e^{\lambda^2a_2^2/2} = e^{\lambda^2(a_1^2+a_2^2)/2}\).
For part 3, Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{uW}\) gives \(\Pr[W > u] \le e^{-u^2}\,\mathbb E[e^{uW}] = e^{-u^2/2}\).
For part 4, write \(\varphi(z) = e^{-z^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) for the density, whose derivative is \(-z\varphi(z)\). On \(z \ge u\) the ratio \(z/u\) is at least \(1\), so \(\Pr[W > u] \le \int_u^\infty \frac zu\varphi(z)\,\mathrm d z = \frac{\varphi(u)}{u}\).


The first step of the plan computes the privacy loss, which is Gaussian, with a mean and a variance set by the distance between \(f(D)\) and \(f(D')\).

Lemma 5.4 Let \(D \sim D'\), let \(M\) be the Gaussian mechanism with noise level \(\sigma\), and write \(v = f(D) - f(D')\). The privacy loss random variable of \(M(D)\) against \(M(D')\) is distributed as
\[
L \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\rho,\ 2\rho\right), \qquad \rho = \frac{\|v\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}.
\tag{5.17}\]


Proof. 

The output is \(f(D) + z\) with \(z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\). Its density under \(D\) is proportional to \(\exp(-\|z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))\). Under \(D'\), the same point is at distance \(z + v\) from the mean \(f(D')\), so its density is proportional to \(\exp(-\|z + v\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))\), with the same constant.
The constants cancel in the ratio, and the logarithm gives

\[
L = \frac{\|z+v\|_2^2 - \|z\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^d\big((z_j+v_j)^2 - z_j^2\big) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^d \big(2z_jv_j + v_j^2\big).
\tag{5.18}\]

The constant part is \(\sum_j v_j^2/(2\sigma^2) = \rho\), the claimed mean.
The random part is \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_j v_jz_j\), and the terms with \(v_j = 0\) vanish. By part 1 of Lemma 5.3 each remaining term \(v_jz_j\) is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2v_j^2)\), and the terms are independent. By part 2 their sum is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2\|v\|_2^2)\). Dividing by \(\sigma^2\) gives \(\mathcal N(0, \|v\|_2^2/\sigma^2) = \mathcal N(0, 2\rho)\).


So the variance of the privacy loss is twice its mean. For a single coordinate, \(d = 1\), the proof is just the identity \(L = vz/\sigma^2 + v^2/(2\sigma^2)\). A Gaussian privacy loss is special to this mechanism: the loss of the Laplace mechanism, by Example 5.1, has atoms.

Proof. Proof of Theorem 5.2.

By part 2 of Theorem 5.1, it suffices to show \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\) for every ordered pair of neighbours. If \(v = 0\) then \(L = 0\), so assume \(v \ne 0\).
By Lemma 5.4 and part 1 of Lemma 5.3, \(L = \rho + \sqrt{2\rho}\,W\) with \(W \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\). So

\[
\Pr[L > \varepsilon] = \Pr\left[W > g(\rho)\right], \qquad g(\rho) = \frac{\varepsilon - \rho}{\sqrt{2\rho}} = \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\rho}} - \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{2}} .
\tag{5.19}\]

The function \(g\) decreases in \(\rho\), and \(\rho \le (\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) by the definition of \(\Delta_2 f\). Write \(t = \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)+\varepsilon}\), so that Equation 5.14 reads \(\sigma = t\,\Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\) and the largest value of \(\rho\) is \(\varepsilon^2/(2t^2)\). Then

\[
g(\rho) \ge g\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2t^2}\right) = t - \frac{\varepsilon}{2t} =: u .
\tag{5.20}\]

The value \(u\) is positive, because \(t^2 \ge \varepsilon > \varepsilon/2\). Its square is \(u^2 = t^2 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/(4t^2) \ge t^2 - \varepsilon = 2\ln(1/\delta)\).
By part 3 of Lemma 5.3, \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \Pr[W > u] \le e^{-u^2/2} \le e^{-\ln(1/\delta)} = \delta\).


Only the upper tail of \(L\) matters in this proof, because part 2 of Theorem 5.1 bounds \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon]\), not \(\Pr[|L| > \varepsilon]\). For \(\varepsilon \le 1\) the noise level Equation 5.14 is at most \(\frac{\Delta_2 f}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{2\ln(1.65/\delta)}\). The sharper tail bound of part 4 of Lemma 5.3 lowers the constant \(1.65\) to \(1.25\), the form that later chapters use.

Corollary 5.1 (Gaussian mechanism for ε ≤ 1) Let \(f\) have \(0 < \Delta_2 f < \infty\), and let \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). The Gaussian mechanism with
\[
\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2 f}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}
\tag{5.21}\]
is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Write \(t = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\), so that \(\sigma = t\,\Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\) and \(e^{-t^2/2} = \delta/1.25\). Steps 1 to 3 of the proof of Theorem 5.2 used only \(\sigma = t\,\Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\), so they give \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \Pr[W > u]\) with \(u = t - \varepsilon/(2t)\).
Since \(\varepsilon \le 1\), the value \(u\) is at least \(t - 1/(2t)\), which increases in \(t\). Also \(u^2 = t^2 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/(4t^2) \ge t^2 - 1\).
Case \(\delta \le 0.74\). Then \(t \ge \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/0.74)} \ge 1.0239\), and by step 2, \(u \ge 0.5356\). By part 4 of Lemma 5.3 and step 2,

\[
\Pr[W > u] \le \frac{e^{-u^2/2}}{u\sqrt{2\pi}} \le \frac{e^{1/2}\,e^{-t^2/2}}{0.5356\sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{e^{1/2}}{1.25 \cdot 0.5356\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\delta \le 0.983\,\delta .
\tag{5.22}\]

Case \(\delta > 0.74\). Then \(t > \sqrt{2\ln 1.25} \ge 0.6680\), and by step 2, \(u > -0.0805\). The density of \(W\) is at most \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), so \(\Pr[W > u] \le \tfrac12 + 0.0805/\sqrt{2\pi} \le 0.533 < \delta\).
In both cases \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\), and part 2 of Theorem 5.1 gives \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


This is the bound of Dwork and Roth (2014, Theorem A.1). On a grid of \(\varepsilon\) from \(0.01\) to \(1\) and \(\delta\) from \(0.89\) down to \(10^{-20}\), the exact \(\delta\) of Proposition 5.3 at this noise level is at most \(0.233\) times the target. Both constants are loose, because the tail bounds of Lemma 5.3 are loose. The exact \(\delta\) comes from the identity of Lemma 5.1 for the Gaussian privacy loss, evaluated instead of bounded.

Proposition 5.3 Let \(\Phi\) be the distribution function of \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), let \(f\) have \(0 < \Delta_2 f < \infty\), and let \(s = \Delta_2 f/\sigma\). For every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), the Gaussian mechanism with noise level \(\sigma\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for
\[
\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\!\left(\frac s2 - \frac\varepsilon s\right) - e^{\varepsilon}\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac s2 - \frac\varepsilon s\right),
\tag{5.23}\]
and for no smaller \(\delta\) when some pair of neighbours has \(\|f(D) - f(D')\|_2 = \Delta_2 f\).


Proof. 

Fix a pair of neighbours and let \(r = \|v\|_2/\sigma \in (0, s]\), so that \(\rho = r^2/2\) and \(L = r^2/2 + rW\). By Lemma 5.1, the smallest \(\delta\) for this pair is \(\mathbb E[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})\mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]]\).
The event \(L > \varepsilon\) is \(W > c\) with \(c = \varepsilon/r - r/2\), so it has probability \(\Phi(r/2 - \varepsilon/r)\).
Write \(\varphi\) for the standard normal density. Completing the square gives \(e^{-rz}\varphi(z) = e^{r^2/2}\varphi(z + r)\), so \(\mathbb E[e^{-rW}\mathbf 1[W > c]] = e^{r^2/2}\,\Phi(-c - r)\). Since \(e^{\varepsilon - L} = e^{\varepsilon - r^2/2}e^{-rW}\) and \(-c-r = -r/2 - \varepsilon/r\),

\[
\mathbb E\big[e^{\varepsilon - L}\mathbf 1[L>\varepsilon]\big] = e^{\varepsilon - r^2/2}\,e^{r^2/2}\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac r2 - \frac\varepsilon r\right) = e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac r2 - \frac\varepsilon r\right).
\tag{5.24}\] 4. Subtracting step 3 from step 2 gives Equation 5.23 with \(r\) in place of \(s\). Call that function \(h(r)\). 5. Write \(c_1 = r/2 - \varepsilon/r\) and \(c_2 = -r/2 - \varepsilon/r\). Then \((c_1^2 - c_2^2)/2 = (c_1-c_2)(c_1+c_2)/2 = -\varepsilon\), so \(e^\varepsilon\varphi(c_2) = \varphi(c_1)\). Differentiating, \(h'(r) = \varphi(c_1)(\tfrac12 + \varepsilon/r^2) + e^\varepsilon\varphi(c_2)(\tfrac12 - \varepsilon/r^2) = \varphi(c_1) > 0\). 6. So \(h\) increases in \(r\), the worst pair is the one with the largest \(r\), and \(h(r) \le h(s) = \delta(\varepsilon)\), with equality when some pair attains \(\Delta_2 f\).

The exact formula shows the graceful degradation promised in Section 5.3: at one noise level, the Gaussian mechanism meets a whole family of guarantees.

Example 5.5 For \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), Equation 5.14 gives \(\sigma = \sqrt{2\ln(10^5) + 1}\,\Delta_2 f = 4.9016\,\Delta_2 f\). At this noise level, Equation 5.23 gives the following guarantees, all at once:

\((0.5,\ 6.1\times 10^{-4})\)-DP,
\((1,\ 3.0\times 10^{-8})\)-DP,
\((2,\ 3.0\times 10^{-24})\)-DP.

The guarantee at \(\varepsilon = 1\) is far better than the \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) that was asked for, and the smallest noise level that gives \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP is \(\sigma = 3.7306\,\Delta_2 f\). As \(\varepsilon\) grows, \(\delta\) falls faster than exponentially, so the privacy loss of this mechanism degrades gracefully.

title: 5  Approximate Differential Privacy
text:
5.5 Properties
The properties of pure DP proved in the Laplace mechanism chapter carry over to approximate DP. Post-processing and composition keep their proofs, with \(\delta\) added to each bound, and group privacy gets a worse \(\delta\).

Theorem 5.3 (Post-processing) Let \(M\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathcal Y\) be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, and let \(F\colon\mathcal Y \to \mathcal Z\) be a randomized map whose coins are independent of those of \(M\). Then \(F \circ M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

The proof of Theorem 4.2 writes \(F\) as a random choice \(g_R\) of deterministic functions and conditions on the coins \(R\). Those steps do not use the definition of privacy, so they are unchanged.
Only its last step changes. For neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an event \(S \subseteq \mathcal Z\), apply Equation 5.2, instead of pure DP, to the event \(g_R^{-1}(S)\), so \(\delta\) joins the bound inside the expectation:

\[
\Pr[F(M(D))\in S] = \mathbb E_R\Big[\Pr[M(D) \in g_R^{-1}(S)]\Big] \le \mathbb E_R\Big[e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in g_R^{-1}(S)] + \delta\Big] = e^\varepsilon\Pr[F(M(D'))\in S] + \delta .
\tag{5.25}\]

For group privacy, recall that an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism meets the bound with \(e^{k\varepsilon}\) on datasets that differ in \(k\) records (Theorem 4.3). With approximate DP, each step of the chain also multiplies the earlier \(\delta\) terms by \(e^\varepsilon\).

Theorem 5.4 (Group privacy) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, and let \(D, D' \in \mathcal X^n\) differ in \(k \ge 1\) records. For every event \(S\),
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S] + k e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta .
\tag{5.26}\]


Proof. 

Change the differing records one at a time to get a chain \(D = D^{(0)} \sim D^{(1)} \sim \dots \sim D^{(k)} = D'\) of neighbours. Write \(P_j = \Pr[M(D^{(j)})\in S]\).
We show \(P_0 \le e^{j\varepsilon}P_j + \delta\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}e^{i\varepsilon}\) by induction on \(j\). The case \(j = 1\) is Equation 5.2.
If the bound holds for \(j\), apply Equation 5.2 to \(D^{(j)} \sim D^{(j+1)}\), which gives \(P_j \le e^{\varepsilon}P_{j+1} + \delta\). Substituting,

\[
P_0 \le e^{j\varepsilon}\big(e^\varepsilon P_{j+1} + \delta\big) + \delta\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}e^{i\varepsilon} = e^{(j+1)\varepsilon}P_{j+1} + \delta\sum_{i=0}^{j}e^{i\varepsilon} .
\tag{5.27}\]

At \(j = k\) this is the first inequality in Equation 5.26. Each of the \(k\) terms of the sum is at most \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), which gives the second.


So the additive term grows exponentially in the group size, and the bound says nothing once \(k\) is a little over \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\).
Composition needs one more tool, because its proof bounds averages of functions with values in \([0,1]\), not only probabilities of events. For pure DP this tool is Lemma 3.2, and the lemma below adds \(\delta\) to it.

Lemma 5.5 Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP and let \(h\colon\mathcal Y \to [0,1]\). For all neighbours \(D \sim D'\),
\[
\mathbb E[h(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h(M(D'))] + \delta .
\tag{5.28}\]


Proof. 

The proof is that of Lemma 3.2 with \(+\delta\). Its first step, which writes \(\mathbb E[h(M(D))] = \int_0^1\Pr[h(M(D)) > t]\,\mathrm d t\), does not use privacy and is unchanged.
Only the bound on each tail changes. Equation 5.2 bounds the probability of the event \(\{y : h(y) > t\}\) by \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[h(M(D')) > t] + \delta\), and integrating over \(t \in [0,1]\) gives \(e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h(M(D'))] + \delta\).


Adaptive composition is as in Definition 4.4: each \(M_i\) may depend on the earlier outputs \(y_{<i}\), and now each \(M_i(\cdot\,; y_{<i})\) is \((\varepsilon_i,\delta_i)\)-DP.

Theorem 5.5 (Basic composition) If each \(M_i(\cdot\,;y_{<i})\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP for every \(y_{<i}\), where the parameters \(\varepsilon_i\) and \(\delta_i\) are fixed in advance, then the adaptive composition of \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) is \(\big(\sum_i\varepsilon_i, \sum_i\delta_i\big)\)-DP.


Proof. The proof is that of Theorem 4.4 for general outputs, with \(\delta\) added. Its steps 1 and 2 do not change. By induction it suffices to treat \(k = 2\). For an event \(S\) of pairs, with \(S_{y_1}\) and \(g_D(y_1) = \Pr[M_2(D; y_1) \in S_{y_1}]\) as there, conditioning on the first output gives \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] = \mathbb E_{y_1\sim M_1(D)}[g_D(y_1)]\). Steps 3 and 4 change, because the bound on \(g_D\) now has an additive term.

Since \(M_2(\cdot\,;y_1)\) is \((\varepsilon_2,\delta_2)\)-DP and \(g_D \le 1\), we have \(g_D(y_1) \le \min\{1, e^{\varepsilon_2}g_{D'}(y_1) + \delta_2\} \le h(y_1) + \delta_2\), where \(h = \min\{1, e^{\varepsilon_2}g_{D'}\}\) takes values in \([0,1]\).
By Lemma 5.5 applied to \(M_1\) and \(h\),

\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le \mathbb E_{M_1(D)}[h] + \delta_2 \le e^{\varepsilon_1}\,\mathbb E_{M_1(D')}[h] + \delta_1 + \delta_2 .
\tag{5.29}\]

Finally \(h \le e^{\varepsilon_2}g_{D'}\), and \(\mathbb E_{y_1\sim M_1(D')}[g_{D'}(y_1)] = \Pr[M(D')\in S]\) by the conditioning identity above, applied to \(D'\). So \(\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}\Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta_1+\delta_2\).


Fix the parameters in advance. If the analyst chooses \(\varepsilon_i\) from earlier outputs, the sum is no longer a valid bound without further work. With \(k\) mechanisms that are each \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, basic composition gives \((k\varepsilon, k\delta)\)-DP. The next chapter proves that, for every \(\delta' > 0\), the same composition is also \((\varepsilon', k\delta + \delta')\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\,(e^\varepsilon - 1).
\tag{5.30}\]
When \(\varepsilon\) is of order \(1/\sqrt k\) or smaller, the second term is no larger than the first, so \(\varepsilon'\) grows like \(\sqrt k\) rather than \(k\). That allows quadratically more analyses for the same privacy, at the price of a \(\delta' > 0\) even when every mechanism is pure.

5.7 References

Cynthia Dwork, Krishnaram Kenthapadi, Frank McSherry, Ilya Mironov and Moni Naor, “Our Data, Ourselves: Privacy via Distributed Noise Generation”, 2006. Defines \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP and first analyses Gaussian noise.
Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, 2014. Covers the privacy loss (Section 3.5), the constant \(\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\) (Theorem A.1) and composition (Theorems 3.16 and 3.20).
Salil Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy”, 2017. Explains in Section 1.6 why an additive bound alone fails.

title: 6  Advanced Composition
text:
6.1 The theorem
When you run \(k\) private analyses on the same data, basic composition says that their privacy costs add up. This chapter shows that the total cost grows much more slowly, about as \(\sqrt{k}\), if you accept a small extra failure probability. The proof turns each step into one simple pair of outputs with four outcomes. Then it bounds \(k\) copies of that pair with Hoeffding’s inequality.
Write \(D \sim D'\) for neighbouring datasets, which differ in one record (the replace-one relation). Recall from the approximate differential privacy (DP) chapter that a mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP if, for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all events \(S\),
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta .
\tag{6.1}\]
The proofs below compare two output distributions at a time, so the next definition names this condition for a pair of random variables.
So \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP exactly when \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable for every pair of neighbours.
The theorem is about the adaptive composition of Definition 4.4: mechanisms \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) run in order on the same \(D\), where \(M_j(D; y_{<j})\) may depend on the earlier outputs \(y_{<j} = (y_1,\dots,y_{j-1})\), and the composition outputs the whole transcript \((y_1,\dots,y_k)\).
Basic composition, proved in the two previous chapters, says that if each \(M_j(\,\cdot\,; y_{<j})\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP for every fixed \(y_{<j}\), then \(M\) is \((k\varepsilon, k\delta)\)-DP. The theorem of this chapter improves the first parameter. Throughout, every output space is countable, so that probabilities are sums over outcomes.
The first term of \(\tilde\varepsilon\) is the important one, and it grows as \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) instead of \(k\varepsilon\). The second term is small when \(\varepsilon\) is small. Its factor is \((e^\varepsilon-1)/(e^\varepsilon+1) = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), and \(\tanh x \le x\) for \(x \ge 0\), so the term is at most \(k\varepsilon^2/2\). That is also at most \(k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), because \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \ge \varepsilon\), so the theorem implies the weaker form that the previous chapter quoted. The extra slack \(\delta'\) is a free parameter, and a larger \(\delta'\) lowers \(\tilde\varepsilon\), so the theorem trades a bigger \(\delta\) for a smaller \(\varepsilon\).
The proof is in Section 6.3. Before it, Example 6.1 and Figure 6.1 say how much the theorem gains.
The exact curve in Figure 6.1 shows that Theorem 6.1 is close to the truth, within 7% of it at \(k = 10{,}000\). So growth as \(\varepsilon\sqrt{k\ln(1/\delta')}\) is how privacy really degrades, not an artefact of the proof. Kairouz, Oh and Viswanath (2015) computed the exact optimal \(\tilde\varepsilon\), which is tighter but harder to use.
With a total budget \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\) for \(k\) analyses, you can invert Equation 6.3. The next corollary gives a simple choice that always works.
The corollary is conservative by about a factor of \(2\). With \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} = 1\), \(k = 1{,}000\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-6}\), it allows \(\varepsilon = 0.00301\) per mechanism, for which Equation 6.3 gives a total of only \(0.5045\). Solving Equation 6.3 numerically allows \(\varepsilon = 0.00591\), almost twice as much, and basic composition with that \(\varepsilon\) would give a total of \(5.911\).
The gain matters most when the number of analyses grows with the problem, as in the next example.

title: 6  Advanced Composition
text:
Definition 6.1 (Indistinguishable pair) Let \(\varepsilon, \delta \ge 0\). Two random variables \(A\) and \(B\) with values in the same space are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable if, for every event \(S\),
\[
\Pr[A\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[B\in S] + \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Pr[B\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[A\in S] + \delta .
\tag{6.2}\]





Theorem 6.1 (Advanced composition) Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), \(\delta \in [0,1)\) and \(\delta' \in (0,1)\). Let \(M\) be the adaptive composition of \(k\) mechanisms such that \(M_j(\,\cdot\,; y_{<j})\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP for every \(j\) and every \(y_{<j}\). Then \(M\) is \((\tilde\varepsilon, \tilde\delta)\)-DP with
\[
\tilde\varepsilon = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\,\frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \qquad \tilde\delta = k\delta + \delta' .
\tag{6.3}\]





Example 6.1 Take \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-6}\), so that \(\ln(1/\delta') = 13.8155\) and \(\tanh(0.05) = 0.04996\). For \(k = 100\) mechanisms, basic composition gives \(10\). Advanced composition gives \(0.1\sqrt{200 \times 13.8155} + 100 \times 0.1 \times 0.04996 = 5.257 + 0.500 = 5.756\). For \(k = 1{,}000\), basic composition gives \(100\) and advanced composition gives \(16.623 + 4.996 = 21.618\). Advanced composition is the smaller of the two from \(k = 31\) on.







Figure 6.1: The total privacy parameter of \(k\) mechanisms that are each \(0.1\)-DP, at \(\delta' = 10^{-6}\). The solid line is basic composition, the dashed line is Equation 6.3, and the dotted line is the exact smallest \(\tilde\varepsilon\) for \(k\) independent randomized responses, which is the worst case for pure DP by Section 6.2. Advanced composition overtakes basic composition at \(k = 31\) and is within 21% of the exact value for every \(k\) from \(100\) to \(10{,}000\).






Corollary 6.1 Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta' \in (0, 1/2]\). If each of \(k\) adaptively composed mechanisms is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}}{2\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}},
\tag{6.4}\]
then the composition is \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}, k\delta + \delta')\)-DP.


Proof. 

By Theorem 6.1, the composition is \((\tilde\varepsilon, k\delta+\delta')\)-DP. Its first term is \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}/2\).
The second term is \(k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \le k\varepsilon^2/2\), because \(\tanh x \le x\). Substituting \(\varepsilon\) gives \(k\varepsilon^2/2 = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}^2/(16\ln(1/\delta'))\).
Since \(\delta' \le 1/2\), we have \(\ln(1/\delta') \ge \ln 2 > 1/8\), and since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} \le 1\), the second term is at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}^2/2 \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}/2\).
Adding the two terms gives \(\tilde\varepsilon \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\). A mechanism that is \((\tilde\varepsilon,\tilde\delta)\)-DP is also \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}},\tilde\delta)\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} \ge \tilde\varepsilon\).





Example 6.2 (Mean estimation with the Laplace mechanism) Each of \(n\) people holds a vector \(x_i \in \{0,1\}^d\), and the analyst wants the mean \(f(D) = \frac1n\sum_i x_i\). Recall the Laplace mechanism: if \(f\) has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f\), meaning that \(\|f(D) - f(D')\|_1 \le \Delta_1 f\) for all neighbours, then adding independent noise from the Laplace distribution with scale \(\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon\) to each coordinate is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. A Laplace variable with scale \(b\) has mean \(0\) and variance \(2b^2\), so the expected squared \(\ell_2\) error of the noise vector is \(2db^2\).
All coordinates at once. Replacing one person changes each coordinate of the mean by at most \(1/n\), so \(\Delta_1 f = d/n\), and the noise has scale \(d/(n\varepsilon)\). The root mean squared \(\ell_2\) error is \(\sqrt{2d}\,d/(n\varepsilon) = \sqrt2\, d^{3/2}/(n\varepsilon)\).
One coordinate at a time. Each coordinate is a mechanism with sensitivity \(1/n\), released with Laplace noise of scale \(1/(n\varepsilon_1)\), which makes it \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP. With \(\varepsilon_1\) from Corollary 6.1 for \(k = d\) and \(\delta = 0\), the \(d\) releases together are \((\varepsilon, \delta')\)-DP for \(\varepsilon \le 1\). The root mean squared error is
\[
\frac{\sqrt{2d}}{n\varepsilon_1} = \frac{\sqrt{2d}\cdot 2\sqrt{2d\ln(1/\delta')}}{n\varepsilon} = \frac{4d\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta')}}{n\varepsilon} .
\tag{6.5}\]
The error now grows as \(d\) instead of \(d^{3/2}\), which is the order the Gaussian mechanism achieves. Take \(n = 100{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-6}\). At \(d = 1{,}000\), the two errors are \(0.4472\) and \(0.1487\). At \(d = 10{,}000\), they are \(14.14\) and \(1.487\), nearly ten times apart. The price is the move from pure to approximate DP.

title: 6  Advanced Composition
text:
6.2 Reduction to four outcomes
A pair of output distributions \(M_j(D)\) and \(M_j(D')\) can be complicated. The first step of the proof replaces every such pair by the simplest \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable pair. It has two ordinary outcomes, \(0\) and \(1\), whose probabilities differ by the factor \(e^\varepsilon\), and two catastrophic outcomes, each with probability \(\delta\), which reveal which distribution the sample came from.

Definition 6.2 (The four-outcome pair) For \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0,1)\), let \(U\) and \(V\) take values in \(\{0, 1, \text{I am } U, \text{I am } V\}\) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr[U = 0] &= \frac{e^\varepsilon(1-\delta)}{1+e^\varepsilon}, & \Pr[U = 1] &= \frac{1-\delta}{1+e^\varepsilon}, & \Pr[U = \text{I am } U] &= \delta, & \Pr[U = \text{I am } V] &= 0, \\
\Pr[V = 0] &= \frac{1-\delta}{1+e^\varepsilon}, & \Pr[V = 1] &= \frac{e^\varepsilon(1-\delta)}{1+e^\varepsilon}, & \Pr[V = \text{I am } U] &= 0, & \Pr[V = \text{I am } V] &= \delta .
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.6}\]

For \(\delta = 0\) this is randomized response with truth probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\), from the first chapter of this part. Here \(U\) is the report of a person whose bit is \(0\) and \(V\) that of a person whose bit is \(1\). The first check is that the pair meets the condition it stands for.

Lemma 6.1 The pair \(U, V\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable.


Proof. 

On the outcomes \(0\) and \(1\), the ratio \(\Pr[U = t]/\Pr[V = t]\) is \(e^\varepsilon\) or \(e^{-\varepsilon}\), so \(\Pr[U = t] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[V = t]\).
Take an event \(S\). Sum step 1 over the outcomes of \(S\) in \(\{0,1\}\). The outcome “I am \(U\)” adds at most \(\delta\) to \(\Pr[U \in S]\), and “I am \(V\)” adds nothing. So \(\Pr[U\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[V\in S] + \delta\).
Swapping the labels \(0 \leftrightarrow 1\) and “I am \(U\)” \(\leftrightarrow\) “I am \(V\)” turns the distribution of \(U\) into that of \(V\) and back, so the same argument gives the other inequality.


Indistinguishability survives any further processing, as privacy does. The proof is that of post-processing in the approximate DP chapter, written for a pair of random variables.

Lemma 6.2 (Post-processing) Let \(A, B\) be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable, and let \(F\) be a randomized map whose coins are independent of \(A\) and \(B\). Then \(F(A)\) and \(F(B)\) are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable.


Proof. 

Functions with values in \([0,1]\). Let \(g\) take values in \([0,1]\). The proof of Lemma 5.5 uses only the bound of the definition on events, so it applies to \(A\) and \(B\) unchanged and gives \(\mathbb E[g(A)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[g(B)] + \delta\).
Post-processing. Fix an event \(S\) and let \(g(a) = \Pr[F(a)\in S]\), a probability over the coins of \(F\). Because those coins are independent of \(A\), \(\Pr[F(A)\in S] = \mathbb E[g(A)]\), and likewise for \(B\).
Step 1 applied to \(g\) gives \(\Pr[F(A)\in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[F(B)\in S] + \delta\). The other direction is the same with \(A\) and \(B\) swapped.


The four-outcome pair is the hardest \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable pair to tell apart, in a strong sense. One randomized map produces any other such pair \(A, B\) from \(U, V\).

Theorem 6.2 (Simulation by the four-outcome pair) Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0,1)\), and let \(A, B\) be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable random variables on a countable space. Then there is a randomized map \(F\) such that \(F(U)\) has the distribution of \(A\) and \(F(V)\) has the distribution of \(B\).

The map sends each of the four outcomes to a distribution on the space. Some outcomes \(y\) are more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely under \(A\) as under \(B\). The definition bounds the total excess of \(A\) on these outcomes by \(\delta\), so “I am \(U\)” can carry it, and “I am \(V\)” carries the reverse excess. What is left is a pair whose probabilities are within a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) at every outcome. The outcome \(0\) puts more weight where \(A\) is the more likely of the two, and \(1\) where \(B\) is. Kairouz, Oh and Viswanath (2015) first proved the theorem, with hypothesis tests and Blackwell’s theorem on the comparison of statistical experiments. The proof below builds the map directly.

Proof. Write \(p(y) = \Pr[A = y]\) and \(q(y) = \Pr[B = y]\).

The excess. Let \(a(y) = \max(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y), 0)\) and \(b(y) = \max(q(y) - e^\varepsilon p(y), 0)\), with totals \(\alpha = \sum_y a(y)\) and \(\beta = \sum_y b(y)\). Take \(S\), the set of outcomes with \(p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\). Then \(\alpha = \Pr[A\in S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr[B\in S] \le \delta\) by the definition. In the same way, \(\beta \le \delta\).
The rest. Let \(p_1(y) = p(y) - a(y) = \min(p(y), e^\varepsilon q(y))\) and \(q_1(y) = q(y) - b(y) = \min(q(y), e^\varepsilon p(y))\). Then \(p_1 \le e^\varepsilon q\) and \(p_1 \le p \le e^{2\varepsilon} p\), so \(p_1 \le e^\varepsilon q_1\). In the same way, \(q_1 \le e^\varepsilon p_1\). The totals of \(p_1\) and \(q_1\) are \(1-\alpha\) and \(1-\beta\).
Equal totals. Suppose \(\alpha \le \beta\); otherwise swap the roles of \(p\) and \(q\). The totals of step 2 differ by \(\sum_y (p_1(y) - q_1(y)) = \beta - \alpha\). So the outcomes with \(p_1(y) > q_1(y)\) carry an excess \(c = \sum_y \max(p_1(y) - q_1(y), 0) \ge \beta - \alpha\). If \(\beta > \alpha\), remove the fraction \(\theta = (\beta-\alpha)/c \le 1\) of that excess: \[
p_2(y) = p_1(y) - \theta\max(p_1(y) - q_1(y), 0) ,
\tag{6.7}\] and if \(\beta = \alpha\), let \(p_2 = p_1\). Let \(q_2 = q_1\). Where \(p_2\) differs from \(p_1\), it lies between \(q_1\) and \(p_1\), so the bounds of step 2 hold for \(p_2\) and \(q_2\). Both now have the total \(1-\beta\).
Scale. Let \(p_0 = t\,p_2\) and \(q_0 = t\,q_2\) with \(t = (1-\delta)/(1-\beta)\), which is in \((0, 1]\) because \(\beta \le \delta < 1\). Then \(p_0\) and \(q_0\) have the total \(1-\delta\), satisfy \(p_0 \le e^\varepsilon q_0\) and \(q_0 \le e^\varepsilon p_0\), and \(p_0 \le p\), \(q_0 \le q\).
The two catastrophic outcomes. If \(\delta > 0\), let \(F\) map “I am \(U\)” to a sample from \(R_U = (p - p_0)/\delta\) and “I am \(V\)” to a sample from \(R_V = (q - q_0)/\delta\). By step 4 both are non-negative, and each sums to \((1 - (1-\delta))/\delta = 1\). If \(\delta = 0\), these two outcomes never occur.
The two ordinary outcomes. If \(\varepsilon = 0\), step 4 gives \(p_0 = q_0\); let \(F\) map \(0\) and \(1\) to a sample from \(p_0/(1-\delta)\). If \(\varepsilon > 0\), define
\[
P_0(y) = \frac{e^\varepsilon p_0(y) - q_0(y)}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)(1-\delta)}, \qquad P_1(y) = \frac{e^\varepsilon q_0(y) - p_0(y)}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)(1-\delta)} .
\tag{6.8}\]
Both are non-negative by step 4, and each sums to \((e^\varepsilon - 1)(1-\delta)/((e^\varepsilon - 1)(1-\delta)) = 1\). Let \(F\) map \(0\) to a sample from \(P_0\) and \(1\) to a sample from \(P_1\).
Check. \(U\) is \(0\) with probability \(e^\varepsilon(1-\delta)/(1+e^\varepsilon)\), \(1\) with probability \((1-\delta)/(1+e^\varepsilon)\) and “I am \(U\)” with probability \(\delta\). So, for \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(F(U)\) equals \(y\) with probability
\[
\frac{e^\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon p_0(y) - q_0(y)) + e^\varepsilon q_0(y) - p_0(y)}{(1+e^\varepsilon)(e^\varepsilon - 1)} + \delta R_U(y) = p_0(y) + p(y) - p_0(y) = p(y) .
\tag{6.9}\]
For \(\varepsilon = 0\), the probability is \((1-\delta)\,p_0(y)/(1-\delta) + p(y) - p_0(y) = p(y)\). In the same way, \(F(V)\) equals \(y\) with probability \(q(y)\).

For \(\delta = 0\), steps 1 to 4 change nothing: \(\alpha = \beta = 0\), \(p_0 = p\) and \(q_0 = q\).

Applying Theorem 6.2 once per step of an adaptive composition reduces the whole transcript to a map of \(k\) independent copies of the four-outcome pair.

Theorem 6.3 Let \(M\) be the adaptive composition of \(M_1,\dots,M_k\) as in Theorem 6.1, and fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\). Let \(U_1,\dots,U_k\) be independent copies of \(U\) and \(V_1,\dots,V_k\) independent copies of \(V\). Then there is a randomized map \(F^*\) such that \(F^*(U_1,\dots,U_k)\) has the distribution of \(M(D)\) and \(F^*(V_1,\dots,V_k)\) has the distribution of \(M(D')\).


Proof. 

Fix a step \(j\) and an earlier transcript \(y_{<j}\). The mechanism \(M_j(\,\cdot\,;y_{<j})\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, so its outputs \(M_j(D; y_{<j})\) and \(M_j(D'; y_{<j})\) are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-indistinguishable. Theorem 6.2 gives a randomized map \(F_j^{y_{<j}}\) that turns \(U\) into \(M_j(D; y_{<j})\) and \(V\) into \(M_j(D'; y_{<j})\).
Define \(F^*\) on an input \((z_1,\dots,z_k)\) step by step. Set \(y_1 = F_1(z_1)\), then \(y_2 = F_2^{y_1}(z_2)\), and in general \(y_j = F_j^{y_{<j}}(z_j)\), with fresh coins at each step. Output \((y_1,\dots,y_k)\).
By induction on \(j\), the prefix \((y_1,\dots,y_j)\) computed from \((U_1,\dots,U_k)\) has the distribution of the first \(j\) outputs of \(M(D)\). For \(j=1\) this is step 1. Given the prefix \(y_{<j}\), the input \(U_j\) is still a fresh copy of \(U\), because it is independent of \(U_1,\dots,U_{j-1}\) and of the coins used so far. So \(y_j = F_j^{y_{<j}}(U_j)\) has the distribution of \(M_j(D;y_{<j})\), which is how \(M\) draws its \(j\)-th output.
The same induction with \(V_1,\dots,V_k\) gives the distribution of \(M(D')\).


The map \(F^*\) depends on \(D\) and \(D'\), but that is harmless, because privacy is a statement about one pair of neighbours at a time and Lemma 6.2 applies to any map. So it remains to show that \((U_1,\dots,U_k)\) and \((V_1,\dots,V_k)\) are \((\tilde\varepsilon,\tilde\delta)\)-indistinguishable.

title: 6  Advanced Composition
text:
6.3 Composing the four-outcome pair
Write \(\mathbf U = (U_1,\dots,U_k)\) and \(\mathbf V = (V_1,\dots,V_k)\). As in the approximate DP chapter, the privacy loss of an outcome compares how likely it is under \(\mathbf U\) and under \(\mathbf V\). An outcome that is possible under \(\mathbf U\) but impossible under \(\mathbf V\) has infinite loss, and for an outcome \(z\) that is possible under \(\mathbf V\), the privacy loss is
\[
L(z) = \ln\frac{\Pr[\mathbf U = z]}{\Pr[\mathbf V = z]} .
\tag{6.10}\]
The plan is to show that, for \(z\) drawn from \(\mathbf U\), the loss rarely exceeds \(\tilde\varepsilon\). Two kinds of outcome are bad. An outcome that contains “I am \(U\)” is impossible under \(\mathbf V\), so its loss is infinite, which happens with probability about \(k\delta\). On the other outcomes, the loss is a sum of \(k\) independent terms, and Hoeffding’s inequality bounds the chance that it strays far above its mean by \(\delta'\). The first step computes the loss on the outcomes with no catastrophe, in which every coordinate is \(0\) or \(1\).

Lemma 6.3 For every \(z \in \{0,1\}^k\), the privacy loss is \(L(z) = \varepsilon\sum_{j=1}^k (1 - 2z_j)\).


Proof. 

The coordinates are independent, so both probabilities factor and the log of the ratio is a sum: \(L(z) = \sum_{j=1}^k \ln\big(\Pr[U = z_j]/\Pr[V = z_j]\big)\).
By Definition 6.2, the ratio is \(e^\varepsilon\) when \(z_j = 0\) and \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) when \(z_j = 1\). In both cases its logarithm is \(\varepsilon(1 - 2z_j)\).


Given no catastrophic outcome, the coordinates of \(\mathbf U\) are independent bits, so the loss is a sum of independent terms, each \(\varepsilon\) or \(-\varepsilon\). Hoeffding’s inequality bounds its tail.
Take \(k\) independent random variables \(W_1,\dots,W_k\), each with values in an interval \([l, u]\) of length \(u - l\). Hoeffding’s inequality bounds the chance that their sum exceeds its mean by a margin \(\tau \ge 0\) or more,
\[
\Pr\left[\sum_{j=1}^k W_j \ge \sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb E[W_j] + \tau\right] \le \exp\left(-\frac{2\tau^2}{k(u-l)^2}\right) .
\tag{6.11}\]
With the loss and its tail bound, the main estimate follows: \(k\) copies of the four-outcome pair are as hard to tell apart as Theorem 6.1 claims.

Proposition 6.1 Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), \(\delta \in [0,1)\) and \(\delta' \in (0,1)\). Then \(\mathbf U\) and \(\mathbf V\) are \((\tilde\varepsilon,\tilde\delta)\)-indistinguishable, with \(\tilde\varepsilon\) and \(\tilde\delta\) as in Equation 6.3.


Proof. 

The events. Let \(E_1\) be the event that some coordinate of \(\mathbf U\) is “I am \(U\)”. Let \(G\) be the set of good outcomes, the \(z \in \{0,1\}^k\) with \(L(z) \le \tilde\varepsilon\). Every outcome \(z\) with \(\Pr[\mathbf U = z] > 0\) that is not in \(G\) either lies in \(E_1\) or lies in \(\{0,1\}^k\) with \(L(z) > \tilde\varepsilon\). Outcomes containing “I am \(V\)” have probability \(0\) under \(\mathbf U\).
The first bad event. Each coordinate avoids “I am \(U\)” with probability \(1-\delta\), independently, so \(\Pr[E_1] = 1 - (1-\delta)^k\). Bernoulli’s inequality \((1-\delta)^k \ge 1 - k\delta\) gives \(\Pr[E_1] \le k\delta\).
The coordinates given no catastrophe. Given that \(U_j\) is not “I am \(U\)”, it is \(0\) with probability \(\frac{e^\varepsilon(1-\delta)/(1+e^\varepsilon)}{1-\delta} = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1+e^\varepsilon}\) and \(1\) otherwise. Conditioned on the complement \(\bar E_1\), the coordinates stay independent, because \(\bar E_1\) is an intersection of independent events, one per coordinate.
The mean of the loss. By Lemma 6.3, given \(\bar E_1\) the loss is \(\sum_j W_j\) with \(W_j = \varepsilon(1-2U_j)\). Each \(W_j\) is \(\varepsilon\) with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\) and \(-\varepsilon\) otherwise, so
\[
\mathbb E\Big[\sum_{j=1}^k W_j \,\Big|\, \bar E_1\Big] = k\varepsilon\,\frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1},
\tag{6.12}\]
which is the second term of \(\tilde\varepsilon\).
The second bad event. If \(\varepsilon = 0\), the loss is \(0 \le \tilde\varepsilon\) and there is nothing to bound. Otherwise apply Equation 6.11, conditioned on \(\bar E_1\), with \([l,u] = [-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\) and \(\tau = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\), the first term of \(\tilde\varepsilon\). The exponent is \(2\tau^2/(4k\varepsilon^2) = \ln(1/\delta')\), so
\[
\Pr\big[L(\mathbf U) > \tilde\varepsilon \,\big|\, \bar E_1\big] \le \delta' .
\tag{6.13}\]
Multiplying by \(\Pr[\bar E_1] \le 1\) bounds the probability that \(\mathbf U \in \{0,1\}^k\) and \(L(\mathbf U) > \tilde\varepsilon\) by \(\delta'\).
Assembly. Take any event \(S\). Split it into \(S \cap G\) and the rest. On \(G\), each outcome has \(\Pr[\mathbf U = z] \le e^{\tilde\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathbf V = z]\) by the definition of \(L\). By step 1, the rest has probability at most that of the two bad events. Steps 2 and 5 then give
\[
\Pr[\mathbf U \in S] \le e^{\tilde\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathbf V \in S\cap G] + k\delta + \delta' \le e^{\tilde\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathbf V \in S] + \tilde\delta .
\tag{6.14}\]
The other direction. Swapping the labels \(0 \leftrightarrow 1\) and “I am \(U\)” \(\leftrightarrow\) “I am \(V\)” in every coordinate maps \(\mathbf U\) to \(\mathbf V\) and back. The same argument then gives \(\Pr[\mathbf V \in S] \le e^{\tilde\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathbf U \in S] + \tilde\delta\).


So the term \(k\delta\) of \(\tilde\delta\) pays for a catastrophic outcome in some step, and \(\delta'\) pays for an unusually long run of outcomes that favour \(\mathbf U\). The proof of the theorem puts the pieces together.

Proof. Proof of Theorem 6.1. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\).

By Theorem 6.3, \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) have the distributions of \(F^*(\mathbf U)\) and \(F^*(\mathbf V)\) for one randomized map \(F^*\).
By Proposition 6.1, \(\mathbf U\) and \(\mathbf V\) are \((\tilde\varepsilon,\tilde\delta)\)-indistinguishable.
By Lemma 6.2, so are \(F^*(\mathbf U)\) and \(F^*(\mathbf V)\). The neighbours were arbitrary, so \(M\) is \((\tilde\varepsilon,\tilde\delta)\)-DP.

text:
6.4 Summary



Table 6.1: The chapter’s results.









Result
Statement

\(k\) adaptive \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP steps are \(\big(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2),\ k\delta+\delta'\big)\)-DP


Corollary 6.1
per-step \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}/(2\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')})\) gives a total of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} \le 1\)

an adaptive composition is a map of \(k\) independent copies of the four-outcome pair
