title: 6  Advanced Composition
text:
6.5 References

Cynthia Dwork, Guy N. Rothblum and Salil Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy”, 2010. First proves the advanced composition theorem.
Peter Kairouz, Sewoong Oh and Pramod Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy”, 2015. Proves the simulation by the four-outcome pair and finds the exact optimal composition.
Wassily Hoeffding, “Probability Inequalities for Sums of Bounded Random Variables”, 1963. Gives the tail bound used for the privacy loss.
Cynthia Dwork and Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy, 2014. Proves advanced composition with the privacy loss in Section 3.5, with \(k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) as the second term.
Salil Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy”, 2017. Presents basic and advanced composition in Section 2.
Jack Murtagh and Salil Vadhan, “The Complexity of Computing the Optimal Composition of Differential Privacy”, 2016. Shows that the exact optimal composition is hard to compute for mixed parameters.

title: 7  The Exponential Mechanism
text:
7.1 Selecting an object
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms release numbers. They work because a small change in a number does little harm. Many tasks instead ask for the best object from a set, such as a price or a classifier, and there a small change in the output can ruin its quality. The exponential mechanism samples each object with a probability that grows exponentially with a score. So good objects are likely, while the choice reveals little about any one person, as differential privacy (DP) requires. This chapter proves that the mechanism is private and nearly optimal, and applies it to three problems.
A seller has a digital good, such as an e-book, that costs nothing to copy, and \(n\) buyers who each want one copy. Buyer \(i\) values the good at \(v_i\) and buys it if the price \(p\) is at most \(v_i\). The seller’s revenue at price \(p\) is the price times the number of buyers,
\[
p \cdot \big|\{i : v_i \ge p\}\big| .
\tag{7.1}\]
The seller could compute the price with the highest revenue from the valuations, but that price can reveal a single buyer. If one buyer values the good far above the others, the best price may be that buyer’s valuation.
Noise added to the best price does not help, because revenue is very sensitive to the price. Take three buyers who value the good at $1 and one who values it at $2.50. At a price of $1 all four buy and the revenue is $4, but at $1.01 only the last buyer buys and the revenue is $1.01. So a cent of noise can cost three quarters of the revenue. It is better to treat the prices as objects with a quality, the revenue, than as numbers to perturb.
In general, the input to the selection problem has three parts:
In the example, \(D\) is the list of valuations, \(\mathcal R\) is the set of prices, and \(u(D,p)\) is the revenue at price \(p\). Only the dataset is private, while the objects and the score function are public. So the sensitivity measures how much the score of a fixed object can move when one record changes.
The score is a single real number, so it needs no choice of norm. The mechanism gives each object \(r\) a weight \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta))\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the privacy parameter and \(\Delta\) is any upper bound on the sensitivity \(\Delta u\). Division by the sum of all weights, the normalizer, turns the weights into probabilities. For an infinite set of objects, such as an interval of prices, the weights become a density. The sum then becomes an integral against a fixed base measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal R\), such as length on the real line.
For finite \(\mathcal R\), Equation 7.4 says that \(\Pr[M_E(D) = r]\) is proportional to \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta))\), so a higher score makes an object more likely. A smaller \(\varepsilon\) or a larger \(\Delta\) flattens the distribution towards uniform, which is more private and less accurate.
The definition says nothing about how to sample. For a finite set, you can compute every weight, add them up and sample, in time proportional to \(|\mathcal R|\), which is slow when \(\mathcal R\) is exponentially large. For an infinite set, the usual remedy is to discretize, as Section 7.4.2 does. So the exponential mechanism always gives an algorithm, but not always an efficient one.

title: 7  The Exponential Mechanism
text:
a dataset \(D \in \mathcal X^n\),
a set \(\mathcal R\) of objects,
a score function \(u\colon \mathcal X^n \times \mathcal R \to \mathbb R\), where \(u(D,r)\) says how good the object \(r\) is for the dataset \(D\).



Definition 7.1 (Sensitivity of a score function) The sensitivity of a score function \(u\) is
\[
\Delta u = \sup_{r \in \mathcal R}\ \sup_{D \sim D'} \big|u(D,r) - u(D',r)\big| ,
\tag{7.2}\]
where the inner supremum is over neighbouring datasets, which differ in one record (the replace-one relation).



Definition 7.2 (Exponential mechanism) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\), and let \(\Delta > 0\) satisfy \(\Delta \ge \Delta u\). Let \(\mu\) be a measure on \(\mathcal R\), taken to be the counting measure, which gives each object weight \(1\), when \(\mathcal R\) is finite. Assume that the normalizer
\[
Z(D) = \int_{\mathcal R} \exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon\, u(D,r')}{2\Delta}\right) \mu(\mathrm d r')
\tag{7.3}\]
is positive and finite for every \(D\). The exponential mechanism \(M_E\) outputs an object \(r \in \mathcal R\) drawn with density, with respect to \(\mu\),
\[
p_D(r) = \frac{1}{Z(D)}\exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon\, u(D,r)}{2\Delta}\right) .
\tag{7.4}\]

title: 7  The Exponential Mechanism
text:
7.2 Privacy
The score of \(r\) changes by at most \(\Delta\) between neighbours, so the weight of \(r\) changes by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\). The normalizer is a sum of such weights, so it also changes by at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), and the two factors together give \(e^\varepsilon\).

Theorem 7.1 The exponential mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an object \(r\). By Equation 7.4, the ratio of the densities is
\[
\frac{p_D(r)}{p_{D'}(r)} = \exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon\,(u(D,r) - u(D',r))}{2\Delta}\right)\cdot\frac{Z(D')}{Z(D)} .
\tag{7.5}\]
By Definition 7.1 and \(\Delta \ge \Delta u\), the difference \(u(D,r) - u(D',r)\) is at most \(\Delta\), so the first factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\).
For every object \(r'\), the same bound gives \(u(D',r') \le u(D,r') + \Delta\), so \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D',r')/(2\Delta)) \le e^{\varepsilon/2}\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r')/(2\Delta))\). Integrating over \(r'\) gives \(Z(D') \le e^{\varepsilon/2} Z(D)\), so the second factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\).
So \(p_D(r) \le e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(r)\) for every \(r\). For an event \(S \subseteq \mathcal R\), integrating over \(S\) gives \(\Pr[M_E(D)\in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M_E(D')\in S]\).


Step 3 spends the factor \(2\) in \(2\Delta\), because it pays for the change in the normalizer. When the normalizer does not depend on the dataset, that half of the budget is not needed.

Corollary 7.1 Suppose that \(Z(D)\), computed with \(\Delta\) in place of \(2\Delta\), is the same for every dataset \(D\). Then the mechanism with density proportional to \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/\Delta)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. In step 1 of the proof of Theorem 7.1, with \(\Delta\) in place of \(2\Delta\), the factor \(Z(D')/Z(D)\) equals \(1\), and the first factor is at most \(\exp(\varepsilon\Delta/\Delta) = e^\varepsilon\). Step 4 then applies unchanged.

title: 7  The Exponential Mechanism
text:
7.3 Utility
The mechanism should output an object whose score is close to the best one. Write the best score and the set of objects that attain it as
\[
\mathrm{OPT}(D) = \max_{r\in\mathcal R} u(D,r), \qquad \mathcal R^*(D) = \{r \in \mathcal R : u(D,r) = \mathrm{OPT}(D)\} .
\tag{7.6}\]
The theorem says that the output’s score is rarely more than about \((2\Delta/\varepsilon)\ln|\mathcal R|\) below \(\mathrm{OPT}(D)\). So the loss grows linearly with the sensitivity and with \(1/\varepsilon\), but only logarithmically with the number of objects.

Theorem 7.2 Let \(\mathcal R\) be finite. For every dataset \(D\) and every \(t \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr\left[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \mathrm{OPT}(D) - \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\frac{|\mathcal R|}{|\mathcal R^*(D)|} + t\right)\right] \le e^{-t} .
\tag{7.7}\]


Proof. 

Fix a threshold \(\tau\). The output has score at most \(\tau\) exactly when it is one of the objects with \(u(D,r) \le \tau\), so
\[
\Pr[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \tau] = \frac{\sum_{r : u(D,r)\le \tau}\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta))}{\sum_{r'\in\mathcal R}\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r')/(2\Delta))} .
\tag{7.8}\]
Numerator. There are at most \(|\mathcal R|\) terms, and each is at most \(\exp(\varepsilon \tau/(2\Delta))\) because its score is at most \(\tau\).
Denominator. Every term is positive, so keeping only the \(|\mathcal R^*(D)|\) terms with score \(\mathrm{OPT}(D)\) gives a lower bound of \(|\mathcal R^*(D)|\exp(\varepsilon\,\mathrm{OPT}(D)/(2\Delta))\).
Together, steps 2 and 3 give
\[
\Pr[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \tau] \le \frac{|\mathcal R|}{|\mathcal R^*(D)|}\exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon\,(\tau - \mathrm{OPT}(D))}{2\Delta}\right) .
\tag{7.9}\]
Set \(\tau = \mathrm{OPT}(D) - (2\Delta/\varepsilon)\big(\ln(|\mathcal R|/|\mathcal R^*(D)|) + t\big)\). The exponent becomes \(-\ln(|\mathcal R|/|\mathcal R^*(D)|) - t\), and the right-hand side becomes \(e^{-t}\).


Since at least one object attains the best score, dropping \(|\mathcal R^*(D)|\) gives the form that is used most often.

Corollary 7.2 Let \(\mathcal R\) be finite. For every dataset \(D\) and every \(t \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr\left[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \mathrm{OPT}(D) - \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\big(\ln|\mathcal R| + t\big)\right] \le e^{-t} .
\tag{7.10}\]


Proof. 

At least one object attains the best score, so \(|\mathcal R^*(D)| \ge 1\) and \(\ln(|\mathcal R|/|\mathcal R^*(D)|) \le \ln|\mathcal R|\). The threshold in Equation 7.10 is therefore at most the threshold of Theorem 7.2 for the same \(t\), so the event here is contained in the event there, and its probability is at most \(e^{-t}\).

title: 7  The Exponential Mechanism
text:
7.4 Applications
Each application below follows the same recipe. It chooses the set of objects and the score function, bounds the sensitivity, and reads off privacy and accuracy from Theorem 7.1 and Corollary 7.2.

7.4.1 The Laplace mechanism
Let \(f\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R\) have sensitivity \(\Delta f\), which means that \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \Delta f\) for all neighbours. Take the real line as the set of objects, with Lebesgue measure, and score each candidate answer by its distance from the true one,
\[
u(D, r) = -|f(D) - r| .
\tag{7.11}\]
By the triangle inequality, \(\big||f(D) - r| - |f(D') - r|\big| \le |f(D) - f(D')| \le \Delta f\), so \(\Delta u \le \Delta f\). With \(\Delta = \Delta f\), the density Equation 7.4 is proportional to \(\exp(-\varepsilon|f(D) - r|/(2\Delta f))\), which is the density of \(f(D)\) plus Laplace noise of scale \(2\Delta f/\varepsilon\). So the exponential mechanism contains a Laplace mechanism, but with twice the noise scale \(\Delta f/\varepsilon\) of the Laplace mechanism. Corollary 7.1 removes the extra factor.

Proposition 7.1 Let \(f\colon\mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R\) have sensitivity \(\Delta f > 0\). The mechanism that outputs \(f(D)\) plus noise from the Laplace distribution with scale \(\Delta f/\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

The output has density proportional to \(\exp(-\varepsilon|f(D) - r|/(\Delta f)) = \exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(\Delta f))\), with the score above, whose sensitivity is at most \(\Delta f\).
The normalizer is \(\int_{\mathbb R}\exp(-\varepsilon|f(D)-r|/(\Delta f))\,\mathrm d r = 2\Delta f/\varepsilon\), after the substitution \(u = r - f(D)\). It does not depend on \(D\).
Corollary 7.1, with \(\Delta = \Delta f\), applies and gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.




7.4.2 Pricing a digital good
Return to the seller of Section 7.1, now with a dataset of valuations \(D = (v_1,\dots,v_n) \in [0,1]^n\) and prices in \([0,1]\). Write \(\gamma\) for the best revenue over all prices,
\[
\gamma = \max_{p\in[0,1]} p\cdot|\{i : v_i \ge p\}| .
\tag{7.12}\]
The maximum exists, because the revenue increases linearly between consecutive valuations and drops just after each one, so it is attained at one of the \(v_i\) or at \(0\).
The set of all prices is infinite, and the revenue has no structure that makes sampling easy, so the mechanism runs on a grid. Fix an integer \(m \ge 1\) and the step \(\alpha = 1/m\), and use the \(m\) prices
\[
\mathcal R = \{\alpha, 2\alpha, \dots, 1\} .
\tag{7.13}\]
Write \(\mathrm{OPT}(D)\) for the best revenue over the grid. Rounding the best price down to the grid loses a little revenue, which the next lemma bounds.

Lemma 7.1 The best revenue on the grid satisfies \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) \ge \gamma - \alpha n\).


Proof. 

Let \(p^*\) attain \(\gamma\). If \(p^* < \alpha\), then \(\gamma \le p^* n < \alpha n\), so \(\gamma - \alpha n < 0\). Revenue is never negative, so \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) \ge 0 > \gamma - \alpha n\).
Otherwise, round \(p^*\) down to the grid, \(p' = \alpha\lfloor p^*/\alpha\rfloor \in \mathcal R\), so that \(p^* - \alpha < p' \le p^*\).
Every buyer with \(v_i \ge p^*\) also has \(v_i \ge p'\). So the revenue at \(p'\) is at least \(p'\cdot|\{i : v_i\ge p^*\}| \ge (p^* - \alpha)|\{i : v_i\ge p^*\}| \ge \gamma - \alpha n\).


So the private price loses revenue twice, once to rounding and once to the random selection. The theorem adds the two losses, with a grid of about \(\varepsilon n\) prices.

Theorem 7.3 Let \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(m = \lceil \varepsilon n\rceil\) and \(\alpha = 1/m\). The exponential mechanism with the grid \(\mathcal R\), the revenue \(u(D,p) = p\cdot|\{i : v_i \ge p\}|\) as score and \(\Delta = 1\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. For every \(D\in[0,1]^n\) and \(t \ge 0\), with probability at least \(1 - e^{-t}\), the revenue at its output price is at least
\[
\gamma - \frac{1 + 2\ln\lceil\varepsilon n\rceil + 2t}{\varepsilon} .
\tag{7.14}\]


Proof. 

Sensitivity. Changing one valuation changes the number of buyers at any price \(p\) by at most \(1\), and \(p \le 1\). So \(\Delta u \le 1 = \Delta\), and Theorem 7.1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Selection. By Corollary 7.2 with \(|\mathcal R| = m\), with probability at least \(1 - e^{-t}\) the output has revenue at least \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) - (2/\varepsilon)(\ln m + t)\).
Discretization. By Lemma 7.1, \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) \ge \gamma - n/m\), and \(n/m \le n/(\varepsilon n) = 1/\varepsilon\) because \(m \ge \varepsilon n\).
Adding the two losses gives Equation 7.14.


The loss is \(O(\log(\varepsilon n)/\varepsilon)\). When a constant fraction of buyers values the good above a constant price, \(\gamma\) grows linearly in \(n\), so the loss is a vanishing fraction of the best revenue. The grid size balances the two losses: a finer grid loses less to rounding, \(\alpha n\), but more to selection, \((2/\varepsilon)\ln(1/\alpha)\). The next example compares the guarantee with the revenue the mechanism actually earns.

Example 7.1 Draw \(n = 1{,}000\) valuations uniformly from \([0,1]\) and take \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), so that the grid has \(m = 500\) prices. The best revenue is \(\gamma = 267.40\), and the best grid price earns \(266.88\). With \(t = \ln 20\), Equation 7.14 guarantees a revenue of at least \(267.40 - 38.84 = 228.56\) with probability \(0.95\). The exact output distribution does much better. Its mean revenue is \(263.86\), and its 5th percentile is \(256.52\), a loss of \(10.88\), so the guarantee is about 3.6 times too pessimistic. Figure 7.1 shows the output distribution on a smaller example.







Figure 7.1: The exponential mechanism for pricing, with \(200\) buyers whose valuations are uniform on \([0,1]\) and a grid of \(200\) prices. Top, the revenue. Bottom, the probability of each output price for \(\varepsilon = 0.2\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). A larger \(\varepsilon\) puts more weight on prices near the best revenue.





7.4.3 Private PAC learning
In the probably approximately correct (PAC) model of learning, a learner sees labelled records and must output a classifier that is accurate on new points from the same source. Here the records are points of the Boolean cube \(\{0,1\}^d\), labelled \(0\) or \(1\). The definition measures accuracy by an error \(\alpha\) and a failure probability \(\beta\), so in this section \(\alpha\) is no longer the grid step of the pricing example.

Definition 7.3 (PAC learning) A concept class is a finite set \(\mathcal C\) of functions \(c\colon\{0,1\}^d\to\{0,1\}\). An unknown target \(c^* \in \mathcal C\) and an unknown distribution \(\mathcal D\) on \(\{0,1\}^d\) generate the dataset. Each record is a point \(x_i\), drawn independently from \(\mathcal D\), together with its label \(y_i = c^*(x_i)\). So the dataset is \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\) with labelled records \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\). The error of a function \(h\) is
\[
\mathrm{err}(h) = \Pr_{x\sim \mathcal D}[h(x) \ne c^*(x)] .
\tag{7.15}\]
A learner is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-accurate if, for every target and every \(\mathcal D\), it outputs a function \(\hat h\) with \(\mathrm{err}(\hat h) \le \alpha\) with probability at least \(1-\beta\).

For example, \(\mathcal C\) might be a finite set of half-spaces, each of which labels \(1\) the points on one side of a hyperplane.
Without privacy, the classic learner outputs any function in \(\mathcal C\) that labels every record correctly, and one exists because the target does. It works because, for every function at once, the fraction of mistakes on the sample is close to the error. Write that fraction as
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h) = \frac1n\big|\{i : h(x_i)\ne y_i\}\big| .
\tag{7.16}\]
The tool is Hoeffding’s inequality: the average of \(n\) independent random variables with values in \([0,1]\) falls below its mean by a margin \(s \ge 0\) or more with probability at most \(\exp(-2ns^2)\). Applied to the mistakes of one function, with a union bound over \(\mathcal C\), it shows that the sample error is close to the true error for every function at once.

Lemma 7.2 Let \(\alpha, \beta \in (0,1)\) and \(n \ge 2\ln(|\mathcal C|/\beta)/\alpha^2\). With probability at least \(1-\beta\) over the sample, every \(h\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(\mathrm{err}(h) \le \widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h) + \alpha/2\). In particular, every function in \(\mathcal C\) that labels the whole sample correctly has error at most \(\alpha/2\).


Proof. 

Fix \(h \in \mathcal C\). The indicators \(W_i = \mathbf 1[h(x_i)\ne c^*(x_i)]\) are independent, lie in \([0,1]\), and have mean \(\mathrm{err}(h)\), because the \(x_i\) are independent draws from \(\mathcal D\). Their average is \(\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h)\).
Hoeffding’s inequality with \(s = \alpha/2\) gives \(\Pr[\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h) \le \mathrm{err}(h) - \alpha/2] \le \exp(-n\alpha^2/2) \le \beta/|\mathcal C|\), by the bound on \(n\).
A union bound over the \(|\mathcal C|\) functions shows that some \(h\) fails with probability at most \(\beta\).
A function that labels the sample correctly has \(\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h) = 0\), so its error is at most \(\alpha/2\).


So about \(\ln|\mathcal C|/\alpha^2\) records suffice.
For privacy, neighbouring datasets differ in one labelled record: any pair \(z_i' = (x_i', y_i')\) can replace \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\). The new point need not come from \(\mathcal D\), and its label need not equal \(c^*(x_i')\). Accuracy is proved for data drawn from the model, but privacy must hold for every dataset, so that a wrong model never costs anyone their privacy.
The private learner keeps the aim of few mistakes on the sample, but chooses the function with the exponential mechanism. Its score is minus the sample error, so a function with fewer mistakes is more likely.

Theorem 7.4 (Private PAC learning) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)\). Run the exponential mechanism with \(\mathcal R = \mathcal C\), the score \(u(D,h) = -\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h)\) and \(\Delta = 1/n\). It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset. If
\[
n \ge \frac{2\ln(2|\mathcal C|/\beta)}{\alpha^2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad n \ge \frac{4\ln(2|\mathcal C|/\beta)}{\alpha\varepsilon},
\tag{7.17}\]
then it is an \((\alpha,\beta)\)-accurate learner.


Proof. 

Privacy. Replacing one labelled record changes the number of mistakes of each \(h\) by at most \(1\), so \(\Delta u \le 1/n\). Theorem 7.1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP for all datasets, whatever their labels.
Selection. The target makes no mistakes, so \(\mathrm{OPT} = 0\). By Corollary 7.2 with \(t = \ln(2/\beta)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta/2\) over the mechanism’s coins, the output \(\hat h\) has
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(\hat h) \le \frac{2}{\varepsilon n}\big(\ln|\mathcal C| + \ln(2/\beta)\big) = \frac{2\ln(2|\mathcal C|/\beta)}{\varepsilon n} \le \frac\alpha2 ,
\tag{7.18}\]
where the last step uses the second bound on \(n\).
Generalization. The first bound on \(n\) is the condition of Lemma 7.2 with \(\beta/2\) in place of \(\beta\). So with probability at least \(1-\beta/2\) over the sample, every \(h\in\mathcal C\), including \(\hat h\), has \(\mathrm{err}(h)\le\widehat{\mathrm{err}}(h)+\alpha/2\).
By a union bound, both events hold with probability at least \(1-\beta\), and then \(\mathrm{err}(\hat h) \le \alpha/2 + \alpha/2 = \alpha\).


The first bound on \(n\) is what learning needs without privacy, and the second is the cost of privacy. Both are logarithmic in \(|\mathcal C|\), and for \(\varepsilon\) of constant size and small \(\alpha\), the cost of privacy is a lower-order term. For instance, with \(|\mathcal C| = 2^{20}\), \(\alpha = \beta = 0.05\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), we have \(\ln(2|\mathcal C|/\beta) = 17.552\), and the two bounds are \(14{,}041\) and \(1{,}404\). The price is computation, because the mechanism scores every function in \(\mathcal C\).

title: Query Release and Its Limits
text:
The second part built mechanisms that answer one question, or a few, under differential privacy (DP). This part asks what happens when an analyst wants many answers from the same dataset. Its first two chapters answer many queries for far less than one budget share per query. The third chapter lets the noise follow the dataset at hand instead of the worst case. The last proves that, under pure DP, no mechanism can do much better than the simple ones on marginals and histograms.



Table 1: The chapters of this part.





Chapter
Question it answers




Private multiplicative weights
How many records are needed to answer a large set of linear queries at once?


Sparse vector
How can a stream of queries be answered when the cost should depend only on the few large ones?


Beyond global sensitivity
When can the noise follow the sensitivity of the actual dataset instead of the worst case?


Packing lower bounds
How much error must any pure DP mechanism incur on marginals and histograms?

title: 8  Private Multiplicative Weights
text:
8.1 Linear queries
An analyst wants the answers to many statistical queries about a dataset, such as the fraction of records in each cell of a table. Independent noise on each answer makes the error grow polynomially with the number of queries. Under approximate differential privacy (DP), this chapter does much better. The number of records it needs grows only with the logarithm of the number of queries and of the size of the universe. The algorithm, private multiplicative weights, comes from online learning. It learns a distribution over the universe that agrees with the data on every query, and it reads the data only through a few private measurements.
Records take values in a set \(\mathcal X\), the universe, and a dataset is a list of \(n\) records. A linear query asks for the average of a bounded function over the records.
A counting query is the special case where \(q\) takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\), and two families of counting queries come up often. In a histogram, there is one query \(q_s(x) = \mathbf 1[x = s]\) for each element \(s\) of the universe, so the answers are the fractions of records equal to each \(s\). In one-way marginals, the universe is \(\{0,1\}^d\), and the query \(q_j(x) = x_j\) for each coordinate \(j\) gives the fraction of records with feature \(j\) set to \(1\). This chapter allows any finite set of linear queries, however irregular.
The analyst wants every query in the set answered at once, so accuracy is the worst error over the set. A mechanism succeeds if, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\), no answer is off by more than a target error \(\alpha\).
The question is how large \(n\) must be for a private mechanism to do this. The sample sizes below are sufficient conditions, and smaller is better.
The first answer uses only earlier chapters. Changing one record changes a linear query by at most \(1/n\), so its sensitivity, the largest change over neighbouring datasets, is at most \(1/n\). The Laplace mechanism adds noise from the Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) of scale \(b\), whose density at \(z\) is \(e^{-|z|/b}/(2b)\). It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP when \(b\) is the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\), and its tails are \(\Pr[|\mathrm{Lap}(b)| \ge tb] = e^{-t}\) for \(t \ge 0\). Independent Laplace noise on every query in \(\mathcal Q\), with the budget split evenly among them, gives the baseline that the rest of the chapter improves on.
Approximate DP does better, through the advanced composition theorem. That theorem implies that \(k\) mechanisms run in sequence, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP and each possibly chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, are together \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with
\[
\varepsilon' = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} + k\varepsilon_0\left(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1\right).
\tag{8.4}\]
To use the theorem, one starts from a target budget \(\varepsilon\) and asks how much each of the \(k\) mechanisms may spend. The next lemma gives a per-mechanism budget \(\varepsilon_0\) that keeps \(\varepsilon'\) at most \(\varepsilon\). It is the budget-splitting corollary of that chapter, proved again here for the form Equation 8.4.
With one Laplace mechanism per query, so \(k = |\mathcal Q|\), the lemma lets each query spend a budget of order \(\varepsilon/\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\) instead of \(\varepsilon/|\mathcal Q|\). So the factor \(|\mathcal Q|\) in the baseline becomes \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\).
The Gaussian mechanism with advanced composition does a little better, \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|\ln|\mathcal Q|\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\), because its lighter tails make the union bound cost \(\sqrt{\ln|\mathcal Q|}\) instead of \(\ln|\mathcal Q|\). These bounds are polynomial in \(|\mathcal Q|\), and in the worst case over query sets nothing better is possible. A smaller universe helps, though, as Table 8.1 shows, up to constants.
The noisy histogram releases one noisy count per element of the universe and answers every query from it. So it pays polynomially in \(|\mathcal X|\), which is \(2^d\) for \(d\) binary features. The fourth row is logarithmic in both \(|\mathcal Q|\) and \(|\mathcal X|\), but its running time is \(|\mathcal X|^{O(\ln|\mathcal Q|/\alpha^2)}\). Private multiplicative weights keeps both logarithms and runs in time polynomial in \(|\mathcal Q|\), \(|\mathcal X|\) and \(n\). This one outputs synthetic data, and for such algorithms that is close to the best possible under standard cryptographic assumptions.

title: 8  Private Multiplicative Weights
text:
Definition 8.1 (Linear query) A linear query is a function \(q \colon \mathcal X \to [0,1]\) on the universe. On a dataset \(D \in \mathcal X^n\) with records \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) it takes the value
\[
q(D) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n q(x_i).
\tag{8.1}\]




Definition 8.2 (Query release) Let \(\mathcal Q\) be a finite set of linear queries, \(\alpha \in (0,1]\) a target error and \(\beta \in (0,1)\) a failure probability. A mechanism \(M \colon \mathcal X^n \to [0,1]^{\mathcal Q}\) outputs one answer \(M(D)_q\) for each query \(q \in \mathcal Q\). It answers \(\mathcal Q\) to accuracy \(\alpha\) with probability \(1-\beta\) if, for every dataset \(D\),
\[
\Pr\Big[\max_{q \in \mathcal Q} |M(D)_q - q(D)| \le \alpha\Big] \ge 1 - \beta .
\tag{8.2}\]




Proposition 8.1 (Laplace baseline) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\). Release \(M(D)_q = q(D) + Z_q\) for every \(q \in \mathcal Q\), with independent \(Z_q \sim \mathrm{Lap}(|\mathcal Q|/(\varepsilon n))\). This mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and it answers \(\mathcal Q\) to accuracy \(\alpha\) with probability \(1-\beta\) whenever
\[
n \ge \frac{|\mathcal Q|\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)}{\alpha\varepsilon} .
\tag{8.3}\]


Proof. 

The vector \((q(D))_{q\in \mathcal Q}\) changes by at most \(1/n\) in each of its \(|\mathcal Q|\) coordinates when one record changes, so its \(\ell_1\) sensitivity is at most \(|\mathcal Q|/n\). The Laplace mechanism with scale \(|\mathcal Q|/(\varepsilon n)\) is therefore \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Write \(b = |\mathcal Q|/(\varepsilon n)\) and \(t = \ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)\). By the tail formula and a union bound over the \(|\mathcal Q|\) coordinates, \(\Pr[\max_q |Z_q| \ge tb] \le |\mathcal Q|e^{-t} = \beta\).
The condition on \(n\) says exactly that \(tb \le \alpha\). So with probability at least \(1-\beta\), every error is below \(\alpha\).






Lemma 8.1 (Splitting a budget) Let \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\), \(\delta \in (0,1/2]\) and \(k \ge 1\). The adaptive composition of \(k\) mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}},
\tag{8.5}\]
is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

The first term of Equation 8.4 is \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} = \varepsilon/2\).
Since \(\ln(1/\delta) \ge \ln 2\), \(\varepsilon \le 1\) and \(k\ge1\), we have \(\varepsilon_0 \le 1\). The function \(e^x\) is convex, so \(e^x - 1\) lies below the chord \((e-1)x \le 2x\) on \([0,1]\). Hence the second term is at most \(2k\varepsilon_0^2 = \varepsilon^2/(4\ln(1/\delta))\).
That is at most \(\varepsilon/2\) because \(\varepsilon \le 1 \le 2\ln 2 \le 2\ln(1/\delta)\). Adding the two terms gives \(\varepsilon' \le \varepsilon\).




Proposition 8.2 (Laplace with advanced composition) Let \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\), \(\delta \in (0,1/2]\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\). Release \(M(D)_q = q(D) + Z_q\) with independent \(Z_q \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon_0 n))\), where \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2|\mathcal Q|\ln(1/\delta)})\). This mechanism is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, and it answers \(\mathcal Q\) to accuracy \(\alpha\) with probability \(1-\beta\) whenever
\[
n \ge \frac{2\sqrt{2|\mathcal Q|\ln(1/\delta)}\,\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)}{\alpha\varepsilon} .
\tag{8.6}\]


Proof. 

Each coordinate is the Laplace mechanism for a query of sensitivity \(1/n\), so it is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP. Lemma 8.1 with \(k = |\mathcal Q|\) makes the whole release \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.
As in Proposition 8.1, \(\Pr[\max_q|Z_q| \ge \ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)/(\varepsilon_0 n)] \le \beta\), and the condition on \(n\) says that \(\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)/(\varepsilon_0 n) \le \alpha\).






Table 8.1: Sufficient sample sizes for answering every query in \(\mathcal Q\) to accuracy \(\alpha\).










Method

\(\lvert \mathcal Q\rvert\ln\lvert \mathcal Q\rvert/(\alpha\varepsilon)\), improvable to \(\lvert \mathcal Q\rvert/(\alpha\varepsilon)\)

title: 8  Private Multiplicative Weights
text:
8.2 Learning from experts
Multiplicative weights is an algorithm for a game of repeated predictions, which has nothing to do with privacy. This section develops it from the simplest case.
A group of \(N\) experts makes predictions over \(T\) days. Each day, every expert predicts whether a stock goes up or down, and the algorithm sees these predictions before it makes its own. Then the true outcome is revealed, and a wrong prediction counts as a mistake. Suppose first that one expert, whose identity is unknown, is always right. Then the algorithm can stop listening to any expert as soon as it errs.

Proposition 8.3 (Halving) Predict with the majority of the experts that have never erred, breaking ties towards “down”, and discard every expert that errs. If some expert never errs, this algorithm makes at most \(\log_2 N\) mistakes.


Proof. 

Let \(S^t\) be the set of experts still kept on day \(t\), so \(|S^1| = N\).
On a day with a mistake, the experts who predicted like the algorithm are wrong. They are at least half of \(S^t\), because the algorithm followed the majority. All of them are discarded, so \(|S^{t+1}| \le |S^t|/2\).
The perfect expert is never discarded, so \(|S^t| \ge 1\) on every day. After \(M\) mistakes, \(1 \le N/2^M\), so \(M \le \log_2 N\).


The algorithm is measured against the best expert in hindsight. Its regret is its total loss minus the total loss of the best single expert. Here the best expert makes no mistakes, so the regret is at most \(\log_2 N\).
Now suppose instead that the best expert makes \(\mathrm{OPT}\) mistakes. Then halving fails, because the best expert may err on the first day and be discarded, after which the rest may all be wrong forever. The repair is to lower trust instead of removing it.

Proposition 8.4 (Weighted majority) Give each expert weight \(1\). Each day, predict with the side whose experts have the larger total weight, breaking ties towards “down”, and then halve the weight of every expert that erred. If the best expert makes \(\mathrm{OPT}\) mistakes, the algorithm makes \(M\) mistakes with
\[
M \le \frac{\mathrm{OPT} + \log_2 N}{\log_2(4/3)} \le 2.41\left(\mathrm{OPT} + \log_2 N\right).
\tag{8.7}\]


Proof. 

Let \(W^t\) be the total weight at the start of day \(t\), so \(W^1 = N\). Weights never increase.
Upper bound. On a day with a mistake, the side the algorithm followed carries at least half of \(W^t\), and all of its weight is halved. So \(W^{t+1} \le W^t - W^t/4 = \tfrac34 W^t\). Over \(T\) days, \(W^{T+1} \le N(3/4)^M\).
Lower bound. The best expert’s weight is halved exactly \(\mathrm{OPT}\) times, so \(W^{T+1} \ge (1/2)^{\mathrm{OPT}}\).
Combining the bounds gives \((4/3)^M \le N\,2^{\mathrm{OPT}}\). Taking \(\log_2\) of both sides gives the first inequality, and \(1/\log_2(4/3) = 2.409\ldots\) gives the second.


The guarantee is competitive with the best expert, but its regret, \(1.41\,\mathrm{OPT} + 2.41\log_2 N\), grows with \(\mathrm{OPT}\). A randomized algorithm with gentler updates removes the factor in front of \(\mathrm{OPT}\).
The general game has losses instead of mistakes. In each of \(T\) rounds, every expert \(i\) suffers a loss \(\ell^t_i \in [-1,1]\), chosen by an adversary, and a negative loss is a gain. A randomized algorithm picks one expert and suffers the loss of that expert. It is cleaner to let the algorithm pick a distribution \(p^t\) over the experts and suffer the average loss \(\ell^t \cdot p^t = \sum_i p^t_i \ell^t_i\). Multiplicative weights keeps one weight per expert and plays the distribution proportional to the weights. After each round it multiplies each weight by a factor that falls as the loss of that expert rises.

Definition 8.3 (Multiplicative weights) Fix a learning rate \(\eta \in (0, 1/2]\). Start with weights \(w^1_i = 1\) for \(i = 1, \dots, N\). In round \(t = 1, 2, \dots\):

Play the distribution \(p^t_i = w^t_i / W^t\), where \(W^t = \sum_{i=1}^N w^t_i\).
Observe the loss vector \(\ell^t \in [-1,1]^N\), which may depend on \(p^1, \dots, p^t\), and suffer \(\ell^t\cdot p^t\).
Update \(w^{t+1}_i = w^t_i\,(1 - \eta\ell^t_i)\) for every \(i\).


The factor \(1 - \eta\ell^t_i\) lies in \([1/2, 3/2]\), so the weights stay positive, and an expert with a positive loss loses weight while one with a negative loss gains it. The analysis takes the logarithm of the total weight, which turns the products of factors \(1 - \eta\ell^t_i\) into sums of \(\ln(1 - \eta\ell^t_i)\). So it needs two bounds on that logarithm, one from above and one from below.

Lemma 8.2 For every \(x < 1\), \(\ln(1-x) \le -x\). For every \(x \in [-1/2, 1/2]\), \(\ln(1-x) \ge -x - x^2\).


Proof. 

The function \(\ln(1-x)\) is concave, so it lies below its tangent line at \(0\), which is \(-x\).
Let \(h(x) = \ln(1-x) + x + x^2\). Then \(h(0) = 0\) and \(h'(x) = -\frac{1}{1-x} + 1 + 2x = \frac{x(1-2x)}{1-x}\).
On \([0,1/2]\), \(h' \ge 0\), so \(h(x) \ge h(0) = 0\). On \([-1/2,0]\), \(h' \le 0\), so \(h\) decreases to \(h(0) = 0\) and is non-negative there too.


The main result compares the total loss of multiplicative weights with the total loss of any fixed distribution \(p\) chosen in hindsight. The difference is the regret, and the theorem bounds it by a term that grows with \(\eta\) and a term that shrinks with it.

Theorem 8.1 (Regret of multiplicative weights) Let \(p^1, p^2, \dots\) be the distributions that multiplicative weights plays. For every learning rate \(\eta \in (0,1/2]\), every number of rounds \(T \ge 1\), every sequence of loss vectors \(\ell^1, \dots, \ell^T\) in \([-1,1]^N\) and every fixed distribution \(p\) over the experts,
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \ell^t\cdot p^t \le \sum_{t=1}^T \ell^t\cdot p + \eta T + \frac{\ln N}{\eta}.
\tag{8.8}\]
If \(N \ge 2\), \(T \ge 4\ln N\) and \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N / T}\), the last two terms add up to \(2\sqrt{T\ln N}\).


Proof. 

Upper bound on the total weight. By the update rule and \(p^t_i = w^t_i/W^t\),

\[
W^{t+1} = \sum_{i=1}^N w^t_i(1 - \eta\ell^t_i) = W^t\left(1 - \eta\,\ell^t\cdot p^t\right).
\tag{8.9}\]
Unrolling from \(W^1 = N\) and applying the first bound of Lemma 8.2 to each factor,
\[
\ln W^{T+1} = \ln N + \sum_{t=1}^T \ln\left(1 - \eta\,\ell^t\cdot p^t\right) \le \ln N - \eta\sum_{t=1}^T \ell^t\cdot p^t .
\tag{8.10}\]

Lower bound through one expert. The total weight is at least the weight of any expert \(i\). Each \(\eta\ell^t_i\) lies in \([-1/2,1/2]\), so the second bound of Lemma 8.2 applies, and \((\ell^t_i)^2 \le 1\):

\[
\ln W^{T+1} \ge \ln w^{T+1}_i = \sum_{t=1}^T \ln(1-\eta\ell^t_i) \ge -\eta\sum_{t=1}^T \ell^t_i - \eta^2 T .
\tag{8.11}\]

Lower bound through a distribution. Multiply the inequality of step 2 by \(p_i\) and sum over \(i\). The weights \(p_i\) sum to \(1\), so \(\ln W^{T+1} \ge -\eta\sum_t \ell^t\cdot p - \eta^2T\).
Combining steps 1 and 3 gives \(-\eta\sum_t \ell^t\cdot p - \eta^2 T \le \ln N - \eta\sum_t \ell^t\cdot p^t\). Dividing by \(\eta\) and rearranging gives Equation 8.8.
With \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\), both \(\eta T\) and \(\ln N/\eta\) equal \(\sqrt{T\ln N}\). The condition \(N \ge 2\) makes \(\eta > 0\), and \(T \ge 4\ln N\) makes \(\eta \le 1/2\).


The regret is of order \(\sqrt T\), while the losses themselves can add up to order \(T\). So on average over rounds the algorithm does as well as the best fixed distribution, up to a term that vanishes as \(\sqrt{\ln N/T}\). With \(p\) a point mass, the distribution that puts all its weight on one expert, the theorem covers the randomized algorithm that picks one expert.

Corollary 8.1 Let \(N \ge 2\). Fix losses \(\ell^1, \dots, \ell^T \in [-1,1]^N\) in advance, with \(T \ge 4\ln N\), and let \(L_i = \sum_t \ell^t_i\). Pick expert \(i_t\) with probability \(p^t_{i_t}\), where \(p^t\) comes from Definition 8.3 with \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\). Then
\[
\mathbb E\Big[\sum_{t=1}^T \ell^t_{i_t}\Big] \le \min_i L_i + 2\sqrt{T\ln N}.
\tag{8.12}\]


Proof. The losses are fixed, so each \(p^t\) is fixed too, and \(\mathbb E[\ell^t_{i_t}] = \ell^t\cdot p^t\). Sum over \(t\) and apply Theorem 8.1 with \(p\) the point mass on the best expert.

title: 8  Private Multiplicative Weights
text:
8.3 Multiplicative weights for queries
To use the game for query release, the experts become the elements of the universe, and the distribution \(p^t\) becomes a candidate dataset. To compare a candidate with the true dataset, we also write the true dataset as a distribution over the universe.

Definition 8.4 (Histogram of a dataset) The histogram of \(D \in \mathcal X^n\) is the distribution \(p_D\) on \(\mathcal X\) with \(p_D(x) = |\{i : x_i = x\}|/n\), the fraction of records equal to \(x\). For a linear query \(q\) and a distribution \(p\) on \(\mathcal X\), write \(\langle q, p\rangle = \sum_{x\in\mathcal X} q(x)p(x)\).

Grouping the records by value gives \(q(D) = \langle q, p_D\rangle\). So answering the queries means finding a distribution \(\hat p\) with \(\langle q, \hat p\rangle\) close to \(\langle q, p_D\rangle\) for every \(q \in \mathcal Q\).
Picture a game in rounds. An adversary picks a query \(q^t \in \mathcal Q\) after the algorithm commits to a distribution \(p^t\), and the algorithm pays its error \(|\langle q^t,p^t\rangle - \langle q^t,p_D\rangle|\). This looks pointless, since the algorithm could play \(p^t = p_D\) from the start. But that move reads the whole dataset, while multiplicative weights reads it only through one query per round and the sign of its error, which are cheap to privatize. And a bound on the total error turns into a bound on the number of rounds with a large error, as shown below.
The loss vector comes from the error itself. Write the error as a function of the candidate, \(f(p') = |\langle q^t, p'\rangle - \langle q^t, p_D\rangle|\). This function is convex, and \(f(p_D) = 0\). Where the error is not zero, its gradient at \(p^t\) is \(s_t q^t\), where \(s_t\) is the sign of \(\langle q^t, p^t - p_D\rangle\), taken as \(+1\) at \(0\). So the loss vector to feed the experts is \(\ell^t = s_t q^t\), and the next lemma shows that it measures the error exactly.

Lemma 8.3 Let \(q\) be a linear query, \(p'\) and \(p\) distributions on \(\mathcal X\), and \(s\) the sign of \(\langle q, p' - p\rangle\), with \(s = +1\) if it is \(0\). The vector \(\ell = s q\) lies in \([-1,1]^{\mathcal X}\), and
\[
\ell\cdot(p' - p) = |\langle q, p'\rangle - \langle q, p\rangle| .
\tag{8.13}\]


Proof. The entries of \(q\) lie in \([0,1]\), so those of \(sq\) lie in \([-1,1]\). By linearity, \(\ell\cdot(p'-p) = s\langle q, p'-p\rangle\), which is the absolute value of \(\langle q, p'-p\rangle\) by the choice of \(s\).

With these losses, the regret of multiplicative weights against the fixed distribution \(p_D\) is exactly the total error of the candidates. So the regret bound also bounds that total.

Theorem 8.2 Run multiplicative weights over the experts \(\mathcal X\) with learning rate \(\eta \in (0,1/2]\), and let \(p^t\) be the distribution it plays in round \(t\). Feed it the losses \(\ell^t = s_tq^t\), where \(q^1, q^2, \dots\) are any queries in \(\mathcal Q\) and \(s_t\) is the sign of \(\langle q^t, p^t - p_D\rangle\). After any number \(U\) of rounds,
\[
\sum_{t=1}^U |\langle q^t,p^t\rangle - q^t(D)| \le \eta U + \frac{\ln|\mathcal X|}{\eta} .
\tag{8.14}\]
With \(|\mathcal X| \ge 2\), \(U \ge 4\ln|\mathcal X|\) and \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln|\mathcal X|/U}\), the right-hand side is \(2\sqrt{U\ln|\mathcal X|}\).


Proof. By Lemma 8.3, the left-hand side equals \(\sum_t \ell^t\cdot p^t - \sum_t\ell^t\cdot p_D\). Apply Theorem 8.1 with \(N = |\mathcal X|\) and the fixed distribution \(p = p_D\).

This bounds a total, while the goal is one distribution that is accurate on every query. Call round \(t\) a mistake if the error there exceeds \(\alpha\). If the adversary always picks a query on which the current distribution makes a mistake, the total grows by more than \(\alpha\) per round, while the regret bound grows only by \(\eta\) per round. So the mistakes cannot go on for long. To use this, the algorithm plays the adversary against itself and always chooses the hardest query it can find.

Definition 8.5 (Multiplicative weights for queries) Given \(D\), \(\mathcal Q\) and \(\alpha \in (0,1]\), set \(\eta = \alpha/2\) and let \(p^1\) be uniform on \(\mathcal X\). In round \(t = 1, 2, \dots\):

If \(|\langle q, p^t\rangle - q(D)| \le \alpha\) for every \(q \in \mathcal Q\), output \(p^t\) and stop.
Otherwise pick \(q^t \in \mathcal Q\) with \(|\langle q^t, p^t\rangle - q^t(D)| > \alpha\), and let \(s_t\) be the sign of \(\langle q^t, p^t\rangle - q^t(D)\).
Update \(p^{t+1}(x) \propto p^t(x)\left(1 - \eta s_tq^t(x)\right)\).


In step 3, the symbol \(\propto\) means that the right-hand side is divided by its sum over \(x\), so that \(p^{t+1}\) is again a distribution. Every update adds more than \(\alpha\) to the total error, while the bound on that total grows by only \(\eta = \alpha/2\) per round. So the updates must stop soon.

Corollary 8.2 (Mistake bound) Let \(|\mathcal X| \ge 2\). The algorithm of Definition 8.5 stops after fewer than \(4\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2\) updates, and its output \(\hat p\) satisfies \(|\langle q,\hat p\rangle - q(D)| \le \alpha\) for every \(q \in \mathcal Q\).


Proof. 

The algorithm is multiplicative weights with \(\eta = \alpha/2 \le 1/2\) and the losses of Theorem 8.2, since normalizing the weights gives the update in step 3.
Suppose it makes \(U\) updates. Each of them has error above \(\alpha\), so by Theorem 8.2

\[
\alpha U < \frac{\alpha}{2}U + \frac{2\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad U < \frac{4\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha^2}.
\tag{8.15}\]

So the algorithm stops, which happens only at step 1, where every query is within \(\alpha\).


The bound is a worst case, and Figure 8.1 runs the algorithm on a small example where the number of updates stays far below it.






Figure 8.1: Multiplicative weights for queries on the universe \(\{0,1\}^8\), with the 128 one-way and two-way marginal queries \(\mathbf 1[x_j = a]\) and \(\mathbf 1[x_j = a, x_k = b]\). The dataset has 2,000 records whose eight features copy a hidden fair bit with probability \(0.8\). Each round picks the query with the largest error. The algorithm stops after about 700 updates for \(\alpha = 0.05\) and about 2,000 for \(\alpha = 0.02\), against the bounds \(4\ln 256/\alpha^2\) of 8,872 and 55,452.

title: 8  Private Multiplicative Weights
text:
8.4 Private multiplicative weights
The algorithm of Definition 8.5 reads the data in two places: it picks a query with a large error, and it reads the sign of that error. Both have private versions. The exponential mechanism picks a query with nearly the largest error, and the Laplace mechanism can measure the error itself, which has sensitivity \(1/n\).
The exponential mechanism takes a finite set \(\mathcal R\) of candidates and a score \(u(D, r)\) whose sensitivity in \(D\) is at most \(\Delta\) for each \(r\). It outputs \(r\) with probability proportional to \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta))\). It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and for every \(t \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr\Big[u(D,\hat r) \le \max_{r\in \mathcal R} u(D,r) - \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\big(\ln|\mathcal R| + t\big)\Big] \le e^{-t},
\tag{8.16}\]
where \(\hat r\) is its output.
The private algorithm replaces the two steps of Definition 8.5 that read the data by these two mechanisms. It also fixes the number of rounds \(T\) in advance, so that the privacy budget can be split among them.

Definition 8.6 (Private multiplicative weights) The inputs are a dataset \(D\in\mathcal X^n\), a finite set \(\mathcal Q\) of linear queries, an accuracy \(\alpha \in (0,1]\) and privacy parameters \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1/2]\). Set
\[
T = \left\lceil \frac{64\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha^2}\right\rceil, \qquad \eta = \frac\alpha8, \qquad \varepsilon_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{4\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)}},
\tag{8.17}\]
and let \(p^1\) be uniform on \(\mathcal X\). In round \(t = 1, \dots, T\):

Choose \(q^t \in \mathcal Q\) with the exponential mechanism, with privacy parameter \(\varepsilon_0\) and score \(u_t(D,q) = |\langle q, p^t\rangle - q(D)|\), whose sensitivity is \(1/n\).
Measure \(y_t = \langle q^t, p^t\rangle - q^t(D) + Z_t\), with \(Z_t \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon_0 n))\).
If \(|y_t| \le \alpha/2\), output \(p^t\) and stop.
Otherwise let \(s_t\) be the sign of \(y_t\) and update \(p^{t+1}(x) \propto p^t(x)\left(1 - \eta s_t q^t(x)\right)\).

If no round stops, output \(p^{T+1}\).

The score \(u_t\) has sensitivity \(1/n\) because \(\langle q, p^t\rangle\) does not depend on \(D\), and \(q(D)\) changes by at most \(1/n\). The threshold \(\alpha/2\) in step 3 sits between the errors that must cause an update and those small enough to stop on. It leaves room on both sides for the noise. Every access to the data goes through one of the two mechanisms, so privacy follows from composing them over the \(T\) rounds.

Theorem 8.3 Private multiplicative weights is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

In round \(t\), the distribution \(p^t\) is a function of the earlier outputs \(q^1, y_1, \dots, q^{t-1}, y_{t-1}\) alone. So each round runs two mechanisms chosen from earlier outputs: the exponential mechanism, which is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, and the Laplace mechanism on a query of sensitivity \(1/n\) with scale \(1/(\varepsilon_0n)\), which is also \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP.
A round after the algorithm stops can be treated as a mechanism with a fixed output, which is \(0\)-DP. So the transcript of all \(T\) rounds is an adaptive composition of \(k = 2T\) mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP.
The value \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(4\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)})\) equals \(\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)})\) for \(k = 2T\). Lemma 8.1 makes the transcript \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.
The output is a function of the transcript, so it is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP by post-processing.


Basic composition would also work, and it would even give pure DP, but only with \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2T)\). Then the condition on \(n\) in the next theorem would grow like \(T\) instead of \(\sqrt T\), which means \(1/\alpha^3\) instead of \(1/\alpha^2\).
Accuracy needs enough records for the errors of both mechanisms to stay below \(\alpha/4\) in every round. Then each update still makes progress, and the algorithm stops on a distribution that is accurate on every query.

Theorem 8.4 (Accuracy of private multiplicative weights) Let \(|\mathcal X| \ge 2\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\), and let the other parameters be as in Definition 8.6. If
\[
n \ge \frac{32\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)}\,\big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + \ln(2T/\beta)\big)}{\alpha\varepsilon},
\tag{8.18}\]
then with probability at least \(1-\beta\) the output \(\hat p\) satisfies \(|\langle q, \hat p\rangle - q(D)| \le \alpha\) for every \(q\in \mathcal Q\).


Proof. 

The good event. Let \(G\) be the event that in every round \(t\) that runs, the chosen query has \(u_t(D,q^t) \ge \max_q u_t(D,q) - \alpha/4\) and the noise has \(|Z_t| < \alpha/4\). Condition Equation 8.18 is the same as \(\frac{2}{n\varepsilon_0}(\ln|\mathcal Q| + \ln(2T/\beta)) \le \frac\alpha4\), by the value of \(\varepsilon_0\). So Equation 8.16 with \(t = \ln(2T/\beta)\) bounds the first failure in each round by \(\beta/(2T)\). The same condition gives \(\ln(2T/\beta)/(\varepsilon_0n) \le \alpha/4\), so the Laplace tail bounds the second failure by \(\beta/(2T)\). A union bound over the two failures and the \(T\) rounds gives \(\Pr[G] \ge 1-\beta\). The rest of the proof assumes \(G\).
Every update makes progress. In a round that updates, \(|y_t| > \alpha/2 > |Z_t|\). So the true error \(\langle q^t,p^t\rangle - q^t(D) = y_t - Z_t\) has the sign \(s_t\) of \(y_t\), and its absolute value exceeds \(\alpha/2 - \alpha/4 = \alpha/4\).
Few updates. By step 2, the update is the one of Theorem 8.2, with \(\eta = \alpha/8 \le 1/2\). If \(U\) rounds update, each has error above \(\alpha/4\), and the theorem gives

\[
\frac\alpha4 U < \frac\alpha8 U + \frac{8\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad U < \frac{64\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha^2} \le T .
\tag{8.19}\]
So the \(T\) rounds cannot all update, and the algorithm stops at step 3 in some round \(t\). 4. The output is accurate. In that round, \(|y_t|\le\alpha/2\) and \(|Z_t| < \alpha/4\), so \(u_t(D,q^t) < 3\alpha/4\). On \(G\), every query then has \(u_t(D,q) \le u_t(D,q^t) + \alpha/4 < \alpha\), and the output is \(\hat p = p^t\).

Since \(\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2 \ge \ln 2 > 1/2\), rounding up adds less than \(2\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2\) and \(T \le 66\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2\). So condition Equation 8.18 asks for
\[
n = O\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{\ln|\mathcal X|\,\ln(1/\delta)}\,\big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + \ln\frac{\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha\beta}\big)}{\alpha^2\varepsilon}\right)
\tag{8.20}\]
records, which is the last row of Table 8.1. It is logarithmic in both \(|\mathcal Q|\) and \(|\mathcal X|\), and the price is a worse dependence on \(\alpha\), \(1/\alpha^2\) instead of \(1/\alpha\). Each round evaluates every query on \(p^t\) and on \(D\), so the running time is \(O\big(T|\mathcal Q|(|\mathcal X| + n)\big)\), linear in \(|\mathcal X|\).
The output is a distribution \(\hat p\) over the universe, a synthetic dataset that agrees with the original on every query in \(\mathcal Q\) and that an analyst can use like the original. The logarithms pay off only when the number of queries is large, as a comparison of the three sufficient sample sizes shows.

Example 8.1 Take records with \(d = 20\) binary features, so \(|\mathcal X| = 2^{20}\), and \(\alpha = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\beta = 0.05\). Private multiplicative weights runs for at most \(T = 354{,}892\) rounds. For \(|\mathcal Q| = 10^6\) queries, the sufficient sample sizes of Proposition 8.1, Proposition 8.2 and Theorem 8.4 are about \(3.4\times10^8\), \(3.5\times10^6\) and \(4.3\times10^7\) records. For \(|\mathcal Q| = 10^9\) they become \(4.7\times10^{11}\), \(1.6\times10^8\) and \(5.3\times10^7\). Private multiplicative weights wins only for very many queries, because the constants in Equation 8.18 are large and its accuracy costs \(1/\alpha^2\).

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text:
9.1 Answering queries online
Queries often arrive one at a time, and each must be answered before the next is seen. Under differential privacy (DP), answering each of them with its own noise makes the error grow polynomially with the number of queries. But often the analyst only needs to know which queries exceed a threshold, and few of them do. This chapter shows, with the sparse vector technique, that the cost then depends on the number of large queries and only logarithmically on the total. Its privacy proof rests on noise on the threshold as well as on the queries. At the end, the technique turns private multiplicative weights into an algorithm that answers queries as they arrive.
The setting is a stream of queries \(f_1, f_2, \dots, f_k \colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R\), each with sensitivity at most \(1\). Two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ by the replacement of one record. Sensitivity at most \(1\) means that \(|f_i(D) - f_i(D')| \le 1\) for every such pair. Counting queries, which count the records with some property, are the typical example. Query \(f_i\) arrives at step \(i\) and must be answered before \(f_{i+1}\) is revealed.
The Laplace mechanism answers each query with noise from the Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) of scale \(b\), whose density at \(z\) is \(e^{-|z|/b}/(2b)\). For a sensitivity-\(1\) query it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP when \(b = 1/\varepsilon\), and its tails are \(\Pr[|\mathrm{Lap}(b)| \ge tb] = e^{-t}\). Under pure DP with a total budget \(\varepsilon\), basic composition forces the scale \(k/\varepsilon\) on each of \(k\) answers, so the error is of order \(k/\varepsilon\). Under approximate DP, the advanced composition theorem brings this down to order \(\sqrt{k\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon\). Both are polynomial in \(k\), and in the worst case no algorithm that answers every query can do much better.
A weaker question has a cheaper answer: which queries are large? If all \(k\) queries were known in advance, the exponential mechanism with score \(f_i(D)\) would pick a query whose value is within \(2(\ln k + t)/\varepsilon\) of the largest, except with probability \(e^{-t}\). Repeating it \(c\) times with budget \(\varepsilon/c\) each finds \(c\) large queries with error of order \(c\ln k/\varepsilon\), or \(\sqrt{c\ln(1/\delta)}\ln k/\varepsilon\) with advanced composition. That is logarithmic in \(k\), but it needs the whole list. Online, the first query cannot be compared with queries not yet seen, so the question becomes absolute.
The idea is to run the Laplace mechanism on each query and report only whether the noisy value exceeds a noisy threshold \(\hat\tau\), not \(\tau\) itself. The details matter, because several published variants are not private.

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text: Given a public threshold \(\tau\), report the first \(c\) queries in the stream with \(f_i(D) \ge \tau\), and stop.

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text:
9.2 AboveThreshold
The case \(c = 1\) finds the first large query and halts. AboveThreshold draws one noisy threshold at the start, compares each noisy query with it, and answers with one of two symbols. The symbol \(\top\) means “above the threshold” and \(\bot\) means “below”.

Definition 9.1 (AboveThreshold) The inputs are a dataset \(D\), a stream of sensitivity-\(1\) queries \(f_1, f_2, \dots\), a threshold \(\tau \in \mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\).

Draw \(\hat\tau = \tau + \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\).
For each query \(f_i\) in turn, draw \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4/\varepsilon)\). If \(f_i(D) + \nu_i \ge \hat\tau\), output \(\top\) and halt. Otherwise output \(\bot\).

All noise draws are independent.

Nothing in the algorithm depends on the number of queries, so the stream may even be infinite, and the privacy guarantee does not change. The accuracy guarantee does, because more noise draws mean a larger largest one.
The queries can be fixed in advance, or an analyst who sees the earlier answers can choose them. Before the algorithm halts every answer is \(\bot\), so in the second case each query is still a fixed function of the analyst’s own coins, which do not depend on the dataset. The proof below applies to the stream fixed by each value of those coins, and averaging the inequality over the coins keeps it.

Theorem 9.1 AboveThreshold is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and a stream, and write \(Y\) and \(Y'\) for the outputs on \(D\) and \(D'\). The outputs are \(y = \bot^{t-1}\top\), which halts at query \(t\), and the output that never halts: \(\bot^k\) for a stream of finite length \(k\), or \(\bot^\infty\) for an infinite one. These form a countable set, so by the pointwise lemma for discrete outputs it suffices to show \(\Pr[Y = y] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[Y' = y]\) for each of them.
Fix the noise of the first \(t-1\) queries. Condition on \(\nu_i = v_i\) for \(i < t\), the same values on both datasets, and let

\[
g(D) = \max_{i < t}\big(f_i(D) + v_i\big),
\tag{9.1}\]
with \(g = -\infty\) if \(t = 1\). With the \(v_i\) fixed, \(g\) is a number, not a random variable. Each \(f_i\) has sensitivity \(1\), so \(|g(D) - g(D')| \le 1\). 3. The output is \(y\) exactly when every earlier query falls below \(\hat\tau\) and query \(t\) does not, that is, when \(g(D) < \hat\tau \le f_t(D) + \nu_t\). Write \(\phi_2\) and \(\phi_4\) for the densities of \(\hat\tau\) and \(\nu_t\), whose subscripts recall the scales \(2/\varepsilon\) and \(4/\varepsilon\). Then
\[
\Pr[Y = y] = \int\!\!\int \phi_2(u)\,\phi_4(v)\,\mathbf 1\big[g(D) < u \le f_t(D) + v\big]\,\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v .
\tag{9.2}\]

Change variables to move from \(D\) to \(D'\). Substitute

\[
u = u' + g(D) - g(D'), \qquad v = v' + g(D) - g(D') + f_t(D') - f_t(D).
\tag{9.3}\]
This is a shift, so \(\mathrm d u\,\mathrm d v = \mathrm d u'\,\mathrm d v'\). The condition \(g(D) < u\) becomes \(g(D') < u'\), and \(u \le f_t(D) + v\) becomes \(u' \le f_t(D') + v'\), so the indicator becomes \(\mathbf 1[g(D') < u' \le f_t(D') + v']\). 5. Pay for the shifts. By step 2, \(|u - u'| \le 1\). By step 2 and the sensitivity of \(f_t\), \(|v - v'| \le 2\). A Laplace density of scale \(b\) changes by at most a factor \(e^{s/b}\) when its argument moves by \(s\), so \(\phi_2(u) \le e^{\varepsilon/2}\phi_2(u')\) and \(\phi_4(v) \le e^{2\varepsilon/4}\phi_4(v') = e^{\varepsilon/2}\phi_4(v')\). Hence
\[
\Pr[Y = y] \le e^{\varepsilon}\int\!\!\int \phi_2(u')\,\phi_4(v')\,\mathbf 1\big[g(D') < u' \le f_t(D') + v'\big]\,\mathrm d u'\,\mathrm d v' = e^\varepsilon\Pr[Y' = y],
\tag{9.4}\]
where both probabilities are conditional on the fixed \(v_1,\dots,v_{t-1}\). 6. The \(v_i\) have the same distribution on both datasets, so averaging step 5 over them gives the unconditional inequality. 7. The output that never halts. It occurs exactly when \(\hat\tau > \sup_i(f_i(D) + \nu_i)\), the supremum over all queries of the stream. Fixing all \(\nu_i\) makes this supremum a number \(g(D)\), possibly \(+\infty\), with \(|g(D) - g(D')| \le 1\) when it is finite, and the output has probability \(0\) on both datasets when it is not. Shifting \(u\) by at most \(1\) as in steps 4 and 5 gives the factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2} \le e^\varepsilon\).

The two noises do different jobs. The noise on \(\hat\tau\) pays, in one draw, for all the \(\bot\) answers: the proof fixes their noise and absorbs the change in their maximum by shifting the threshold. The noise \(\nu_t\) pays for the single \(\top\). So the privacy cost does not grow with the number of \(\bot\) answers.
The output carries no numbers, so accuracy means making no mistakes, with some slack around the threshold.

Definition 9.2 (Accuracy for threshold answers) Let an algorithm answer a stream of queries \(f_1, f_2, \dots\) with \(\top\) or \(\bot\), compared with a threshold \(\tau\), and write \(a_i\) for its answer to \(f_i\). Let \(\alpha \ge 0\) be a slack and \(\beta \in (0,1)\) a failure probability. The algorithm is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-accurate on \(D\) if, with probability at least \(1-\beta\), every answered query satisfies
\[
a_i = \top \implies f_i(D) \ge \tau - \alpha \qquad\text{and}\qquad a_i = \bot \implies f_i(D) \le \tau + \alpha .
\tag{9.5}\]

In words, no query more than \(\alpha\) below the threshold gets a \(\top\), and no query more than \(\alpha\) above it gets a \(\bot\). AboveThreshold meets this definition with a slack \(\alpha\) that grows only with the logarithm of the number of queries. The theorem also asks that every query before the last be at least \(\alpha\) below the threshold, so that the algorithm does not halt early.

Theorem 9.2 (Accuracy of AboveThreshold) Let \(\beta \in (0,1)\), and let \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) be a stream with \(f_i(D) \le \tau - \alpha\) for every \(i < k\), where
\[
\alpha = \frac{8\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{9.6}\]
Then AboveThreshold is \((\alpha,\beta)\)-accurate on \(D\), and with probability at least \(1-\beta\) it does not halt before query \(k\).


Proof. 

The good event. Let \(G\) be the event that \(|\hat\tau - \tau| < \alpha/2\) and \(|\nu_i| < \alpha/2\) for every \(i \le k\).
Accuracy on \(G\). If \(a_i = \top\), then \(f_i(D) \ge \hat\tau - \nu_i > (\tau - \alpha/2) - \alpha/2 = \tau - \alpha\). If \(a_i = \bot\), then \(f_i(D) < \hat\tau - \nu_i < \tau + \alpha\).
No early halt on \(G\). By step 2, a \(\top\) at query \(i\) needs \(f_i(D) > \tau - \alpha\), which the hypothesis rules out for \(i < k\).
\(G\) is likely. The threshold noise has scale \(2/\varepsilon\), so the tail formula gives \(\Pr[|\hat\tau - \tau| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-\varepsilon\alpha/4}\). Each \(\nu_i\) has scale \(4/\varepsilon\), so a union bound gives \(\Pr[\max_{i\le k}|\nu_i| \ge \alpha/2] \le k e^{-\varepsilon\alpha/8}\).
With Equation 9.6, \(ke^{-\varepsilon\alpha/8} = k\cdot\frac{1}{k}\cdot\frac{\beta}{2} = \beta/2\). Also \(e^{-\varepsilon\alpha/4} = (\beta/(2k))^2 \le \beta/2\). So \(\Pr[G] \ge 1-\beta\).


The error grows only logarithmically in \(k\), like that of the exponential mechanism, but the queries can arrive online.

Example 9.1 Take \(k = 10^6\) counting queries, \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\). Then Equation 9.6 gives \(\alpha = 8(\ln 10^6 + \ln 40) = 8(13.82 + 3.69) = 140.0\). On a dataset of \(n = 10^5\) records, a query is placed correctly unless its count lies within \(140\) of the threshold. Answering every query with the Laplace mechanism and basic composition would instead add noise of scale \(10^6\), ten times the size of the dataset.

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text:
9.3 Sparse vector
To find \(c\) large queries, restart AboveThreshold after each \(\top\), with a fresh threshold, until \(c\) of them have been found.

Definition 9.3 (Sparse vector) The inputs are those of AboveThreshold, a count \(c \ge 1\) of \(\top\) answers to find, and a parameter \(\delta\), with either \(\delta = 0\) or \(\delta \in (0,1/2]\). Set the Laplace noise scale \(b\) to
\[
b = \frac{2c}{\varepsilon} \ \text{ if } \delta = 0, \qquad b = \frac{\sqrt{32c\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon} \ \text{ if } \delta > 0 .
\tag{9.7}\]

Draw \(\hat\tau = \tau + \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and set \(\mathrm{count} = 0\).
For each query \(f_i\) in turn, draw \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2b)\). If \(f_i(D) + \nu_i < \hat\tau\), output \(\bot\). Otherwise output \(\top\) and add \(1\) to \(\mathrm{count}\). If \(\mathrm{count} = c\), halt. If not, draw a fresh \(\hat\tau = \tau + \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and continue.


Between two \(\top\) answers the algorithm runs AboveThreshold with parameter \(\varepsilon' = 2/b\), whose noise scales are \(2/\varepsilon' = b\) and \(4/\varepsilon' = 2b\). The fresh threshold matters, because reusing \(\hat\tau\) after a \(\top\) would break this equivalence, and with it the proof. With the equivalence, sparse vector is a composition of \(c\) runs of AboveThreshold, and its privacy follows from the composition theorems.

Theorem 9.3 Sparse vector with \(\delta = 0\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon > 0\). With \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1/2]\) it is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

The output is the concatenation of at most \(c\) runs of AboveThreshold, each with parameter \(\varepsilon' = 2/b\) and fresh noise. Each run takes the rest of the stream, which may depend on the earlier outputs, so the whole is an adaptive composition of \(c\) mechanisms. A run that never starts, because the algorithm halted, has a fixed output. Each run is \(\varepsilon'\)-DP by Theorem 9.1.
If \(\delta = 0\), then \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/c\), and basic composition gives \(c\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\).
If \(\delta > 0\), then \(\varepsilon' = 2\varepsilon/\sqrt{32c\ln(1/\delta)} = \varepsilon/\big(2\sqrt{2c\ln(1/\delta)}\big)\). The budget-splitting lemma says that \(m\) adaptively composed mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2m\ln(1/\delta)})\)-DP, are together \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP when \(\varepsilon \le 1\) and \(\delta \le 1/2\). Apply it with \(m = c\).


Accuracy is proved as for AboveThreshold. The only change is that the union bound now runs over every threshold drawn, one per run, as well as over the noise on each query.

Theorem 9.4 (Accuracy of sparse vector) Let \(\beta \in (0,1)\), let \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) be a stream, and let
\[
\alpha = 4b\ln(2k/\beta) .
\tag{9.8}\]
With probability at least \(1-\beta\), every answered query satisfies the two implications of Definition 9.2. If moreover fewer than \(c\) of the queries have \(f_i(D) > \tau - \alpha\), the algorithm answers all \(k\) queries. In terms of the parameters, the accuracy is
\[
\alpha = \frac{8c\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} \ \text{ if } \delta = 0, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\sqrt{512\,c\ln(1/\delta)}\,\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} \ \text{ if } \delta > 0 .
\tag{9.9}\]


Proof. 

Let \(G\) be the event that every threshold drawn and every \(\nu_i\) with \(i \le k\) lies within \(\alpha/2\) of its centre. On \(G\), steps 2 and 3 of the proof of Theorem 9.2 apply to each query, with whichever threshold is current. So the implications hold, and a \(\top\) needs \(f_i(D) > \tau - \alpha\).
If fewer than \(c\) queries have \(f_i(D) > \tau-\alpha\), then on \(G\) there are fewer than \(c\) answers \(\top\), and the algorithm never halts.
The query noise has scale \(2b\), and \(\alpha/(4b) = \ln(2k/\beta)\). A union bound over the \(k\) draws bounds its failure by \(k e^{-\alpha/(4b)} = \beta/2\).
At most \(k+1\) thresholds are drawn, each with scale \(b\). Their failure is at most \((k+1)e^{-\alpha/(2b)} = (k+1)\beta^2/(4k^2) \le \beta/2\), since \(k + 1 \le 2k\) and \(\beta \le 1\).
Substituting the two values of \(b\) into \(4b\ln(2k/\beta)\) gives Equation 9.9, because \(4\sqrt{32} = \sqrt{512}\).


With \(c = 1\) and \(\delta = 0\) this is Theorem 9.2 again. The error is polynomial in the number \(c\) of large queries and logarithmic in the total number \(k\). So sparse vector can scan a very long stream, as long as few of its queries are large.

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text:
9.4 Numeric sparse vector
Sparse vector already pays in proportion to the number \(c\) of large queries. A noisy value for each of those \(c\) queries takes \(c\) more Laplace mechanisms, which cost the same order of budget. So sparse vector can also release the values of the large queries for a constant factor.

Definition 9.4 (Numeric sparse vector) Run sparse vector with \(\delta = 0\) and budget \(\varepsilon/2\), so \(b = 4c/\varepsilon\). Whenever it would output \(\top\) for query \(f_i\), output instead \(a_i = f_i(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(2c/\varepsilon)\), with fresh noise.

Each answer is now either \(\bot\) or a number. The guarantee combines the two implications of Definition 9.2 with an error bound on every released number.

Theorem 9.5 Numeric sparse vector is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Let \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) be a stream, \(\beta\in(0,1)\) and \(\alpha = 16c\ln(4k/\beta)/\varepsilon\). With probability at least \(1-\beta\), every answered query satisfies the following, where \(a_i \in \mathbb R\) means that the answer to \(f_i\) is a released number:
\[
a_i = \bot \implies f_i(D) \le \tau + \alpha, \qquad a_i \in \mathbb R \implies f_i(D) \ge \tau - \alpha \ \text{ and } \ |a_i - f_i(D)| \le \alpha ,
\tag{9.10}\]
and if fewer than \(c\) queries have \(f_i(D) > \tau - \alpha\), all \(k\) are answered.


Proof. 

Privacy. The algorithm is an adaptive composition of at most \(c\) runs of AboveThreshold, each with parameter \(2/b = \varepsilon/(2c)\), and at most \(c\) Laplace mechanisms. Each Laplace mechanism measures one sensitivity-\(1\) query, chosen from the earlier outputs, with scale \(2c/\varepsilon\), so it is \(\varepsilon/(2c)\)-DP. Basic composition over the \(2c\) mechanisms gives \(\varepsilon\).
Accuracy of the labels. Theorem 9.4 with \(b = 4c/\varepsilon\) and failure probability \(\beta/2\) gives accuracy \(4b\ln(4k/\beta) = \alpha\) for the labels, and no early halt, with probability at least \(1-\beta/2\).
Accuracy of the values. At most \(k\) values are released, one per query. By the tail formula and a union bound, some noise exceeds \(\alpha\) with probability at most \(k\,e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(2c)} = k\,(\beta/(4k))^8 \le \beta/2\).


The fresh noise in the released value matters. Releasing \(f_i(D) + \nu_i\), the value already compared with the threshold, is not private, and published variants that did so were wrong.

title: 9  Sparse Vector
text:
9.5 Online private multiplicative weights
The previous chapter built private multiplicative weights for a fixed set of linear queries \(q \colon \mathcal X \to [0,1]\), with \(q(D) = \frac1n\sum_i q(x_i)\). This section uses four of its facts. For a distribution \(p\) on \(\mathcal X\), write \(\langle q, p\rangle = \sum_x q(x)p(x)\) for the average of \(q\) under \(p\). The histogram \(p_D\) of the dataset, the fraction of records equal to each \(x\), satisfies \(q(D) = \langle q, p_D\rangle\). Multiplicative weights over the experts \(\mathcal X\) with learning rate \(\eta\) and losses \(s_tq^t\), where \(s_t\) is the sign of the error \(\langle q^t, p^t\rangle - q^t(D)\), has total error at most \(\eta U + \ln|\mathcal X|/\eta\) after \(U\) updates. And the offline algorithm used the exponential mechanism to find a query with a large error.
Online, the exponential mechanism cannot be used, because the queries arrive one at a time, so sparse vector replaces it. The algorithm keeps a distribution \(\hat p\) and answers each query from it while it is accurate. When sparse vector reports a large error, the algorithm answers with a noisy true value and updates \(\hat p\).
These queries have sensitivity \(1/n\), not \(1\). Sparse vector on \(f_i/\Delta\) with threshold \(\tau/\Delta\) handles sensitivity \(\Delta\). It is the same algorithm with every noise scale multiplied by \(\Delta\), so it has the same privacy and \(\Delta\) times the accuracy \(\alpha\). The algorithm runs this rescaled sparse vector on the errors of \(\hat p\), with threshold \(\alpha/2\). Its count \(c\) of large errors is set to the bound on the number of updates from the previous chapter, and \(\varepsilon_0\) is the budget of each of the \(2c\) mechanisms it may run.

Definition 9.5 (Online private multiplicative weights) The inputs are a dataset \(D\in\mathcal X^n\), a stream of linear queries \(f_1, f_2, \dots\), an accuracy \(\alpha \in (0,1]\), and \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta\in(0,1/2]\). Set
\[
c = \left\lceil\frac{64\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha^2}\right\rceil, \qquad \eta = \frac\alpha8, \qquad \varepsilon_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{4\sqrt{c\ln(1/\delta)}} ,
\tag{9.11}\]
let \(\hat p\) be uniform on \(\mathcal X\), set \(\mathrm{count} = 0\), and draw \(\hat\tau = \alpha/2 + \mathrm{Lap}(2/(\varepsilon_0n))\). For each query \(f_i\) in turn:

Let \(e_i = |\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle - f_i(D)|\) and draw \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4/(\varepsilon_0n))\).
If \(e_i + \nu_i < \hat\tau\), answer \(\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle\).
Otherwise answer \(a_i = f_i(D) + Z_i\) with \(Z_i \sim\mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon_0 n))\). Let \(s_i\) be the sign of \(\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle - a_i\), update \(\hat p(x) \propto \hat p(x)\big(1 - \eta s_if_i(x)\big)\), and add \(1\) to \(\mathrm{count}\). If \(\mathrm{count} = c\), halt. Otherwise draw a fresh \(\hat\tau = \alpha/2 + \mathrm{Lap}(2/(\varepsilon_0n))\).


Steps 1 to 3 follow numeric sparse vector, run on the errors \(e_i\) with threshold \(\alpha/2\), except that the fresh measurement in step 3 is of \(f_i(D)\) rather than of \(e_i\). The answer in step 2 uses only \(\hat p\), which depends on the earlier outputs alone, so it costs no privacy.

Theorem 9.6 Online private multiplicative weights is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Between two updates \(\hat p\) is fixed, so the errors \(e_i\) form a stream of queries determined by the earlier outputs and the analyst. Each \(e_i\) has sensitivity \(1/n\), since \(\langle f_i,\hat p\rangle\) does not depend on \(D\) and \(f_i(D)\) changes by at most \(1/n\).
Each stretch between updates is therefore AboveThreshold with parameter \(\varepsilon_0\), rescaled to sensitivity \(1/n\), and so \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP by Theorem 9.1. Each measurement in step 3 is the Laplace mechanism on a query of sensitivity \(1/n\) with scale \(1/(\varepsilon_0n)\), so it is also \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP. The answers of step 2 and the updates are post-processing.
There are at most \(c\) stretches and \(c\) measurements, so the algorithm is an adaptive composition of \(2c\) mechanisms, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP. Since \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2\sqrt{2\cdot 2c\ln(1/\delta)})\), the budget-splitting lemma with \(m = 2c\) mechanisms makes it \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Accuracy follows the proof for the offline algorithm. When all the noise is small, every answer from \(\hat p\) is accurate, every measured answer is accurate, and every update makes progress, so the count of updates never reaches \(c\).

Theorem 9.7 (Accuracy of online private multiplicative weights) Let \(|\mathcal X|\ge 2\), \(\beta\in(0,1)\) and a stream of \(k\) queries, and let the other parameters be as in Definition 9.5. If
\[
n \ge \frac{128\sqrt{c\ln(1/\delta)}\,\ln\big((2c+k)/\beta\big)}{\alpha\varepsilon},
\tag{9.12}\]
then with probability at least \(1-\beta\) the algorithm answers all \(k\) queries, each within \(\alpha\) of \(f_i(D)\).


Proof. 

The good event. Let \(G\) be the event that every threshold noise, every \(\nu_i\) and every \(Z_i\) is less than \(\alpha/8\) in absolute value. These are at most \(2c + k\) draws, because there are at most \(c\) thresholds and \(c\) measurements. The widest scale is \(4/(\varepsilon_0n)\), so each draw fails with probability at most \(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon_0n/32}\). Condition Equation 9.12 is the same as \(\alpha\varepsilon_0n/32 \ge \ln((2c+k)/\beta)\), by the value of \(\varepsilon_0\). A union bound gives \(\Pr[G] \ge 1-\beta\), and the rest assumes \(G\).
Answers from \(\hat p\). In step 2, \(e_i < \hat\tau - \nu_i < \alpha/2 + \alpha/8 + \alpha/8 = 3\alpha/4\), so the answer is within \(\alpha\).
Measured answers. In step 3, \(|a_i - f_i(D)| = |Z_i| < \alpha/8\). Also \(e_i \ge \hat\tau - \nu_i > \alpha/2 - \alpha/4 = \alpha/4\). The difference \(\langle f_i,\hat p\rangle - a_i\) is the true error minus \(Z_i\), and \(|Z_i| < \alpha/8 < e_i\), so \(s_i\) is the sign of the true error.
Few updates. By step 3, the updates are those of multiplicative weights for queries with \(\eta = \alpha/8\), and each has error above \(\alpha/4\). If there are \(U\) of them, the regret bound gives

\[
\frac\alpha4U < \frac\alpha8U + \frac{8\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad U < \frac{64\ln|\mathcal X|}{\alpha^2} \le c .
\tag{9.13}\]
So the count never reaches \(c\), the algorithm never halts, and all \(k\) queries are answered.

As in the previous chapter, \(c \le 66\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2\). So condition Equation 9.12 asks for
\[
n = O\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{\ln|\mathcal X|\,\ln(1/\delta)}\;\ln\frac{k + \ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2}{\beta}}{\alpha^2\varepsilon}\right)
\tag{9.14}\]
records. This matches the offline algorithm, with the length \(k\) of the stream in place of the number \(|\mathcal Q|\) of queries.
