title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
text:
10.1 Local sensitivity
The Laplace mechanism adds noise scaled to the global sensitivity of a function, the largest change one record can cause on any pair of neighbouring datasets. For many functions that worst case is far from the dataset at hand, or infinite. This chapter asks whether the noise can be scaled to the dataset actually held instead, while keeping differential privacy (DP).
Done naively, it cannot, because the amount of noise then depends on the data and leaks it. Four techniques make the idea work. Propose-test-release checks privately that the dataset is far from any dataset where the function is sensitive. A stability argument built on it finds the most frequent element and every count of a histogram, whatever the size of the domain. The last two techniques bound the sensitivity privately, or smooth it, before they use it.
Throughout the chapter, \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R\) is a real-valued function of the dataset. Its global sensitivity is the largest change that replacing one record can cause, over neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) (the replace-one relation),
\[
\Delta f = \max_{D \sim D'} |f(D) - f(D')| ,
\tag{10.1}\]
and the Laplace mechanism adds to \(f(D)\) a noise term drawn from \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta f/\varepsilon)\), which makes the release \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The maximum ranges over all pairs of neighbours, including datasets that look nothing like the one held. Fixing the first dataset gives a local version.
The global sensitivity is the largest local sensitivity, \(\Delta f = \max_D \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\), and the local sensitivity can be much smaller. The natural mechanism releases \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)/\varepsilon)\). It fails, because the scale of the noise is itself a function of the data. The distance between the two closest records shows how the local sensitivity can jump from one dataset to a neighbour.
On these two neighbours, the naive mechanism adds no noise to one and some noise to the other, and that difference alone gives the dataset away.
The failure is that \(D\) has low local sensitivity while a neighbour has high local sensitivity, and the noise level tells them apart. So the local sensitivity is itself a statistic of the data, which leaks even through the scale of the noise. Each technique below accounts for the sensitivity of nearby datasets, not just of \(D\).

title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
text:
Definition 10.1 (Local sensitivity) The local sensitivity of \(f\) at a dataset \(D \in \mathcal X^n\) is
\[
\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D' \sim D} |f(D) - f(D')| .
\tag{10.2}\]



Example 10.1 Let \(\mathcal X = \mathbb R\), \(n = 3\), and let \(f(D)\) be the distance between the two closest records. On the real line \(f\) has infinite global sensitivity. For example, \((0, c, 2c)\) and its neighbour \((0, 0, 2c)\) have \(f\) equal to \(c\) and \(0\), for every \(c > 0\), so the Laplace mechanism does not apply. Take \(D = (0, 0, 0)\). Replacing any one record leaves two records at \(0\), so \(f\) stays \(0\) and \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = 0\). Now take the neighbour \(D' = (0, 0, 5)\). It also has \(f(D') = 0\), but replacing one of its zeros by \(10\) gives \((0, 10, 5)\) with closest distance \(5\), so \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D') \ge 5\).



Proposition 10.1 The mechanism \(M(D) = f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)/\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathrm{Lap}(0)\) means no noise, is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\) when \(f\) is the closest-pair distance of Example 10.1.


Proof. 

On \(D = (0,0,0)\) the local sensitivity is \(0\), so \(M(D) = 0\) with probability \(1\).
On the neighbour \(D' = (0,0,5)\) the local sensitivity is positive, so \(M(D')\) has a continuous distribution and \(\Pr[M(D') = 0] = 0\).
So the event \(\{0\}\) has probability \(1\) on \(D\) and \(0\) on \(D'\), and no factor \(e^{\varepsilon}\) with finite \(\varepsilon\) can bound the first by the second.

title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
text:
10.2 Propose-test-release
The first technique proposes a bound \(b\) on the local sensitivity and tests privately that the bound holds at \(D\) and at every dataset near \(D\). Only if the test passes does it release \(f(D)\) with noise scaled to \(b\). The test measures how many records must change before the bound fails. The Hamming distance \(d(D, D')\) between two datasets is the number of records in which they differ.

Definition 10.2 (Distance to instability) For a proposed bound \(b \ge 0\) on the local sensitivity \(\mathrm{LS}_f\), the distance to instability of \(D\) is
\[
\gamma_b(D) = \min\{\, d(D, D') : D' \in \mathcal X^n,\ \mathrm{LS}_f(D') > b \,\},
\tag{10.3}\]
the fewest records that must change to reach a dataset whose local sensitivity exceeds \(b\), where \(d\) is the Hamming distance. If no dataset has local sensitivity above \(b\), set \(\gamma_b(D) = \infty\) for every \(D\).

So \(\gamma_b(D) = 0\) exactly when \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) > b\). The distance is a count of records, and that gives it sensitivity \(1\) whatever \(f\) is.

Lemma 10.1 If \(\gamma_b\) is finite, then \(|\gamma_b(D) - \gamma_b(D')| \le 1\) for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\).


Proof. 

If some dataset \(W\) has \(\mathrm{LS}_f(W) > b\), every dataset is within distance \(n\) of \(W\), so \(\gamma_b\) is finite everywhere.
Let \(W\) attain the minimum for \(D'\), so \(d(D', W) = \gamma_b(D')\) and \(\mathrm{LS}_f(W) > b\). The Hamming distance satisfies the triangle inequality, so \(d(D, W) \le d(D, D') + d(D', W) = 1 + \gamma_b(D')\). Hence \(\gamma_b(D) \le \gamma_b(D') + 1\).
Swapping the roles of \(D\) and \(D'\) gives the other inequality.


Because the distance has sensitivity \(1\), the Laplace mechanism can release it privately, and that noisy distance is the test. The threshold of the test is set so that a dataset whose local sensitivity exceeds \(b\) passes only with probability \(\delta/2\).

Definition 10.3 (Propose-test-release) The mechanism takes a proposed bound \(b > 0\) and privacy parameters \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). On input \(D\), it does three steps.

compute \(\hat\gamma = \gamma_b(D) + Z_1\) with \(Z_1 \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\);
if \(\hat\gamma \le \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), output \(\bot\), meaning “no answer”;
otherwise output \(f(D) + Z_2\) with \(Z_2 \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b/\varepsilon)\), independent of \(Z_1\).


The test spends one budget of \(\varepsilon\), and the release spends another. The test can wrongly pass on a sensitive dataset, and \(\delta\) pays for that. The release step is the naive mechanism of Proposition 10.1 with the scale \(b\) in place of \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)\). It is safe now because \(b\) is fixed in advance. The decision to use it depends on the data only through the private estimate \(\hat\gamma\).

Theorem 10.1 Propose-test-release is \((2\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an event \(S \subseteq \mathbb R \cup \{\bot\}\). Write \(\tau = \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) for the threshold. If \(\gamma_b\) is infinite at every dataset, the test always passes and \(b \ge \Delta f\), so the output is the Laplace mechanism and is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Assume from now on that \(\gamma_b\) is finite.

The test is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. By Lemma 10.1, \(\gamma_b\) has sensitivity \(1\), so \(\hat\gamma\) is the Laplace mechanism and is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The events \(\{\hat\gamma \le \tau\}\) and \(\{\hat\gamma > \tau\}\) are post-processing of \(\hat\gamma\), so each has probability on \(D\) at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\) times its probability on \(D'\).
Case \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) > b\). Then \(\gamma_b(D) = 0\), and the test passes only if \(Z_1 > \tau\), which has probability \(\frac12 e^{-\varepsilon\tau} = \delta/2\). Splitting on whether the output is \(\bot\) and using step 1,

\[
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) = \bot]\,\mathbf 1[\bot \in S] + \Pr[M(D) \ne \bot] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \tfrac\delta2 .
\tag{10.4}\]

Case \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le b\). Then \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le b\), so the release step is the Laplace mechanism for a pair at distance at most \(b\), with scale \(b/\varepsilon\). Its density at any \(y\) changes by a factor at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\) between \(D\) and \(D'\). Write \(S_{\mathbb R} = S \cap \mathbb R\). The two steps use independent noise, so

\[
\Pr[M(D) \in S] = \Pr[\hat\gamma \le \tau]\,\mathbf 1[\bot \in S] + \Pr[\hat\gamma > \tau]\,\Pr[f(D) + Z_2 \in S_{\mathbb R}] .
\tag{10.5}\]
Each probability on the right is at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\) times the same probability on \(D'\), by step 1 and by the Laplace mechanism. So \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S]\).

In both cases \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta\). The pair was arbitrary, so this holds for every ordered pair of neighbours.


The test passes with high probability on datasets far from instability, because if \(\gamma_b(D) \ge 2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), then the output is \(\bot\) only if \(Z_1 \le -\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability \(\delta/2\). The price is computation, because \(\gamma_b\) is a minimum over all \(|\mathcal X|^n\) datasets. So the distance to instability has to be worked out by hand for each function, and the median is the standard case where this is efficient.

title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
section: 10.3 Stability: the mode and the histogram
text:
10.3 Stability: the mode and the histogram
Propose-test-release is most striking with the bound \(b = 0\). Then the test checks that the answer does not change at all near \(D\), and the release step adds no noise. The mode, the most frequent element, is the standard example. If all \(n\) records equal the same value \(v\), the mode stays \(v\) until about \(n/2\) records change, so the mode is far from instability.
Let \(\mathcal X\) be any set with a fixed total order, used only to break ties. Write \(c_x(D)\) for the number of records of \(D\) equal to \(x\), and \(c_{(1)}(D) \ge c_{(2)}(D)\) for the largest and second-largest of these counts, with \(c_{(2)}(D) = 0\) if all records are equal. The mode \(\mathrm{mode}(D)\) is the element with the largest count, the least one in the order among ties. To change the mode, records must move from the most frequent element to the runner-up until it overtakes. So half the gap between the two largest counts is, up to \(1\), the distance to instability, and it is computed in one pass over the data whatever the domain.

Lemma 10.2 Let \(g(D) = \big(c_{(1)}(D) - c_{(2)}(D)\big)/2\). For all neighbours \(D \sim D'\):

\(|g(D) - g(D')| \le 1\);
if \(g(D) > 1\), then \(\mathrm{mode}(D') = \mathrm{mode}(D)\).



Proof. 

Replacing one record lowers one count by \(1\) and raises another by \(1\), so every count changes by at most \(1\).
The \(j\)-th largest count is the maximum, over sets \(S\) of \(j\) elements, of \(\min_{x \in S} c_x\). If every count rises by at most \(1\), each such minimum rises by at most \(1\), and so does the maximum. The same holds for decreases, so \(c_{(1)}\) and \(c_{(2)}\) each change by at most \(1\), and \(g\) changes by at most \((1 + 1)/2 = 1\). This is claim 1.
For claim 2, let \(a = \mathrm{mode}(D)\). In \(D'\), the count of \(a\) is at least \(c_{(1)}(D) - 1\), and every other count is at most \(c_{(2)}(D) + 1\). The condition \(g(D) > 1\) means \(c_{(1)}(D) - 1 > c_{(2)}(D) + 1\), so \(a\) has the strictly largest count in \(D'\).


The stable mode is propose-test-release with \(b = 0\), with the gap \(g\) in place of the distance to instability. Its threshold has an extra \(1\) because claim 2 protects the mode only when \(g(D) > 1\).

Definition 10.4 (Stable mode) Given \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), on input \(D\), compute \(\hat g = g(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\), where \(g(D)\) is half the gap between the two largest counts. If \(\hat g \le 1 + \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), output \(\bot\), and otherwise output \(\mathrm{mode}(D)\) exactly.

The guarantee has two parts. The test costs \(\delta\) in privacy, and it fails, by outputting \(\bot\), only on datasets whose two largest counts are close.

Theorem 10.2 The stable mode is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. On every dataset whose two largest counts differ by at least \(2 + 4\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), it outputs the mode with probability at least \(1 - \delta/2\).


Proof. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an event \(S\), and write \(\tau = 1 + \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\).

The gap is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. By Lemma 10.2, claim 1, \(\hat g\) is the Laplace mechanism for a function of sensitivity \(1\), so it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Case \(\mathrm{mode}(D') = \mathrm{mode}(D)\). The output on both datasets is the same function of \(\hat g\), namely \(\bot\) below the threshold and the common mode above it. Post-processing gives \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S]\).
Case \(\mathrm{mode}(D') \ne \mathrm{mode}(D)\). By Lemma 10.2, claim 2, \(g(D) \le 1\). The mode is released only if \(Z > \tau - g(D) \ge \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability at most \(\delta/2\). As in the proof of Theorem 10.1, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta/2\).
Accuracy. If \(c_{(1)} - c_{(2)} \ge 2 + 4\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), then \(g(D) \ge \tau + \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\). The output is \(\bot\) only if \(Z \le -\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability \(\delta/2\).


With typical parameters, the gap the theorem needs is a few dozen records.

Example 10.2 With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the threshold is \(1 + \ln(10^6) = 14.82\). A gap of \(2 + 4 \times 13.82 = 57.3\), so \(58\) records, between the most frequent element and the runner-up is enough. The domain plays no part. It may be the set of all strings, which is infinite.

The stable mode costs \(\varepsilon\), not \(2\varepsilon\), because the release step adds no noise and spends no budget. Its accuracy depends on the gap, not on the domain, and under pure DP no such bound is possible. The packing chapter shows that an \(\varepsilon\)-DP algorithm that finds the mode of a dataset over \(k\) elements needs at least \(\ln(k/2)/\varepsilon\) records, even when all records are equal. So approximate DP replaces the cost \(\ln k\) of a large domain by \(\ln(1/\delta)\).
The same idea estimates every count at once. The algorithm adds noise only to the counts of elements that appear in the data. It reports only those whose noisy count clears a threshold. An element that appears once in \(D\) and not at all in a neighbour is the only danger, and the threshold hides it except with probability \(\delta/2\).

Definition 10.5 (Stability-based histogram) Given \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), let \(\tau = 1 + 2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\). On input \(D\), for each element \(x\) whose count \(c_x(D)\) of records is positive, draw an independent \(Z_x \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) and set \(\hat c_x = c_x(D) + Z_x\). Output the list of pairs \((x, \hat c_x)\) with \(\hat c_x > \tau\). An element not on the list has estimate \(\hat c_x = 0\).

The noise has scale \(2/\varepsilon\) because replacing one record changes two counts. The threshold costs \(\delta\) in privacy. In accuracy, it adds at most \(\tau\) to the noise on each count, because a count is reported as \(0\) only when its noisy value is at most \(\tau\).

Theorem 10.3 The stability-based histogram is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. For every \(\beta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every element \(x \in \mathcal X\) has
\[
|\hat c_x - c_x(D)| \le \tau + \frac{2}{\varepsilon}\ln\frac{n}{\beta} .
\tag{10.6}\]


Proof. Privacy. Let \(D'\) be \(D\) with one record equal to \(a\) replaced by \(a' \ne a\). Let \(C\) be the set of elements that appear in both datasets. Any element that appears only in \(D\) is \(a\), with count \(1\), and any element that appears only in \(D'\) is \(a'\), with count \(1\). Write \(O(D) = O_C(D) \cup O_A(D)\) for the output list on \(D\), where \(O_C\) is the part of the list from \(C\) and \(O_A\) the part from elements only in \(D\), which can only be \(a\). Define \(O_C(D')\) and \(O_{A'}(D')\) in the same way, where \(O_{A'}\) can only contain \(a'\). Fix an event \(S\) and let \(p_C = \Pr[O_C(D') \in S]\).

The extra element of \(D\). An element with count \(1\) is listed only if its noise exceeds \(\tau - 1 = 2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability \(\frac12 e^{-\ln(1/\delta)} = \delta/2\). When \(O_A(D)\) is empty, \(O(D) = O_C(D)\), so \(\Pr[O(D) \in S] \le \Pr[O_C(D) \in S] + \delta/2\).
The common elements. On \(C\), the counts of \(D\) and \(D'\) differ by at most \(1\) at \(a\) and at \(a'\), so in \(\ell_1\) by at most \(2\). Laplace noise of scale \(2/\varepsilon\) makes the noisy counts on \(C\) \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and the list is post-processing of them. So \(\Pr[O_C(D) \in S] \le \min(1, e^{\varepsilon} p_C)\).
The extra element of \(D'\). The parts \(O_C(D')\) and \(O_{A'}(D')\) are independent, and \(O_{A'}(D')\) is empty with probability at least \(1 - \delta/2\) by the computation of step 1. When it is empty, \(O(D') = O_C(D')\). So \(\Pr[O(D') \in S] \ge (1 - \delta/2)\, p_C\).
Combining. If \(e^{\varepsilon}p_C \le 1\), then \(\min(1, e^\varepsilon p_C) - e^{\varepsilon}(1-\delta/2)p_C = e^{\varepsilon}p_C\,\delta/2 \le \delta/2\). Otherwise \(1 - e^{\varepsilon}(1-\delta/2)p_C < 1 - (1 - \delta/2) = \delta/2\). In both cases, steps 1 to 3 give

\[
\Pr[O(D) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}(1 - \delta/2)\,p_C + \tfrac\delta2 + \tfrac\delta2 \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[O(D') \in S] + \delta .
\tag{10.7}\]
Accuracy.

At most \(n\) elements appear in \(D\). A Laplace variable of scale \(2/\varepsilon\) exceeds \(s\) in absolute value with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon s/2}\), so by a union bound all of them satisfy \(|Z_x| \le (2/\varepsilon)\ln(n/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).
On that event, take any element \(x\). If it is listed, its error is \(|Z_x|\). If it appears in \(D\) but is not listed, then \(c_x + Z_x \le \tau\), so its error is \(c_x \le \tau + |Z_x|\). If it does not appear, both its count and its estimate are \(0\). In every case the error is at most Equation 10.6.


In the usual regime \(\delta \le 1/n\), the bound Equation 10.6 is at most \(1 + (2/\varepsilon)\big(2\ln(1/\delta) + \ln(1/\beta)\big)\). So every count is accurate to within a number of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), whatever the size of the domain. The Laplace histogram under pure DP pays \(\ln|\mathcal X|\) instead, and by the packing chapter pure DP cannot avoid that cost.

title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
text:
10.4 Privately bounding the local sensitivity
Propose-test-release guesses a bound and checks it. A second technique estimates the local sensitivity itself, privately, and uses the estimate as the noise scale. It applies when the local sensitivity does not change fast between neighbours, that is, when \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) has bounded global sensitivity.

Definition 10.6 (Noisy local sensitivity) Suppose that the local sensitivity changes by at most \(\lambda > 0\) between neighbours, that is, \(|\mathrm{LS}_f(D) - \mathrm{LS}_f(D')| \le \lambda\) for all \(D \sim D'\). Given \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), on input \(D\):

compute \(\hat s = \mathrm{LS}_f(D) + Z_1 + \lambda\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) with \(Z_1 \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\lambda/\varepsilon)\);
if \(\hat s \le 0\), output \(\bot\), and otherwise output \(f(D) + Z_2\) with \(Z_2 \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\hat s/\varepsilon)\).


The shift \(\lambda\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) makes the estimate \(\hat s\) an overestimate of \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)\) except with probability \(\delta/2\). On that good event, the noise is large enough for privacy. Paying both for the noisy estimate and for the release gives the factor \(2\varepsilon\) in the next theorem.

Theorem 10.4 Let \(\lambda > 0\) satisfy \(|\mathrm{LS}_f(D) - \mathrm{LS}_f(D')| \le \lambda\) for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), and let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). Then noisy local sensitivity with these parameters is \((2\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\). It suffices to prove the guarantee for the pair \((\hat s, \text{output})\), since the output alone is post-processing of it.

The good event. Let \(G = \{\hat s \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\}\), computed with the data \(D\). It fails only if \(Z_1 < -\lambda\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability \(\delta/2\).
Density of the scale. The function \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) has sensitivity \(\lambda\), so the density of \(\hat s\) on \(D\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\) times its density on \(D'\), at every value \(s\).
Density of the release. Fix a value \(s\) with \(s \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\) and \(s > 0\). Then \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le s\), so the Laplace density of scale \(s/\varepsilon\) at any \(y\) changes by a factor at most \(e^{\varepsilon |f(D) - f(D')|/s} \le e^{\varepsilon}\) between \(D\) and \(D'\).
Combining. On values of \(\hat s\) in \(G\), the joint density of \((\hat s, \text{output})\) on \(D\) is at most \(e^{2\varepsilon}\) times that on \(D'\), by steps 2 and 3. For an event \(S\), split on \(G\):

\[
\Pr[(\hat s, M(D)) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[(\hat s, M(D')) \in S] + \Pr[\text{not } G] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[(\hat s, M(D')) \in S] + \tfrac\delta2 .
\tag{10.8}\]

For each function, the local sensitivity at \(D\) and a bound \(\lambda\) on how fast it changes must be worked out by hand. The first takes up to \(n(|\mathcal X| - 1)\) evaluations of \(f\), one per neighbour. For some functions it is much faster, such as the mode, whose local sensitivity depends only on the two largest counts. The technique is simpler to run than propose-test-release, but it applies to fewer functions, because it needs the local sensitivity to change slowly everywhere.

title: 10  Beyond Global Sensitivity
text:
10.5 Smooth sensitivity
The last technique also lets the local sensitivity grow away from \(D\), but discounts each dataset by its distance. Take the closest-pair function of Example 10.1 on the bounded domain \(\mathcal X = [0, 10]\), so that its global sensitivity is finite. The dataset \(D = (0,0,0)\) still has local sensitivity \(0\), while its neighbour \((0,0,5)\) has local sensitivity at least \(5\). A safe noise scale at \(D\) must account for that neighbour, but less than for \(D\) itself.

Definition 10.7 (Smooth sensitivity) For a smoothing parameter \(s > 0\), the smooth sensitivity of \(f\) at \(D\) discounts the local sensitivity of every dataset \(D'\) by a factor \(e^{-s}\) for each record in which \(D'\) differs from \(D\):
\[
S_{f,s}(D) = \sup_{D' \in \mathcal X^n} \mathrm{LS}_f(D')\, e^{-s\, d(D, D')} ,
\tag{10.9}\]
where \(d\) is the Hamming distance.

The supremum ranges over all datasets, not only neighbours. Every dataset is within distance \(n\) of every other, so \(e^{-sn}\Delta f \le S_{f,s}(D) \le \Delta f\). The smooth sensitivity is therefore finite exactly when the global sensitivity is, and it can be smaller by a factor up to \(e^{sn}\). Two properties follow from the definition, and they are all that privacy needs.

Lemma 10.3 For every \(D\), \(S_{f,s}(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D)\). For all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), \(S_{f,s}(D) \le e^{s} S_{f,s}(D')\).


Proof. 

The term \(D' = D\) in the supremum is \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)\), so the supremum is at least that.
For any dataset \(W\), the triangle inequality gives \(d(D, W) \ge d(D', W) - 1\), so \(\mathrm{LS}_f(W)e^{-s\,d(D,W)} \le e^{s}\,\mathrm{LS}_f(W)e^{-s\,d(D',W)} \le e^{s} S_{f,s}(D')\). Taking the supremum over \(W\) gives the second claim.


Laplace noise scaled to the smooth sensitivity is not enough for pure DP. The scale moves by a factor up to \(e^{s}\) between neighbours, and far in the tail a Laplace density changes by much more than that when its scale changes. Noise with polynomial tails changes little under rescaling, and it works. The standard Cauchy distribution is such a noise, with density at a point \(z\) equal to
\[
h(z) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+z^2)} .
\tag{10.10}\]

Theorem 10.5 (Smooth sensitivity with Cauchy noise) Let \(f\) be non-constant with finite global sensitivity \(\Delta f\), let \(\varepsilon > 0\), and write \(S^* = S_{f, \varepsilon/2}\). The mechanism
\[
M(D) = f(D) + \frac{2\,S^*(D)}{\varepsilon}\, Z, \qquad Z \sim \text{standard Cauchy},
\tag{10.11}\]
is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

The scale is positive and finite. Some dataset \(W_0\) has \(\mathrm{LS}_f(W_0) > 0\) because \(f\) is not constant, and every \(D\) is within distance \(n\) of it, so \(S^*(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(W_0)e^{-\varepsilon n/2} > 0\). Every term of the supremum is at most \(\Delta f\), so \(S^*(D) \le \Delta f < \infty\).
Two facts about \(h\). The derivative of \(\ln(1+z^2)\) is \(2z/(1+z^2)\), which lies in \([-1, 1]\), so \(h(z)/h(z + u) \le e^{|u|}\) for all \(z\) and \(u\). For every real \(\kappa\) and \(v\), \(e^{-\kappa}h(v)/h(e^{\kappa}v) = e^{-\kappa}(1 + e^{2\kappa}v^2)/(1+v^2) \le e^{-\kappa}\max(1, e^{2\kappa}) = e^{|\kappa|}\).
The ratio of densities. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and write \(a = \varepsilon/2\). The density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is \((a/S^*(D))\,h\big(a(y - f(D))/S^*(D)\big)\). Set \(u = a(y - f(D))/S^*(D)\), \(w = a(f(D) - f(D'))/S^*(D)\) and \(e^{\kappa} = S^*(D)/S^*(D')\). Then \(a(y - f(D'))/S^*(D') = e^{\kappa}(u + w)\), and the ratio of the densities on \(D\) and \(D'\) is

\[
e^{-\kappa}\,\frac{h(u)}{h(e^{\kappa}(u+w))} = \frac{h(u)}{h(u+w)} \cdot \frac{e^{-\kappa}\,h(u+w)}{h(e^{\kappa}(u+w))} \le e^{|w|}\,e^{|\kappa|} ,
\tag{10.12}\]
by the two facts of step 2.

Bounding the exponents. By Lemma 10.3, \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le S^*(D)\), so \(|w| \le a = \varepsilon/2\). By the same lemma applied in both directions, \(|\kappa| \le \varepsilon/2\). The densities therefore differ by a factor at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\), and integrating over any event gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


The Cauchy distribution has such heavy tails that it has no mean. Its tail is \(\Pr[|Z| > z] = \frac2\pi\arctan(1/z) \le 2/(\pi z)\), so the error exceeds \(4S^*(D)/(\pi\varepsilon\beta)\) with probability at most \(\beta\). That bound grows as \(1/\beta\), while the exponential tails of Laplace or Gaussian noise give \(\ln(1/\beta)\). Those two noises, scaled to the smooth sensitivity with a smaller smoothing parameter, give approximate DP with lighter tails. Computing \(S_{f,s}\) means a maximum over all datasets, which is hard in general, but for the median it takes polynomial time.

title: 11  Packing Lower Bounds
text:
11.1 Two problems and their upper bounds
Every chapter so far has given an algorithm and proved how much data it needs. This chapter asks whether a cleverer algorithm could need less. For pure differential privacy (DP), a short argument called packing answers it. An accurate algorithm must put its output in a different region for each of many datasets. But a private one barely moves its output distribution between them. Both can hold only when the dataset is large enough.
The resulting lower bounds hold for every \(\varepsilon\)-DP algorithm, however it is built. On one-way marginals and histograms, they show that the simple Laplace-noise algorithms are optimal up to a constant or a logarithmic factor. They also show that pure DP costs strictly more than approximate DP there.
Both problems ask for many counting queries at once, answered as fractions of the dataset. The first has records that are \(d\) yes-or-no answers, and asks for the fraction of yes answers to each question.
The second problem has records that are symbols from a finite set, and asks for the fraction of records equal to each symbol.
For both problems, an answer \(y\) is judged by its worst coordinate, the \(\ell_\infty\) error \(\max_j |y_j - f_j(D)|\). So an answer with error at most \(\alpha\) gets every query right to within \(\alpha\) at once.
The upper bounds come from the Laplace mechanism. Suppose the vector of answers \(f\) has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity at most \(\Delta_1 f\), which means that \(\sum_j |f_j(D) - f_j(D')| \le \Delta_1 f\) for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), datasets that differ in one record (the replace-one relation). The Laplace mechanism releases \(f(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_d)\), where the noise terms \(Z_j\) are independent Laplace variables with scale \(\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon\), and it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The analysis needs only the tail of a Laplace variable \(Z\) with scale \(b\), for every \(s \ge 0\),
\[
\Pr[|Z| \ge s] = e^{-s/b} .
\tag{11.3}\]
Computing the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of each problem and applying this tail to every coordinate gives the two upper bounds that the rest of the chapter tries to beat.
Approximate DP does better on both problems. For the marginals, the Gaussian mechanism of the approximate DP chapter uses the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt d/n\) instead of the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(d/n\), and needs \(n\) only of order \(\sqrt{d \ln(1/\delta)\ln d}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\), a factor of about \(\sqrt d\) less. For histograms, the stability-based histogram of the previous chapter needs \(n\) of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) when \(\delta \le 1/n\), with no dependence on \(k\) at all. The rest of the chapter shows that under pure DP neither gain is possible.

title: 11  Packing Lower Bounds
text:
Definition 11.1 (One-way marginals) Let \(\mathcal X = \{0,1\}^d\). For a record \(x_i\), write \(x_{ij}\) for its coordinate \(j\). The one-way marginals of a dataset \(D \in \mathcal X^n\) are the \(d\) averages
\[
f_j(D) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}, \qquad j = 1, \dots, d .
\tag{11.1}\]



Definition 11.2 (Histogram) Let \(\mathcal X = [k] = \{1, \dots, k\}\). The normalized histogram of a dataset \(D \in [k]^n\) is the vector \(h(D) \in [0,1]^k\) with coordinates
\[
h_j(D) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf 1[x_i = j], \qquad j = 1, \dots, k ,
\tag{11.2}\]
where \(\mathbf 1[x_i = j]\) is \(1\) if record \(i\) equals \(j\) and \(0\) otherwise.






Proposition 11.1 Let \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\alpha > 0\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\). With probability at least \(1 - \beta\):

the Laplace mechanism for the \(d\) one-way marginals, with scale \(d/(n\varepsilon)\), has error at most \(d\ln(d/\beta)/(n\varepsilon)\);
the Laplace mechanism for the histogram over \([k]\), with scale \(2/(n\varepsilon)\), has error at most \(2\ln(k/\beta)/(n\varepsilon)\).

Both are \(\varepsilon\)-DP. So error at most \(\alpha\) with probability at least \(1/2\) needs only
\[
n \ge \frac{d \ln(2d)}{\alpha\varepsilon} \quad \text{for marginals}, \qquad n \ge \frac{2\ln(2k)}{\alpha\varepsilon} \quad \text{for histograms}.
\tag{11.4}\]


Proof. 

Sensitivity of the marginals. Replacing one record changes each average \(f_j\) by at most \(1/n\), so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of \((f_1, \dots, f_d)\) is at most \(d/n\). The Laplace mechanism with scale \(d/(n\varepsilon)\) is therefore \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Sensitivity of the histogram. Replacing a record equal to \(a\) by a record equal to \(a' \ne a\) lowers \(h_a\) by \(1/n\) and raises \(h_{a'}\) by \(1/n\), so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of \(h\) is \(2/n\). The scale \(2/(n\varepsilon)\) gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Union bound. For \(m\) Laplace variables with scale \(b\), the chance that some \(|Z_j|\) is at least \(s\) is at most \(m e^{-s/b}\). Setting this equal to \(\beta\) gives \(s = b \ln(m/\beta)\). With \(m = d\) and \(b = d/(n\varepsilon)\) this is claim 1, and with \(m = k\) and \(b = 2/(n\varepsilon)\) it is claim 2.
Sample size. Each error bound is at most \(\alpha\) exactly when \(n\) satisfies Equation 11.4 with \(\beta = 1/2\).

title: 11  Packing Lower Bounds
text:
11.2 The packing argument
The name comes from packing balls into a box, where only a limited number fit because the balls cannot overlap. Here the balls are regions of the output space that do not overlap, one for each of many datasets. Accuracy forces each dataset to send its output into its own region, and privacy forces every dataset to give every region some probability. The probabilities of disjoint regions add up to at most \(1\), so only a limited number of datasets can be packed.
The tool that connects datasets far apart is group privacy, from the Laplace mechanism chapter. The Hamming distance between two datasets in \(\mathcal X^n\) is the number of records in which they differ. Group privacy says that an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism \(M\) is \(t\varepsilon\)-DP for datasets at Hamming distance at most \(t\). So for such datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) and every event \(S\),
\[
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{t\varepsilon}\, \Pr[M(D') \in S] .
\tag{11.5}\]

11.2.1 A first example: the mode
The simplest instance of the argument is the mode of a dataset over \([k]\), the most frequent symbol. Take the \(k\) datasets \(D_1, \dots, D_k\), where \(D_j\) consists of \(n\) copies of the symbol \(j\). The mode of \(D_j\) is \(j\), and any two of these datasets are at Hamming distance \(n\). An accurate mechanism must answer \(j\) on \(D_j\) at least half the time, for every \(j\). Group privacy then forces each answer \(j\) to keep some probability on every other dataset as well, and \(k\) such probabilities cannot all fit into a total of \(1\) unless \(n\) is large.

Proposition 11.2 (Lower bound for the mode) Let \(k \ge 2\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\), and for each \(j \in [k]\) let \(D_j\) be the dataset of \(n\) copies of the symbol \(j\). Let \(M \colon [k]^n \to [k]\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and suppose that \(\Pr[M(D_j) = j] \ge 1/2\) for every \(j \in [k]\). Then
\[
n \ge \frac{\ln(k/2)}{\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.6}\]


Proof. 

Pigeonhole. Fix any \(j\). The \(k\) probabilities \(\Pr[M(D_j) = \ell]\), for \(\ell \in [k]\), sum to \(1\). So at least one symbol \(\ell\) has \(\Pr[M(D_j) = \ell] \le 1/k\), since otherwise the sum would exceed \(1\).
Accuracy. The mechanism is correct on \(D_\ell\) with probability at least \(1/2\), so \(\Pr[M(D_\ell) = \ell] \ge 1/2\).
Group privacy. The datasets \(D_\ell\) and \(D_j\) are at Hamming distance at most \(n\). By Equation 11.5 with the event \(\{\ell\}\),

\[
\frac12 \le \Pr[M(D_\ell) = \ell] \le e^{n\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D_j) = \ell] \le \frac{e^{n\varepsilon}}{k} .
\tag{11.7}\]

Rearranging. The chain gives \(e^{n\varepsilon} \ge k/2\), and taking logarithms gives \(n\varepsilon \ge \ln(k/2)\).


So a private mode needs a number of records of order \(\ln k/\varepsilon\). With \(k = 1{,}000\) symbols and \(\varepsilon = 1\), the bound is \(\ln 500 = 6.21\), so no \(1\)-DP algorithm finds the mode reliably from \(6\) records.


11.2.2 The packing theorem
The proof used three things: many datasets, disjoint sets of correct answers, and group privacy across a bounded distance. The theorem below keeps exactly these. It also lets the datasets be close to one common centre \(D\), at distance \(t\) that may be much smaller than \(n\), which the histogram bound will need.

Theorem 11.1 (Packing) Let \(D_1, \dots, D_m \in \mathcal X^n\) be datasets, each at Hamming distance at most \(t\) from a fixed dataset \(D \in \mathcal X^n\). Let \(S_1, \dots, S_m\) be pairwise disjoint subsets of the output space \(\mathcal Y\). If \(M\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathcal Y\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and, for some \(p > 0\),
\[
\Pr[M(D_\ell) \in S_\ell] \ge p \qquad \text{for every } \ell \in [m],
\tag{11.8}\]
then
\[
\frac1m \ge p\, e^{-t\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.9}\]


Proof. 

Accuracy and group privacy. Fix \(\ell\). The datasets \(D_\ell\) and \(D\) are at Hamming distance at most \(t\), so Equation 11.5 gives \(p \le \Pr[M(D_\ell) \in S_\ell] \le e^{t\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D) \in S_\ell]\). Hence \(\Pr[M(D) \in S_\ell] \ge p e^{-t\varepsilon}\).
Disjointness. The sets \(S_\ell\) are disjoint, so the probability of their union is the sum of their probabilities:

\[
1 \ge \Pr\Big[M(D) \in \bigcup_{\ell=1}^m S_\ell\Big] = \sum_{\ell=1}^m \Pr[M(D) \in S_\ell] \ge m\, p\, e^{-t\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.10}\]

Rearranging. Dividing by \(m\) gives Equation 11.9.


Taking logarithms, the theorem says that \(t\varepsilon \ge \ln(mp)\). With the trivial distance \(t = n\) and \(p = 1/2\), this reads \(n \ge \ln(m/2)/\varepsilon\), which is Proposition 11.2 again with \(m = k\). A lower bound on \(n\) therefore needs a packing with many datasets \(m\), accuracy regions that do not overlap, and a small distance \(t\) in terms of \(n\).

title: 11  Packing Lower Bounds
text:
11.3 One-way marginals
To make the answers on different datasets as different as possible, take datasets made of one repeated record. For each \(w \in \{0,1\}^d\), let \(D_w\) consist of \(n\) copies of \(w\). Its marginals are \(f(D_w) = w\), a corner of the cube \([0,1]^d\), and there are \(2^d\) corners. Two distinct corners differ by \(1\) in some coordinate, so an answer with every error below \(1/2\) points to a single corner. The packing theorem then applies with \(2^d\) datasets.

Theorem 11.2 (Lower bound for one-way marginals) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Let \(M\colon (\{0,1\}^d)^n \to \mathbb R^d\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and suppose that on every dataset \(D\), with probability at least \(1/2\), it answers every one-way marginal with error less than \(1/2\):
\[
\Pr\Big[\max_{j} |M(D)_j - f_j(D)| < \tfrac12\Big] \ge \tfrac12 .
\tag{11.11}\]
Then
\[
n \ge \frac{(d-1)\ln 2}{\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.12}\]


Proof. 

The packing. Use the \(m = 2^d\) datasets \(D_w\). For each \(w\), let \(S_w = \{y \in \mathbb R^d : |y_j - w_j| < 1/2 \text{ for all } j\}\) be the open \(\ell_\infty\) ball of radius \(1/2\) around the corner \(w\). Since \(f(D_w) = w\), the hypothesis says exactly that \(\Pr[M(D_w) \in S_w] \ge 1/2\).
Disjointness. Let \(w \ne w'\) differ in coordinate \(j\), so \(|w_j - w'_j| = 1\). For any \(y\), the triangle inequality gives \(|y_j - w_j| + |y_j - w'_j| \ge 1\), so the two distances cannot both be less than \(1/2\). Hence \(S_w\) and \(S_{w'}\) are disjoint.
Distance. Any two datasets in \(\mathcal X^n\) differ in at most \(n\) records, so every \(D_w\) is within Hamming distance \(t = n\) of \(D = D_{0}\), the all-zero dataset.
Packing. Theorem 11.1 with \(m = 2^d\), \(p = 1/2\) and \(t = n\) gives \(2^{-d} \ge \frac12 e^{-n\varepsilon}\). Taking logarithms, \(n\varepsilon \ge d\ln 2 - \ln 2\).


So \(n = \Omega(d/\varepsilon)\) records are necessary for error below \(1/2\) under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, against the upper bound \(d\ln(2d)/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) of Proposition 11.1. Under approximate DP, \(n\) of order \(\sqrt d\) suffices, so pure DP costs a factor \(\sqrt d\) more. A matching lower bound of order \(\sqrt d\) under approximate DP also holds. Packing cannot give it, because group privacy under \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP degrades too fast with \(t\), and the proof needs fingerprinting codes instead.
The bound above does not depend on \(\alpha\), because the packing uses corners of the cube, which are far apart. Datasets with only a few records changed have marginals closer together, and they give the factor \(1/\alpha\).

Corollary 11.1 Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\alpha \in (0, 1/2)\). If an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism \(M\colon (\{0,1\}^d)^n \to \mathbb R^d\) answers every one-way marginal with error at most \(\alpha\), with probability at least \(1/2\) on every dataset, then
\[
n \ge \frac{(d-1)\ln 2 - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.13}\]


Proof. 

The packing. Let \(t = \lfloor 2\alpha n\rfloor + 1\), so that \(t/n > 2\alpha\), and \(t \le n\) because \(2\alpha < 1\). For each \(w \in \{0,1\}^d\), let \(D_w\) consist of \(t\) copies of \(w\) and \(n - t\) copies of the all-zero record. Its marginals are \(f(D_w) = (t/n)\,w\).
Disjointness. Let \(S_w\) be the closed \(\ell_\infty\) ball of radius \(\alpha\) around \((t/n)\,w\), so that \(\Pr[M(D_w) \in S_w] \ge 1/2\) by hypothesis. If \(w \ne w'\) differ in coordinate \(j\), the centres differ by \(t/n > 2\alpha\) in that coordinate, and two closed intervals of half-width \(\alpha\) whose centres are more than \(2\alpha\) apart do not meet. So the sets \(S_w\) are pairwise disjoint.
Distance. Each \(D_w\) differs from the all-zero dataset in at most \(t\) records.
Packing. Theorem 11.1 with \(m = 2^d\) and \(p = 1/2\) gives \(\ln(2^{d-1}) \le t\varepsilon \le (2\alpha n + 1)\varepsilon\). Rearranging gives the claim.


For concrete parameters, the lower bound and the Laplace upper bound of Proposition 11.1 are within a modest factor of each other.

Example 11.1 With \(d = 1{,}000\) questions, \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), Corollary 11.1 says that \(n \ge 3{,}458\) is necessary, and Equation 11.4 says that \(n \ge 76{,}010\) suffices. The ratio, \(22.0\), is the factor \(\ln(2d) = 7.60\) times constants, and it grows only logarithmically with \(d\).

title: 11  Packing Lower Bounds
text:
11.4 Histograms
For histograms, the corner construction gives only the mode bound \(\ln(k/2)/\varepsilon\), with no \(\alpha\). The factor \(1/\alpha\) comes from datasets that are all close to one centre, as in Corollary 11.1. Take the centre \(D_1\) to be \(n\) copies of the symbol \(1\), and move a small block of records to another symbol.

Theorem 11.3 (Lower bound for histograms) Let \(k \ge 2\), \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\alpha \in (0, 1/2)\). If an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism \(M\colon [k]^n \to \mathbb R^k\) estimates the normalized histogram with error at most \(\alpha\),
\[
\Pr\Big[\max_j |M(D)_j - h_j(D)| \le \alpha\Big] \ge \tfrac12 \qquad\text{for every } D \in [k]^n,
\tag{11.14}\]
then
\[
n \ge \frac{\ln(k/2) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon} .
\tag{11.15}\]


Proof. 

The packing. Let \(t = \lfloor 2\alpha n\rfloor + 1\), so that \(t/n > 2\alpha\), and \(t \le n\) because \(2\alpha < 1\). Let \(D_1\) be \(n\) copies of the symbol \(1\), so its histogram puts all its mass on the symbol \(1\). For \(\ell = 2, \dots, k\), let \(D_\ell\) consist of \(t\) copies of \(\ell\) and \(n - t\) copies of \(1\). Its histogram \(h(D_\ell)\) puts mass \(t/n\) on the symbol \(\ell\), mass \(1 - t/n\) on the symbol \(1\), and nothing elsewhere.
Accuracy regions. Let \(S_\ell\) be the closed \(\ell_\infty\) ball of radius \(\alpha\) around \(h(D_\ell)\). The hypothesis applied to the dataset \(D_\ell\) says that \(\Pr[M(D_\ell) \in S_\ell] \ge 1/2\).
Disjointness. Take \(\ell \ne \ell'\). At least one of them is not \(1\), say \(\ell \ne 1\). In coordinate \(\ell\), the centre \(h(D_\ell)\) has value \(t/n\) and the centre \(h(D_{\ell'})\) has value \(0\), because \(D_{\ell'}\) contains only the symbols \(1\) and \(\ell'\). These differ by more than \(2\alpha\), so \(S_\ell\) and \(S_{\ell'}\) are disjoint.
Distance. Each \(D_\ell\) differs from \(D_1\) in at most \(t\) records, the ones not equal to \(1\).
Packing. Theorem 11.1 with \(m = k\), \(p = 1/2\) and centre \(D_1\) gives \(1/k \ge \frac12 e^{-t\varepsilon}\), that is, \(\ln(k/2) \le t\varepsilon\). Since \(t \le 2\alpha n + 1\), this gives \(\ln(k/2) \le (2\alpha n + 1)\varepsilon\), which rearranges to Equation 11.15.


Figure 11.1 shows the construction for \(k = 5\), \(n = 20\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\), where \(t = 5\) and each moved block holds a quarter of the records. In coordinate \(\ell\), the band of acceptable answers for \(D_\ell\) starts at \(0.15\), above the band of every other dataset, which ends at \(0.1\).






Figure 11.1: The packing behind Theorem 11.3, for \(k = 5\), \(n = 20\) and \(\alpha = 0.1\). Each panel shows the normalized histogram of one dataset as bars and the band of answers within \(\alpha\) of each count as a shaded box. Three of the five datasets are shown. Any two datasets have non-overlapping bands in at least one coordinate, so no answer is acceptable for both.



The choice of \(t\) produces the factor \(1/\alpha\). Moving the whole dataset, \(t = n\), would also give disjoint regions, but then the packing theorem would bound only \(n\varepsilon\), as in Proposition 11.2. A block of about \(2\alpha n\) records is just enough to separate the answers, and group privacy pays \(e^{t\varepsilon}\) for those \(t\) records only.

Example 11.2 With \(k = 10^6\) symbols, \(\alpha = 0.01\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), Equation 11.15 says that \(n \ge 607\) is necessary, and the Laplace histogram of Proposition 11.1 succeeds once \(n \ge 2{,}902\). The ratio is \(4.8\), and as \(k\) grows it falls towards \(4\), because the upper bound is \(2\ln(2k)/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) and the lower bound is about \(\ln k/(2\alpha\varepsilon)\). The union bound in Proposition 11.1 is nearly tight. In simulation with \(k = 10^4\) and \(n = 1{,}981\), the value Equation 11.4 gives for that \(k\), the Laplace histogram met error \(\alpha\) in \(217\) of \(400\) runs, \(54\%\), against the \(50\%\) that the bound guarantees.

So under pure DP the Laplace histogram is optimal up to a constant factor, and the \(\ln k\) in its sample size cannot be removed. The stability-based histogram, which replaces \(\ln k\) by \(\ln(1/\delta)\), shows that this cost belongs to pure DP and not to the problem.

title: Private Learning and Statistics
text:
The earlier parts released statistics of a fixed dataset under differential privacy (DP). This part turns to the goals of machine learning and statistics, which are to fit models and to learn about the population that the data comes from. It starts with the question of what privacy must protect, because a model can predict a person’s sensitive label without any use of that person’s record. Then it trains convex models and neural networks privately, and finds how many samples a private estimate of a population mean needs. Last, it shows that a private mechanism lets one dataset answer adaptively chosen questions without overfitting. Table 1 gives the question of each chapter.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




What differential privacy protects
Which inferences from a trained model are privacy violations, and which are learning at work?


Private empirical risk minimization
How can a convex model be fitted privately, and at what cost in accuracy?


Private deep learning
How are neural networks trained privately, and how tightly can their privacy be accounted?


Private mean estimation
How many samples does a private estimate of a population mean need?


Adaptive data analysis
How can one dataset answer adaptively chosen questions without overfitting?

title: 12  What Differential Privacy Protects
text:
12.1 What the definition promises
Machine learning on sensitive data often gives results that feel invasive, but not each of them is a privacy violation. This chapter gives a test that separates the inferences that differential privacy (DP) must prevent from those it allows. Two facts support the test. A private learner can still find a rule that predicts a person’s sensitive label, but it cannot memorize a secret that is only in one person’s records.
Recall the definition from the randomized response chapter. Two datasets \(D \sim D'\) are neighbours if they differ by the replacement of one record. A mechanism \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if, for all such pairs and all sets \(S\) of outputs,
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr[M(D')\in S].
\tag{12.1}\]
So the output changes little when one record changes, and the definition says nothing more. Two properties from the Laplace mechanism chapter turn the definition into a statement about attackers. Post-processing says that a function of the output of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism, computed with coins independent of the data, is again \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Group privacy says that if \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in some number \(k\) of entries, then
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in S].
\tag{12.2}\]
Write \(D^{(i \leftarrow z)}\) for the dataset \(D\) with entry \(i\) replaced by a record \(z\). An attacker is any function \(\mathcal A\) of the output, possibly randomized, that answers \(1\) when it believes it has learned something harmful. The attacker may know every other record and any side information, because all of that is fixed in \(\mathcal A\). The first fact compares its chance to answer \(1\) on the real dataset and on the dataset with one record replaced.
So a harm that the output causes a person is about as likely when a placeholder replaces their record. The definition does not try to stop that harm. This gives three questions to ask of an alleged violation.
The second question matters most. If an inference about a person is exactly what an accurate model predicts, the only way to prevent it is to release an inaccurate model, for example one that ignores the data. That is always possible and always useless.

title: 12  What Differential Privacy Protects
text:
Proposition 12.1 (What an attacker gains from one record) Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and let \(\mathcal A\) be a randomized function of the output whose coins are independent of the coins of \(M\). Then for every dataset \(D\), every index \(i\) and every record \(z\),
\[
\Pr\big[\mathcal A(M(D)) = 1\big] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr\big[\mathcal A(M(D^{(i\leftarrow z)})) = 1\big].
\tag{12.3}\]


Proof. 

The composed algorithm \(\mathcal A \circ M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by post-processing.
The datasets \(D\) and \(D^{(i\leftarrow z)}\) differ in at most one entry, so they are neighbours or equal. The definition, applied to the event \(\{1\}\), gives the inequality.




Is the result substantially different if one person’s record is changed or left out?
Is the harmful inference the same thing as the accuracy of the learned model?
If the inference still feels wrong, at what point, and by whom, was the information given away?

title: 12  What Differential Privacy Protects
section: 12.2 Learning a rule is not a violation
text:
12.2 Learning a rule is not a violation
A learning algorithm takes a training set of pairs \((x_i, y_i)\), where \(x_i\) is a feature vector and \(y_i\) a label. It outputs a classifier, a function that maps a feature vector to a predicted label. In the private setting, the training set is the sensitive dataset, and the classifier is the output that must be differentially private. The test points that measure its accuracy are not protected.
Take a simple training set of real pairs,
\[
(0, 1),\ (2, 3),\ (5, 6),\ (-6, -5),\ (0.5, 1.5),\ (\pi, \pi+1),\ \dots
\tag{12.4}\]
in which every label is one more than its feature. Any reasonable learner finds the rule \(y = x + 1\). At \(x = 4\), which is not in the training set, it predicts \(5\). At \(x = \pi\), it predicts \(\pi + 1\), which is the true label of a training record. That is not a violation, because the learner found a fact about the population. The prediction at \(x = \pi\) is the same if the record \((\pi, \pi+1)\) was never collected.
A private algorithm makes this exact. Each record gives an offset \(y_i - x_i\), and a rule \(y = x + b\) is a choice of offset. The stability-based histogram of the chapter on beyond global sensitivity releases the offsets that many records share, although offsets are real numbers with infinitely many possible bins. Its guarantee is approximate DP, \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, from the approximate DP chapter, which adds a slack \(\delta\) to the bound of the definition:
\[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta \quad\text{for all } D \sim D' \text{ and all } S.
\tag{12.5}\]
The algorithm adds Laplace noise to the count of each offset and releases the offsets whose noisy count is above a threshold.

Definition 12.1 (Stable histogram of offsets) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), and set the threshold
\[
\tau = 1 + \frac{2\ln(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{12.6}\]
On input \(D = ((x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n))\), a list of \(n\) records with real entries, let \(c_b = |\{i : y_i - x_i = b\}|\) be the number of records whose offset is \(b\). For each \(b\) with \(c_b > 0\), draw an independent \(Z_b\) from the Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) with scale \(2/\varepsilon\), and output the set
\[
M(D) = \{\, b : c_b > 0 \text{ and } c_b + Z_b > \tau \,\}.
\tag{12.7}\]

This is the stability-based histogram on the offsets \(y_i - x_i\), with the noisy counts dropped from its output. Bins with count zero are never released, and the threshold \(\tau\) stops the release of a bin that one record holds, except with small probability. So the guarantee of the histogram carries over.

Theorem 12.1 The stable histogram of offsets is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Replacing one record changes at most one offset, so when \(D \sim D'\) the two lists of offsets are neighbours or equal.
The stability-based histogram is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP on datasets of offsets, by the theorem of that chapter.
The output \(M(D)\) is the set of elements on the histogram’s list, a function of that output alone. So it is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP by post-processing, which holds for approximate DP as well.


The privacy cost does not depend on how many records follow the rule. Accuracy only needs enough of them to clear the threshold.

Proposition 12.2 Suppose every record satisfies \(y_i = x_i + 1\), let \(\tau\) be the threshold of Definition 12.1, and let \(\beta \in (0, 1/2)\) be a failure probability. If
\[
n \ge \tau + \frac{2}{\varepsilon}\ln\frac{1}{2\beta},
\tag{12.8}\]
then with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) the output is exactly \(\{1\}\), and the released rule predicts \(y = x + 1\) at every feature value.


Proof. 

Only the offset \(1\) has a positive count, \(c_1 = n\), because all \(n\) records have that offset. So the output is either \(\{1\}\) or empty.
The output is empty when the Laplace noise \(Z_1\) on that count satisfies \(n + Z_1 \le \tau\). A \(\mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\) variable \(Z\) has \(\Pr[Z \le -s] = \tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon s/2}\) for every \(s \ge 0\). With \(s = n - \tau\), which is not negative because \(n \ge \tau\), this gives \[
\Pr[Z_1 \le -(n-\tau)] = \tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon(n-\tau)/2}.
\tag{12.9}\]
The assumed bound on \(n\) makes this at most \(\beta\).



Example 12.1 Take \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(\beta = 0.01\). With these values the threshold is \(\tau = 1 + 2\ln(10^{6}) = 1 + 2 \times 13.82 = 28.63\). The bound on \(n\) adds \(2\ln 50 = 7.82\) to it, which gives \(36.45\). So \(37\) records that follow the rule are enough for the private algorithm to output it with probability at least \(0.99\).

So Proposition 12.1 protects the record \((\pi, \pi+1)\), but the rule predicts the label of that record exactly. The prediction follows from the rule, and the rule is a fact about nature. If this still feels like a leak, the third question finds the point of the leak. It is the moment when someone revealed that the person’s feature value is \(\pi\), because after that anyone who knows the rule can calculate the label.

title: 12  What Differential Privacy Protects
text:
12.3 Inferences from what people reveal
The same pattern explains examples that people often present as privacy failures. Take a smoker who must decide whether to join a study of whether smoking causes cancer, and fears higher insurance premiums if the study publishes the link. This is the rule \(y = x + 1\) in another form. The feature is “smokes”, the label is “likely to develop cancer”, and the study reaches the same conclusion without this person. The only way to prevent the harm is not to run the study. The person gave up privacy when their smoking became known.

title: 12  What Differential Privacy Protects
text:
12.4 What a violation looks like
A violation is an inference that depends on the presence of the person’s own sensitive record in the dataset.
The Netflix Prize. Netflix released movie ratings with dates under pseudonymous user identifiers. Narayanan and Shmatikov linked them to public reviews on the Internet Movie Database, and so found films that the matched users had rated but never reviewed in public. Without a user’s record, that reidentification is impossible, so it fails the first question. In contrast, an analyst who sees that a user reviewed the first and third films of a trilogy may guess that they watched the second. That guess uses only what the user chose to publish, so it is not a violation.
Memorized secrets. Carlini and coauthors trained language models on text with a secret, such as a nine-digit identification number, that one person had typed several times. The model gave the secret an unusually high likelihood, and a search guided by those scores could extract it. This is a violation. A model that learned only the language has no reason to prefer one nine-digit number to another, so the preference comes from that person’s records. DP prevents it, with group privacy for the repetitions, as the next proposition shows.

Proposition 12.3 (Secrets are not memorized) Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite set of \(N\) possible secrets. For each \(s \in \mathcal S\), let \(D(s)\) be a training set in which \(k\) entries depend on \(s\) and the other entries do not. Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and let \(G\) be any guessing rule, with coins independent of \(M\), that maps the trained model to an element of \(\mathcal S\). If the secret \(s\) is drawn uniformly from \(\mathcal S\), then
\[
\Pr\big[G(M(D(s))) = s\big] \le \frac{e^{k\varepsilon}}{N}.
\tag{12.10}\]


Proof. 

Let \(D_0\) be the training set with the \(k\) entries that depend on the secret replaced by fixed placeholder records. For every \(s\), the datasets \(D(s)\) and \(D_0\) differ in at most \(k\) entries.
By post-processing and group privacy, \(\Pr[G(M(D(s))) = s] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[G(M(D_0)) = s]\) for every \(s\).
The guess on \(D_0\) does not depend on \(s\), and it equals at most one secret, so \(\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\Pr[G(M(D_0)) = s] \le 1\).
The average of step 2 over the uniform secret, with step 3, gives \[
\Pr\big[G(M(D(s))) = s\big] = \frac1N\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\Pr\big[G(M(D(s))) = s\big] \le \frac{e^{k\varepsilon}}{N}.
\tag{12.11}\]


For a nine-digit number, \(N = 10^9\). With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and a secret typed \(k = 4\) times, the chance of the attacker is at most \(e^4/10^9 = 5.5\times10^{-8}\), against \(10^{-9}\) for a blind guess. The bound grows exponentially in \(k\). So a person who contributes many records needs a guarantee per person, not per record.
