title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
text:
13.1 Empirical risk minimization
Most of machine learning fits a model by minimizing its average loss on a training set. This chapter asks how to do that under differential privacy (DP) when the loss is convex. Noise can go into the output of a non-private solver, into the objective that the solver minimizes, or into each step of gradient descent. The chapter proves a privacy guarantee for each of the three methods. It also proves an accuracy guarantee for the third, which the next chapter scales to neural networks.
Each record \(z = (x, y)\) is a pair of a feature vector \(x\) and a label \(y\), and the dataset \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\) holds \(n\) records. A parameter vector \(\theta\) in \(\mathbb R^d\) describes a model. A loss function \(\ell(\theta; z)\) measures how badly the model \(\theta\) fits the record \(z\). To fit a model is to choose \(\theta\) from a set of allowed values so that the total loss over the dataset is small. The definition also says how to measure an algorithm that only comes close to the best choice.
The problem is called empirical risk minimization (ERM). In practice the loss on new data matters. But where a uniform convergence argument applies, a good empirical minimizer also has a small loss on new data. So this chapter studies only the empirical problem.
In this generality the problem is hopeless, so the chapter makes three assumptions. The set of allowed parameters is bounded, which its diameter measures. The loss is convex, so that a local minimum is a global one, and Lipschitz, so that it cannot change quickly. The definitions below make these terms precise, with the subgradient, which replaces the gradient where a convex function has a kink.
So the chapter assumes that \(\Theta\) has finite diameter. It also assumes that, for every record \(z\), the loss \(\theta \mapsto \ell(\theta; z)\) is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\). A convex function that is finite on all of \(\mathbb R^d\) has a subgradient at every point. Write \(\nabla\ell(\theta; z)\) for a gradient, or a subgradient where \(\ell\) is not differentiable. Lipschitz continuity matters to privacy because it bounds every gradient, and so the effect of one record on a gradient step.
The most common losses are convex, and most of them are Lipschitz when the features are bounded.
Stronger assumptions, such as strong convexity or smoothness of the loss, give faster rates, but the chapter does not need them. Until Section 13.5, the solver of this convex problem is a black box.

title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
text:
Definition 13.1 (Empirical risk minimization) Let \(\Theta \subseteq \mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty, closed, convex set of allowed parameters. The empirical risk of \(\theta\) on \(D\) is the total loss
\[
\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\theta; z_i),
\tag{13.1}\]
and \(\theta^* \in \Theta\) denotes a minimizer of \(\mathcal L(\cdot\,; D)\) over \(\Theta\). An algorithm that outputs \(\tilde\theta \in \Theta\) has excess empirical risk \(\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D)] - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), where the expectation is over the algorithm’s coins only. The dataset is fixed.




Definition 13.2 (Diameter, convexity, Lipschitz continuity)  

The diameter of \(\Theta\) is \(\|\Theta\|_2 = \sup_{\theta, \theta' \in \Theta}\|\theta - \theta'\|_2\).
A function \(f\) on a convex set \(K\) is convex if \(f(t\theta + (1-t)\theta') \le t f(\theta) + (1-t)f(\theta')\) for all \(\theta, \theta' \in K\) and \(t \in [0,1]\).
A function \(f\) on \(K\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz if \(|f(\theta) - f(\theta')| \le L\|\theta - \theta'\|_2\) for all \(\theta, \theta' \in K\).
A vector \(g\) is a subgradient of a convex \(f\) at \(\theta\) if \(f(\theta') \ge f(\theta) + \langle g, \theta' - \theta\rangle\) for all \(\theta'\). Where \(f\) is differentiable, its gradient \(\nabla f(\theta)\), the vector of partial derivatives, is the only subgradient.




Lemma 13.1 If a convex function \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\), then every subgradient \(g\) of \(f\) satisfies \(\|g\|_2 \le L\).


Proof. 

Suppose \(g \ne 0\), take any point \(\theta\), and set \(u = g/\|g\|_2\). The definition of a subgradient at \(\theta' = \theta + u\) gives \(f(\theta + u) - f(\theta) \ge \langle g, u\rangle = \|g\|_2\).
The Lipschitz condition gives \(f(\theta+u) - f(\theta) \le L\|u\|_2 = L\). The two bounds together give \(\|g\|_2 \le L\).




Example 13.1 (Common losses) Take \(x, \theta \in \mathbb R^d\).

Linear regression, \(y \in \mathbb R\): the squared loss \(\ell(\theta; x, y) = (\langle x, \theta\rangle - y)^2\). It is convex, and Lipschitz only on bounded sets.
Logistic regression, \(y \in \{-1, 1\}\): \(\ell(\theta; x, y) = \ln\big(1 + e^{-y\langle x, \theta\rangle}\big)\). Its gradient is \(-y\,x/(1 + e^{y\langle x,\theta\rangle})\), of norm at most \(\|x\|_2\), so it is \(\|x\|_2\)-Lipschitz.
Geometric median, no label: \(\ell(\theta; x) = \|\theta - x\|_2\). By the triangle inequality it is \(1\)-Lipschitz. In one dimension it is \(|\theta - x|\), and its minimizer is the median.
Support vector machine (SVM), \(y \in \{-1, 1\}\): the hinge loss \(\ell(\theta; x, y) = \max(0, 1 - y\langle x, \theta\rangle)\). It is a maximum of two functions that are linear in \(\theta\), so it is convex and \(\|x\|_2\)-Lipschitz.

title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
section: 13.2 Why the minimizer is not private
text:
13.2 Why the minimizer is not private
An exact minimizer can reveal records outright, and the median is the simplest case.

Proposition 13.1 Let \(d = 1\), \(\ell(\theta; x) = |\theta - x|\), records in \([-R, R]\) with \(R > 0\), \(\Theta = [-R, R]\), and \(n\) odd. Then the empirical risk has a unique minimizer, the median \(x_{(m)}\) with \(m = (n+1)/2\), where \(x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}\) are the sorted records. The algorithm that outputs it is not \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta < 1\).


Proof. 

Away from the records, the function \(\theta \mapsto \sum_i |\theta - x_i|\) has slope equal to the number of records below \(\theta\) minus the number above. For \(\theta < x_{(m)}\) at least \(m\) records lie above, so the slope is at most \((m-1) - m = -1\). For \(\theta > x_{(m)}\) the slope is at least \(1\) in the same way. The function is continuous, so \(x_{(m)}\) is its unique minimizer.
On the dataset with every record equal to \(-R\) the output is \(-R\), and on the dataset with every record equal to \(R\) it is \(R\). A path of \(n\) replacements joins the two datasets, so some neighbours \(D \sim D'\) along it have different outputs \(v \ne v'\).
The algorithm is deterministic. For the event \(S = \{v\}\) this gives \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = 1\) and \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = 0\), and \(1 \le e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 + \delta\) fails for every \(\delta < 1\).


To privatize each record before any non-private algorithm is local DP, which needs far more data for the same accuracy. So the three methods below add noise after the data is pooled.

title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
text:
13.3 Output perturbation
The obvious method computes the minimizer and adds noise scaled to its sensitivity. But Proposition 13.1 shows that the minimizer can have large sensitivity, and regularization is the fix.
Polynomial regression shows the problem. With records \((x_i, y_i) \in \mathbb R^2\) and the squared loss \(\ell(\theta; x, y) = \big(\sum_{j=0}^{p}\theta_j x^j - y\big)^2\), the model is a polynomial of degree \(p\). If the degree is as high as \(p = n - 1\), then for distinct features the minimizer passes through every point. Its excess risk is zero, but it fits new data poorly and swings wildly when one point moves. These are two views of the same instability, as the left panel of Figure 13.1 shows.
Regularization adds a penalty that favours simple models. For a function \(N\) of the parameters alone, called the regularizer, and a weight \(\lambda > 0\), the regularized objective is
\[
F_D(\theta) = \mathcal L(\theta; D) + \lambda N(\theta).
\tag{13.2}\]
At \(\lambda = 0\) there is no regularization, and as \(\lambda \to \infty\) the data is ignored. The usual choice is \(N(\theta) = \tfrac12\|\theta\|_2^2\). Its effect on sensitivity comes from strong convexity, which asks that the function curve upward by at least a fixed amount everywhere. For the regularized objective, that amount is the weight \(\lambda\).

Definition 13.3 (Strong convexity) For \(\lambda > 0\), a function \(f\) on a convex set \(K\) is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex if, for all \(\theta, \theta' \in K\) and \(t \in [0,1]\),
\[
f(t\theta + (1-t)\theta') \le t f(\theta) + (1-t) f(\theta') - \frac\lambda2\, t(1-t)\,\|\theta - \theta'\|_2^2 .
\tag{13.3}\]

The function \(\tfrac12\|\theta\|_2^2\) is \(1\)-strongly convex, with equality, by the identity \(t\|a\|^2 + (1-t)\|b\|^2 - \|ta + (1-t)b\|^2 = t(1-t)\|a - b\|^2\). A \(\lambda\)-strongly convex function plus a convex function is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex. The next lemma shows that such a function grows at least quadratically away from its minimizer.

Lemma 13.2 Let \(f\) be \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on a convex set \(K\), with a minimizer \(\hat\theta\) over \(K\). Then for every \(\theta \in K\),
\[
f(\theta) - f(\hat\theta) \ge \frac\lambda2\|\theta - \hat\theta\|_2^2 .
\tag{13.4}\]
In particular, the minimizer is unique.


Proof. 

For \(t \in (0, 1)\), the point \(\hat\theta + t(\theta - \hat\theta)\) lies in \(K\), so its value is at least \(f(\hat\theta)\).
Strong convexity, applied with weight \(t\) on \(\theta\), bounds that value by \(t f(\theta) + (1-t) f(\hat\theta) - \frac\lambda2 t(1-t)\|\theta - \hat\theta\|_2^2\).
The two bounds together, divided by \(t\), give \(f(\theta) - f(\hat\theta) \ge \frac\lambda2(1-t)\|\theta - \hat\theta\|_2^2\). Letting \(t \to 0\) gives the claim.
A second minimizer \(\theta\) would have \(f(\theta) - f(\hat\theta) = 0\), which forces \(\theta = \hat\theta\).


This growth keeps the regularized minimizer stable. When one record changes, the two regularized objectives differ by a Lipschitz function. Each objective grows quadratically around its own minimizer, so the two minimizers cannot be far apart.

Theorem 13.1 (Sensitivity of the regularized minimizer) Let \(\Theta\) be nonempty, closed, convex and bounded. Suppose that for every record \(z\) the loss \(\ell(\cdot\,; z)\) is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\Theta\), and that \(N\) is continuous and \(1\)-strongly convex. For each dataset \(D\), let \(\theta_D\) be the minimizer of \(F_D = \mathcal L(\cdot\,; D) + \lambda N\) over \(\Theta\). Then for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), which differ in one replaced record,
\[
\|\theta_D - \theta_{D'}\|_2 \le \frac{2L}{\lambda}.
\tag{13.5}\]


Proof. 

\(F_D\) is continuous on the closed bounded set \(\Theta\), so it has a minimizer, and it is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, so the minimizer is unique by Lemma 13.2. The same holds for \(F_{D'}\).
Write \(\theta = \theta_D\) and \(\theta' = \theta_{D'}\). Lemma 13.2 applied to each function gives \[
F_D(\theta') - F_D(\theta) \ge \frac\lambda2\|\theta - \theta'\|_2^2, \qquad F_{D'}(\theta) - F_{D'}(\theta') \ge \frac\lambda2\|\theta - \theta'\|_2^2 .
\tag{13.6}\]
Add the two inequalities. The left side becomes \(h(\theta') - h(\theta)\), where \(h = F_D - F_{D'}\), and the right side becomes \(\lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|_2^2\).
If \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in record \(j\), then \(h(\cdot) = \ell(\cdot\,; z_j) - \ell(\cdot\,; z'_j)\) is a difference of two \(L\)-Lipschitz functions, so \(h(\theta') - h(\theta) \le 2L\|\theta - \theta'\|_2\).
So \(\lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|_2^2 \le 2L\|\theta - \theta'\|_2\), and dividing by \(\lambda\|\theta - \theta'\|_2\) gives the claim. If \(\theta = \theta'\), there is nothing to prove.


The bound depends on neither \(n\) nor the dimension, and the Gaussian mechanism of the approximate DP chapter does the rest. Take a function \(f\) whose \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the largest change in Euclidean norm between neighbours, is \(\Delta_2 f\). The mechanism adds Gaussian noise \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) with standard deviation \(\sigma\) in each coordinate. For every \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\) it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the relaxation that allows an additive slack \(\delta\), when
\[
\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2 f}{\varepsilon}\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon}.
\tag{13.7}\]
The mechanism applied to the regularized minimizer \(f(D) = \theta_D\), with \(\Delta_2 f = 2L/\lambda\), gives the first private algorithm.

Theorem 13.2 (Output perturbation) Under the assumptions of Theorem 13.1, let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). The algorithm that outputs \(\tilde\theta = \theta_D + b\), where \(\theta_D\) is the regularized minimizer, with \(b \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) and
\[
\sigma = \frac{2L}{\lambda}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta) + \varepsilon}}{\varepsilon},
\tag{13.8}\]
is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. So is its projection onto \(\Theta\).


Proof. The map \(D \mapsto \theta_D\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity at most \(2L/\lambda\) by Theorem 13.1, so the Gaussian mechanism gives the guarantee. The projection is post-processing.







Figure 13.1: Polynomials of degree \(9\) fitted by least squares to \(10\) points, on a dataset and on a neighbour with one label raised (the square). Without regularization, both fits pass through every point, and one moved point changes the whole curve. With the penalty \(\tfrac\lambda2\|\theta\|_2^2\), the two fits stay close.



Output perturbation is simple and works with any exact solver. But its accuracy is often weak, because the regularization that privacy needs can be far from the one that fits the data best.

title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
text:
13.4 Objective perturbation
The second method adds noise to the objective instead of the output. It minimizes
\[
J_b(\theta) = \mathcal L(\theta; D) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|_2^2 + \langle b, \theta\rangle
\tag{13.9}\]
for a random vector \(b\), and releases the exact minimizer. The linear term rewards or penalizes each direction of the parameter space by a random amount.
The proof below is for losses of generalized linear form, such as logistic regression and smoothed versions of the hinge loss. Such a loss is \(\ell(\theta; x, y) = \phi(\langle x, \theta\rangle, y)\). For each label \(y\), the scalar function \(u \mapsto \phi(u, y)\) is convex and twice continuously differentiable, with derivatives \(|\phi'| \le L\) and \(0 \le \phi'' \le \beta\). The features satisfy \(\|x\|_2 \le 1\). So the gradient \(\nabla\ell = \phi'(\langle x,\theta\rangle, y)\,x\) has norm at most \(L\). The Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, is \(\nabla^2\ell = \phi''(\langle x,\theta\rangle, y)\,xx^\top\), with rank at most one and eigenvalues in \([0, \beta]\).
The proof compares the densities of the output on two neighbouring datasets. So it needs a criterion in terms of densities, from the approximate DP chapter. Write \(p_D\) for the density of the output when the dataset is \(D\). The privacy loss of an output \(\theta\) is \(\ln\big(p_D(\theta)/p_{D'}(\theta)\big)\), which is large when \(\theta\) is much more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\). The criterion says that \(M\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP if, for every ordered pair of neighbours, an output drawn from \(M(D)\) has privacy loss above \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\).

Theorem 13.3 (Objective perturbation) Let \(\Theta = \mathbb R^d\), and let \(\ell\) be a generalized linear loss as above, with \(|\phi'| \le L\), \(0 \le \phi'' \le \beta\) and features of norm at most \(1\). Let \(\varepsilon \in (0, 4]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), and set
\[
\lambda \ge \frac{\beta}{e^{\varepsilon/2} - 1}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{4L\big(1 + \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\big)}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{13.10}\]
Then the algorithm that draws \(b \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\) and outputs the exact minimizer \(\tilde\theta\) of \(J_b\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

The output as a function of the noise. For each \(b\), the function \(J_b\) is continuous and \(\lambda\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^d\), so it has a unique minimizer, where its gradient vanishes. So \(\tilde\theta = \theta\) exactly when \(b = g_D(\theta)\), where \(g_D(\theta) = -\nabla\mathcal L(\theta; D) - \lambda\theta\). Every \(\theta\) is the minimizer for the noise \(g_D(\theta)\), and each noise has one minimizer, so \(g_D\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb R^d\) and \(\tilde\theta = g_D^{-1}(b)\).
The density of the output. The map \(g_D\) is continuously differentiable with Jacobian \(-(H_D(\theta) + \lambda I)\), where \(H_D(\theta) = \sum_i \nabla^2\ell(\theta; z_i)\) is positive semidefinite. By the change of variables formula, \(\tilde\theta\) has density \[
p_D(\theta) = \varphi_\sigma\big(g_D(\theta)\big)\,\det\big(H_D(\theta) + \lambda I\big),
\tag{13.11}\] where \(\varphi_\sigma\) is the density of \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2 I_d)\).
The determinants. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in the last record, \(z = (x, y)\) in \(D\) and \(z' = (x', y')\) in \(D'\). Fix \(\theta\) and write \(A = \sum_{i<n}\nabla^2\ell(\theta; z_i) + \lambda I\), which satisfies \(A \succeq \lambda I\). Then \(H_D + \lambda I = A + a\,xx^\top\) with \(a = \phi''(\langle x,\theta\rangle, y) \in [0,\beta]\). The matrix determinant lemma gives \[
\det(A + a\,xx^\top) = \det(A)\,\big(1 + a\,x^\top A^{-1}x\big) \in \big[\det A,\ (1 + \beta/\lambda)\det A\big],
\tag{13.12}\] because \(0 \le x^\top A^{-1} x \le \|x\|_2^2/\lambda \le 1/\lambda\). The same holds for \(D'\). So the ratio of the two determinants is at most \(1 + \beta/\lambda \le e^{\varepsilon/2}\), by the choice of \(\lambda\).
The Gaussian factors. The two noise vectors that lead to \(\theta\) differ by \(u = g_{D'}(\theta) - g_D(\theta) = \nabla\ell(\theta; z) - \nabla\ell(\theta; z')\). This vector has norm at most \(2L\), and it lies in the subspace \(V\) spanned by \(x\) and \(x'\), which does not depend on \(\theta\). With \(b = g_D(\theta)\) and \(P_V\) the orthogonal projection onto \(V\), \[
\ln\frac{\varphi_\sigma(b)}{\varphi_\sigma(b + u)} = \frac{2\langle b, u\rangle + \|u\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2} \le \frac{2L\,\|P_V b\|_2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{2L^2}{\sigma^2},
\tag{13.13}\] by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to \(\langle b, u\rangle = \langle P_V b, u\rangle\).
The privacy loss. When the output is drawn from \(M(D)\), the vector \(g_D(\tilde\theta)\) is the noise \(b\) itself. Steps 2 to 4 bound the privacy loss at the output by \[
\ln\frac{p_D(\tilde\theta)}{p_{D'}(\tilde\theta)} \le \frac\varepsilon2 + \frac{2L\,\|P_V b\|_2}{\sigma^2} + \frac{2L^2}{\sigma^2}.
\tag{13.14}\]
The tail. The subspace \(V\) has dimension \(d_V \le 2\), so \(\|P_V b\|_2^2/\sigma^2\) is chi-squared with \(d_V\) degrees of freedom. Its tail is at most that of two degrees of freedom, which is \(e^{-r/2}\) beyond \(r\). Write \(s = \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) for the cut-off. Then \[
\Pr\big[\|P_V b\|_2 > \sigma s\big] \le e^{-s^2/2} = \delta .
\tag{13.15}\]
Outside that event, substituting \(\sigma = 4L(1+s)/\varepsilon\) into step 5 gives \[
\ln\frac{p_D(\tilde\theta)}{p_{D'}(\tilde\theta)} \le \frac\varepsilon2 + \frac\varepsilon2\left(\frac{s}{1+s} + \frac{\varepsilon}{4(1+s)^2}\right) \le \frac\varepsilon2 + \frac\varepsilon2\cdot\frac{s + 1}{1+s} = \varepsilon,
\tag{13.16}\] where the second step uses \(\varepsilon \le 4\) and \(1/(1+s)^2 \le 1/(1+s)\).
The privacy loss criterion turns this bound into \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


The theorem has a practical weakness. It holds only for the exact minimizer, and a real solver never returns one. Iterative solvers such as gradient descent only approach the minimizer. Floating-point arithmetic cannot represent most real numbers, and even a naive floating-point Laplace mechanism leaks the data through the low-order bits of its output (Mironov). Later versions of objective perturbation need only an approximate minimizer.

title: 13  Private Empirical Risk Minimization
text:
13.5 Gradient perturbation
The third method, now the standard one, runs gradient descent and adds noise to each gradient. Its analysis starts from the non-private algorithm. Write \(\Pi_\Theta(u) = \arg\min_{\theta\in \Theta}\|\theta - u\|_2\) for the projection onto \(\Theta\), the closest point of \(\Theta\), which exists and is unique because \(\Theta\) is closed and convex.
The definition leaves the step direction \(G_t\) random, so that one analysis covers exact gradients, gradients of one sampled record, and the noisy gradients of the private algorithm.

Definition 13.4 (Projected stochastic gradient descent) Fix a start \(\theta_0 \in \Theta\), a number of steps \(T\) and a learning rate \(\eta > 0\), also called the step size. For \(t = 1, \dots, T\), draw a random vector \(G_t\) and set
\[
\theta_t = \Pi_\Theta(\theta_{t-1} - \eta\,G_t).
\tag{13.17}\]
Output the average \(\bar\theta = \frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\theta_t\). With \(G_t = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_{t-1}; D)\) this is projected gradient descent. With \(G_t = n\,\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t})\), for an index \(I_t\) drawn uniformly from \(\{1,\dots,n\}\), it is projected stochastic gradient descent (SGD).

A step moves against the gradient, the direction of steepest increase. The projection brings a step that leaves \(\Theta\) back to the nearest allowed point. The convergence proof compares each iterate with the minimizer, and for that it uses the fact that projection never moves a point farther from any point of \(\Theta\).

Lemma 13.3 For every \(u \in \mathbb R^d\) and every \(\theta \in \Theta\), \(\|\Pi_\Theta(u) - \theta\|_2 \le \|u - \theta\|_2\).


Proof. 

Let \(v = \Pi_\Theta(u)\). For \(t \in (0,1]\) the point \(v + t(\theta - v)\) is in \(\Theta\), so it is no closer to \(u\) than \(v\): \(\|u - v - t(\theta-v)\|^2 \ge \|u - v\|^2\). Expanding, dividing by \(t\) and letting \(t \to 0\) gives \(\langle u - v, \theta - v\rangle \le 0\).
Then \(\|u - \theta\|^2 = \|u - v\|^2 + \|v - \theta\|^2 + 2\langle u - v, v - \theta\rangle \ge \|v - \theta\|^2\), because the last term is nonnegative by step 1.


The convergence theorem asks only that each \(G_t\) is right on average and not too large.

Theorem 13.4 (Convergence of projected SGD) Let \(F\) be convex on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\theta^*\) minimize \(F\) over \(\Theta\). Suppose that, given \(\theta_0, \dots, \theta_{t-1}\), the conditional mean \(\mathbb E[G_t \mid \theta_0, \dots, \theta_{t-1}]\) is a subgradient of \(F\) at \(\theta_{t-1}\), and that \(\mathbb E\|G_t\|_2^2 \le G^2\) for every \(t\). With learning rate \(\eta = \|\Theta\|_2/(G\sqrt T)\),
\[
\mathbb E[F(\bar\theta)] - F(\theta^*) \le \frac{\|\Theta\|_2\, G}{\sqrt T}.
\tag{13.18}\]


Proof. 

By Lemma 13.3 with \(\theta = \theta^*\), \[
\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2 \le \|\theta_{t-1} - \eta G_t - \theta^*\|^2 = \|\theta_{t-1} - \theta^*\|^2 - 2\eta\langle G_t, \theta_{t-1} - \theta^*\rangle + \eta^2\|G_t\|^2 .
\tag{13.19}\]
Condition on the past and let \(g\) be the conditional mean of \(G_t\), a subgradient at \(\theta_{t-1}\). The definition of a subgradient gives \(\langle g, \theta_{t-1} - \theta^*\rangle \ge F(\theta_{t-1}) - F(\theta^*)\). Taking expectations in step 1, \[
\mathbb E[F(\theta_{t-1})] - F(\theta^*) \le \frac{\mathbb E\|\theta_{t-1} - \theta^*\|^2 - \mathbb E\|\theta_t - \theta^*\|^2}{2\eta} + \frac{\eta G^2}{2}.
\tag{13.20}\]
Summing over \(t = 1, \dots, T\), the distances telescope. The first is at most \(\|\Theta\|_2^2\) and the last is nonnegative, so \[
\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\big(\mathbb E[F(\theta_t)] - F(\theta^*)\big) \le \frac{\|\Theta\|_2^2}{2\eta} + \frac{T\eta G^2}{2}.
\tag{13.21}\]
The average \(\bar\theta\) lies in \(\Theta\), and convexity gives \(F(\bar\theta) \le \frac1T\sum_t F(\theta_t)\). Step 3 divided by \(T\), with the value of \(\eta\), makes both terms \(\|\Theta\|_2 G/(2\sqrt T)\).


For the empirical risk, the theorem gives the number of steps that each method needs. The bound \(G\) on the step comes from the bound \(L\) on every gradient.

Corollary 13.1 Suppose that \(\Theta\) has finite diameter \(\|\Theta\|_2\) and that every loss \(\ell(\cdot\,; z)\) is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\). Then gradient descent and SGD both reach excess empirical risk at most \(\alpha\) after \(T = \lceil n^2L^2\|\Theta\|_2^2/\alpha^2\rceil\) steps. Gradient descent evaluates \(nT\) gradients of \(\ell\), and SGD evaluates \(T\).


Proof. 

For gradient descent, \(G_t = \sum_i\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i)\) is a subgradient of \(\mathcal L\), and by Lemma 13.1 its norm is at most \(nL\).
For SGD, the conditional mean of \(G_t = n\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t})\) is \(\frac1n\sum_i n\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i)\), the same subgradient. Its second moment is \(\frac1n\sum_i n^2\|\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i)\|^2 \le n^2L^2\).
In both cases \(G = nL\), and Theorem 13.4 gives excess risk at most \(\|\Theta\|_2 nL/\sqrt T \le \alpha\).


For a constant \(\alpha\), gradient descent costs about \(n^3\) gradient evaluations and SGD about \(n^2\). SGD is also easier to make private, because each step touches one record. Private SGD adds Gaussian noise to each sampled gradient, at the level \(\sigma\) that the privacy proof below needs, and its learning rate allows for the extra noise.

Definition 13.5 (Private SGD) Let \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\). Run projected SGD for \(T = n^2\) steps with
\[
G_t = n\,\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t}) + b_t, \qquad b_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d), \qquad \sigma = \frac{16\,nL\sqrt{\ln(3.3n/\delta)\,\ln(2/\delta)}}{\varepsilon},
\tag{13.22}\]
with fresh, independent indices \(I_t\) and noise \(b_t\), and learning rate \(\eta = \|\Theta\|_2/(G\sqrt T)\) where \(G^2 = n^2L^2 + d\sigma^2\).

Accuracy is the easier half, because the noise has mean zero and only makes the second moment larger.

Theorem 13.5 With \(\ell(\cdot\,;z)\) convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\), private SGD satisfies
\[
\mathbb E[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)] - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D) \le \|\Theta\|_2\sqrt{L^2 + \frac{d\sigma^2}{n^2}} \le \|\Theta\|_2\,L\left(1 + \frac{16\sqrt{d\,\ln(3.3n/\delta)\ln(2/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\right).
\tag{13.23}\]


Proof. 

Given the past, \(b_t\) has mean zero and is independent of \(I_t\), so the conditional mean of \(G_t\) is the subgradient of step 2 of Corollary 13.1.
Expanding the square, \[
\mathbb E\|G_t\|^2 = n^2\,\mathbb E\|\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t})\|^2 + 2n\,\mathbb E\langle\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_{I_t}), b_t\rangle + \mathbb E\|b_t\|^2 \le n^2L^2 + 0 + d\sigma^2 .
\tag{13.24}\] The first term is bounded by Lemma 13.1. The middle term vanishes because \(b_t\) is independent of the gradient and has mean zero. The last is a sum of \(d\) squared Gaussians of variance \(\sigma^2\).
Theorem 13.4 with \(T = n^2\) gives \(\|\Theta\|_2 G/n\), which is the first bound. The second uses \(\sqrt{a + b} \le \sqrt a + \sqrt b\) and the value of \(\sigma\).


Up to logarithmic factors, the excess risk is \(O\big(\|\Theta\|_2 L\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon\big)\), so the average excess risk per record falls as \(1/n\). The price of privacy is the factor \(\sqrt d\), and Bassily, Smith and Thakurta proved that some dependence of this kind is unavoidable. But the constant \(16\) comes from a loose chain of bounds. For example, with \(n = 10{,}000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the noise is \(\sigma = 299.9\,nL\). With \(d = 100\), the bound per record is \(\|\Theta\|_2L(1 + 2999)/10{,}000 = 0.30\,\|\Theta\|_2L\). The next chapter replaces this chain with a much tighter one.
The privacy proof uses three tools. The first is the Gaussian mechanism, restated above. The second is amplification by subsampling, which says that a mechanism run on one random record is more private than the same mechanism run on a fixed record.

Lemma 13.4 (Amplification by sampling one record) Let \(M_0\) be a mechanism whose input is a single record and which satisfies \(\Pr[M_0(z)\in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\Pr[M_0(z')\in S] + \delta_0\) for all records \(z, z'\) and all events \(S\). Let \(M(D) = M_0(z_I)\) with \(I\) uniform on \(\{1,\dots,n\}\). Then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon_1, \delta_0/n)\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon_1 = \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{n}\right) \le \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}-1}{n}.
\tag{13.25}\]


Proof. 

Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in record \(j\), fix an event \(S\), and write \(p_i = \Pr[M_0(z_i)\in S]\) and \(p'_j = \Pr[M_0(z'_j)\in S]\). Let \(r\) be the average of \(p_i\) over \(i \ne j\), and write \(q = 1/n\) for the sampling rate. Then \[
P = \Pr[M(D)\in S] = (1-q)r + q p_j, \qquad P' = \Pr[M(D')\in S] = (1-q)r + q p'_j .
\tag{13.26}\]
The hypothesis, applied to \(z_j\) against \(z'_j\) and against each \(z_i\) and then averaged, gives two bounds: \[
p_j - p'_j \le (e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)p'_j + \delta_0, \qquad p_j - p'_j \le e^{\varepsilon_0}r - p'_j + \delta_0 .
\tag{13.27}\]
Let \(c = e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1\) and take the convex combination of the two bounds with weights \(w\) and \(1-w\), where \(1 - w = c(1-q)/e^{\varepsilon_0} \in [0,1)\). The coefficient of \(r\) becomes \(c(1-q)\), and that of \(p'_j\) becomes \(we^{\varepsilon_0} - 1 = cq\). So \[
p_j - p'_j \le c\big((1-q)r + q p'_j\big) + \delta_0 = cP' + \delta_0 .
\tag{13.28}\]
Then \(P = P' + q(p_j - p'_j) \le (1 + q c)P' + q\delta_0\), which is the claim. The inequality \(\ln(1+x) \le x\) gives the simpler bound on \(\varepsilon_1\).


For \(\varepsilon_0 \le 1\), convexity of the exponential gives \(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1 \le (e-1)\varepsilon_0 \le 2\varepsilon_0\). So a sample of one record of \(n\) cuts the privacy parameter by a factor of about \(n/2\).
The third tool is advanced composition, from the advanced composition chapter. Take \(k\) mechanisms in sequence, each \((\varepsilon_0,\delta_0)\)-DP and each chosen adaptively from the outputs of the previous ones. Their sequence is \((\varepsilon, k\delta_0 + \delta')\)-DP for every \(\delta' \in (0,1)\), where
\[
\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon_0\,\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} \le \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + \frac{k\varepsilon_0^2}{2},
\tag{13.29}\]
and the inequality uses \((e^{x}-1)/(e^{x}+1) = \tanh(x/2) \le x/2\) for \(x \ge 0\).
The proof uses the three tools in turn. The Gaussian noise protects the sampled record in one step, the random choice of that record makes the step more private, and advanced composition adds up the steps.

Theorem 13.6 (Privacy of private SGD) For \(\varepsilon \in (0,1]\) and \(\delta \in (0,1)\), private SGD is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, even if it releases every iterate \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\).


Proof. 

One step, fixed index. Fix the previous iterate and the index \(i\). The step releases a post-processing of \(n\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i) + b_t\). As a function of the single record \(z_i\), the vector \(n\nabla\ell\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity at most \(2nL\), by Lemma 13.1. Set \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/\big(4\sqrt{2\ln(2/\delta)}\big)\), which is below \(1\), and \(\delta_0 = \delta/(2n)\). The Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon_0,\delta_0)\)-DP with respect to \(z_i\) at the noise level \[
\sigma_0 = \frac{2nL}{\varepsilon_0}\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta_0) + \varepsilon_0} \le \frac{2nL}{\varepsilon_0}\sqrt{2\ln\frac{2\sqrt e\,n}{\delta}} \le \frac{2nL}{\varepsilon_0}\sqrt{2\ln\frac{3.3n}{\delta}} = \sigma,
\tag{13.30}\] where the first inequality uses \(\varepsilon_0 \le 1 = 2\ln\sqrt e\), and the last equality is the \(\sigma\) of Definition 13.5. Noise of variance \(\sigma^2 \ge \sigma_0^2\) is noise of variance \(\sigma_0^2\) plus an independent Gaussian of variance \(\sigma^2 - \sigma_0^2\), a post-processing, so the step is \((\varepsilon_0,\delta_0)\)-DP with respect to \(z_i\).
One step, random index. By Lemma 13.4, each step is \((\varepsilon_1, \delta_0/n)\)-DP with respect to the dataset, where \(\varepsilon_1 \le (e^{\varepsilon_0}-1)/n \le 2\varepsilon_0/n\).
All steps. Each step is chosen adaptively from the previous iterates. Advanced composition over \(T = n^2\) steps with \(\delta' = \delta/2\) gives total failure probability \(n^2\cdot\delta/(2n^2) + \delta/2 = \delta\), and privacy parameter \[
\varepsilon_1\sqrt{2n^2\ln(2/\delta)} + \frac{n^2\varepsilon_1^2}{2} \le 2\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2\ln(2/\delta)} + 2\varepsilon_0^2 = \frac\varepsilon2 + 2\varepsilon_0^2 .
\tag{13.31}\]
Finally, the second term is small because \(\varepsilon \le 1\) and \(\ln(2/\delta) > \ln 2 > 1/8\): \[
2\varepsilon_0^2 = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{16\ln(2/\delta)} \le \frac\varepsilon2 .
\tag{13.32}\] The average \(\bar\theta\) is a post-processing of the iterates.


The privacy cost per step is about \(\varepsilon/n\), and composition over \(n^2\) steps multiplies it by only \(\sqrt{n^2} = n\). Each piece of the argument is generic, so the same recipe extends to models with no convergence theorem.

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
14.1 Neural networks
The private stochastic gradient descent (SGD) of the previous chapter needs a convex, Lipschitz loss, and its privacy analysis loses large constants. The losses of neural networks are neither convex nor Lipschitz, and in practice the constants decide whether a guarantee is meaningful. This chapter adapts noisy SGD to neural networks under differential privacy (DP) by clipping each gradient. Then it replaces composition with a tighter accounting, built on the moments of the privacy loss. Last, it turns any non-private learner into a private one by a vote among models trained on disjoint data.
The setting is that of the previous chapter. Each record is a pair of a feature vector and a label, and training minimizes the total loss of the records over a parameter vector \(\theta\),
\[
\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\theta; x_i, y_i).
\tag{14.1}\]
Here a feature vector \(x\) lies in \(\mathbb R^{m_0}\), and a label is one of \(K\) classes, \(y \in \{1, \dots, K\}\). A neural network maps a feature vector to one score per class, and training adjusts its parameters \(\theta\). The simplest network is a stack of layers, each a linear map followed by a fixed nonlinear function.
Without the activation, the network is a composition of linear maps, and so a single linear map. Common activations are the rectified linear unit \(\phi(u) = \max(0, u)\), the usual choice without privacy, and the bounded \(\tanh(u) = (e^u - e^{-u})/(e^u + e^{-u})\).
The softmax function turns the scores into a probability vector over the classes, \(\hat y_k = e^{o_k}/\sum_{j=1}^K e^{o_j}\), which gives the confidence of the network in each class. The prediction is the class with the largest \(\hat y_k\). The loss is the cross-entropy, the negative log of the probability of the true class,
\[
\ell(\theta; x, y) = -\ln \hat y_y = -\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf 1[k = y]\,\ln \hat y_k ,
\tag{14.3}\]
where \(\hat y\) depends on \(\theta\) through every layer. The analysis of the previous chapter does not apply to this loss. It is not convex in \(\theta\), so no convergence theorem holds, although SGD works well in practice. It is not Lipschitz either, because in a two-layer network the second-layer weights multiply the gradient of the first-layer weights, and they can be arbitrarily large. So a single gradient has unbounded sensitivity.

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
Definition 14.1 (Multilayer perceptron) A network with \(J\) layers sets \(v^{(0)} = x\) and, for \(j = 1, \dots, J\),
\[
v^{(j)} = \phi\big(W^{(j)}v^{(j-1)} + c^{(j)}\big),
\tag{14.2}\]
where \(W^{(j)}\) is an \(m_j \times m_{j-1}\) matrix of weights, \(c^{(j)} \in \mathbb R^{m_j}\) is a vector of offsets, and the activation function \(\phi\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb R\) is applied to each coordinate. The last layer has no activation and outputs \(o \in \mathbb R^K\), one score per class. The parameter vector \(\theta\) collects all weights and offsets.

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
14.2 Differentially private SGD
Two changes make noisy SGD practical. First, each gradient is clipped to a fixed norm, which bounds sensitivity directly. Clipping shrinks a vector that is too long and leaves a short one alone. Second, each step uses a random batch of records, called a lot, chosen by Poisson sampling.

Definition 14.2 (Clipping) For a clipping norm \(C\), a positive number, the clipping of a vector \(g\) is
\[
\mathrm{clip}_C(g) = g\cdot\min\left(1, \frac{C}{\|g\|_2}\right).
\tag{14.4}\]

So every clipped vector has norm at most \(C\).
DP-SGD combines the two changes. Each step clips the gradient of every record in the lot, adds Gaussian noise to the sum, and divides by the expected lot size \(qn\). The noise multiplier \(\sigma\) sets the noise, as the ratio of its standard deviation to the clipping norm. So, unlike the \(\sigma\) of the previous chapter, it is not the standard deviation itself.

Definition 14.3 (DP-SGD) Let the parameter vector \(\theta\) have \(d\) coordinates. Fix a sampling rate \(q\) in \((0, 1]\), a noise multiplier \(\sigma > 0\), a clipping norm \(C\), a number of steps \(T\), learning rates \(\eta_t\) and a start \(\theta_0\). For \(t = 1, \dots, T\):

Form the lot \(B_t\) by including each index \(i \in \{1,\dots,n\}\) independently with probability \(q\).
Compute the noisy average of clipped gradients, \[
\tilde g_t = \frac{1}{qn}\left(\sum_{i\in B_t}\mathrm{clip}_C\big(\nabla\ell(\theta_{t-1}; z_i)\big) + b_t\right), \qquad b_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2 I_d).
\tag{14.5}\]
Step: \(\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \eta_t\,\tilde g_t\).

Output \(\theta_T\).

Unlike the private SGD of the previous chapter, a step uses a lot of expected size \(qn\) instead of one record. And clipping, not an assumption, bounds the gradient. The noise is calibrated to \(C\), the most that one record can contribute to the sum.

Lemma 14.1 Adding or removing one record changes the clipped sum \(\sum_{i\in B}\mathrm{clip}_C(\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i))\) by a vector of norm at most \(C\). Replacing one record changes it by at most \(2C\).


Proof. Adding or removing a record adds or removes one clipped vector, of norm at most \(C\). A replacement does both, and the triangle inequality gives \(2C\).

Clipping has a cost, because the clipped average is a biased estimate of the gradient. So even for convex losses the convergence theorem no longer applies, but clipped SGD works well in practice.
The privacy analysis depends on how the lot is drawn. Poisson sampling includes each record independently with probability \(q\), so the lot size is random. Even at \(q = 1/n\), this is not the same as the choice of one record, because the lot may be empty or hold several records. Other schemes, such as sampling without replacement of a lot of fixed size, need other analyses. The analyses below are for Poisson sampling. They use the add/remove relation, under which neighbours \(D \sim D'\) differ by one record, so Lemma 14.1 gives sensitivity \(C\).
Implementations often shuffle the data once and cut it into consecutive batches of fixed size. Each batch is then a uniform sample, but the batches are dependent, so the Poisson analysis does not apply to them.

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
14.3 Privacy accounting
The analysis of the previous chapter applies to DP-SGD too, because without sampling a single step is the Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma\). If that step is \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\)-DP, then amplification by Poisson sampling makes it about \((2q\varepsilon_0, q\delta_0)\)-DP, and advanced composition over \(T\) steps gives
\[
\Big(O\big(q\varepsilon_0\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)}\big),\ Tq\delta_0 + \delta\Big)\text{-DP}.
\tag{14.6}\]
Abadi and coauthors proved a better bound for the same algorithm, which needs less noise for the same guarantee.

Theorem 14.1 (Moments accountant, asymptotic form) There are constants \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) such that, for every sampling rate \(q\) and number of steps \(T\), every \(\varepsilon < c_1q^2T\) and every \(\delta > 0\), DP-SGD is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP under add/remove neighbours if
\[
\sigma \ge c_2\,\frac{q\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}.
\tag{14.7}\]


The proof is Theorem 1 of Abadi and coauthors, 2016, and the rest of this section proves its ingredients. Compared with composition, the gain is a factor of order \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta_0)}\) in \(\sigma\) and no failure probability \(Tq\delta_0\), as Corollary 14.1 shows below. Such factors in \(\varepsilon\) separate a meaningful guarantee from an empty one.
The accountant starts from the privacy loss. For a mechanism \(M\) whose output has density \(p_D\) on dataset \(D\), the privacy loss at an output \(y\) is \(\ln\big(p_D(y)/p_{D'}(y)\big)\). It is a random variable when \(y\) is drawn from \(M(D)\). By the privacy loss criterion of the approximate DP chapter, \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP follows if, for every ordered pair of neighbours, the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\). But tail probabilities do not compose simply, and moments do, by addition. So the accountant takes, for an order \(\lambda > 0\), the logarithm of the average \(\lambda\)-th power of the ratio \(p_D(y)/p_{D'}(y)\), for the worst pair of neighbours.

Definition 14.4 (Log-moments of the privacy loss) Let \(p_D\) be the density of the output \(M(D)\). For \(\lambda > 0\), the \(\lambda\)-th log-moment of \(M\) is
\[
\kappa_M(\lambda) = \sup_{D \sim D'}\ \ln\ \mathbb E_{y\sim M(D)}\left[\left(\frac{p_D(y)}{p_{D'}(y)}\right)^{\lambda}\right].
\tag{14.8}\]

Up to a factor, it is the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\) between the two output distributions. A bound on it for every pair of neighbours is Rényi differential privacy (RDP). By Markov’s inequality, a bound on one log-moment already gives approximate DP.

Theorem 14.2 (From moments to approximate DP) For every \(\lambda > 0\) and \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), the mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with
\[
\delta = \exp\big(\kappa_M(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon\big).
\tag{14.9}\]


Proof. 

Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and write \(L = \ln(p_D(Y)/p_{D'}(Y))\) for the privacy loss random variable, with \(Y \sim M(D)\). The map \(u \mapsto e^{\lambda u}\) is increasing, so \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \Pr[e^{\lambda L} \ge e^{\lambda\varepsilon}]\).
Markov’s inequality bounds the right side by \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]\,e^{-\lambda\varepsilon}\), and \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}] \le e^{\kappa_M(\lambda)}\) by definition.
So the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\), and the privacy loss criterion gives \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.


The conversion is useful because log-moments are easy to track over many steps. The next lemma shows that they add up when mechanisms run in sequence, even when the outputs of the previous mechanisms choose the next one.

Lemma 14.2 (Composition of moments) Let \(M_1\) have output \(y_1\), and let \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) be a mechanism chosen as a function of \(y_1\) with \(\kappa_{M_2(\cdot;y_1)}(\lambda) \le \kappa_2\) for every \(y_1\). The mechanism \(M\) that outputs \((y_1, y_2)\) satisfies \(\kappa_M(\lambda) \le \kappa_{M_1}(\lambda) + \kappa_2\). By induction, \(T\) adaptive steps have log-moments at most the sum of theirs.


Proof. 

The density of \((y_1, y_2)\) on \(D\) is \(p_D(y_1)\,p_D(y_2 \mid y_1)\), so the ratio for neighbours factors as \(r_1(y_1)\,r_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\). Here \(r_1\) is the density ratio of \(y_1\), and \(r_2\) is the density ratio of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\).
The expectation over \(y_2\) first, given \(y_1\), gives \[
\mathbb E\big[r_1^\lambda r_2^\lambda\big] = \mathbb E_{y_1}\Big[r_1(y_1)^\lambda\ \mathbb E_{y_2}\big[r_2(y_2\mid y_1)^\lambda \,\big|\, y_1\big]\Big] \le e^{\kappa_2}\,\mathbb E_{y_1}\big[r_1(y_1)^\lambda\big] \le e^{\kappa_2 + \kappa_{M_1}(\lambda)}.
\tag{14.10}\]
The logarithm and the supremum over neighbours give the claim.


For the Gaussian mechanism the log-moments have a closed form.

Lemma 14.3 Let \(M(D) = f(D) + b\) with \(b \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I_d)\), where \(f\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\). Then for every \(\lambda > 0\),
\[
\kappa_M(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda(\lambda + 1)(\Delta_2 f)^2}{2\sigma^2}.
\tag{14.11}\]


Proof. 

Fix neighbours, write \(\mu = f(D)\) and \(\mu' = f(D')\), and let \(r = \|\mu - \mu'\|_2 \le \Delta_2 f\). For \(y = \mu + \sigma \xi\) with \(\xi\) standard normal, the privacy loss is \[
\frac{\|y - \mu'\|^2 - \|y - \mu\|^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{r^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\langle \xi, \mu - \mu'\rangle}{\sigma}.
\tag{14.12}\]
So the privacy loss is normal with mean \(m = r^2/(2\sigma^2)\) and variance \(r^2/\sigma^2 = 2m\).
A normal variable \(Z\) with mean \(m\) and variance \(s^2\) has \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda Z}] = e^{\lambda m + \lambda^2s^2/2}\). Here the exponent is \(\lambda m + \lambda^2 m = \lambda(\lambda+1)r^2/(2\sigma^2)\).
This increases with \(r\), and the supremum is reached at \(r = \Delta_2 f\).


The three results give a guarantee for many Gaussian steps without sampling. The log-moments of the steps add up, and the conversion turns their sum into \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP at the best order \(\lambda\).

Corollary 14.1 Let \(\rho = (\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Any adaptive sequence of \(T\) Gaussian mechanisms, each with sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\) and noise \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2I_d)\), is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), with
\[
\varepsilon = T\rho + 2\sqrt{T\rho\ln(1/\delta)}.
\tag{14.13}\]


Proof. 

By Lemma 14.3 and Lemma 14.2, the sequence has \(\kappa(\lambda) \le \lambda(\lambda+1)T\rho\).
By Theorem 14.2, it is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP whenever \(\lambda(\lambda+1)T\rho - \lambda\varepsilon \le \ln\delta\), that is, whenever \(\varepsilon \ge (\lambda+1)T\rho + \ln(1/\delta)/\lambda\).
The right side is smallest at \(\lambda = \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/(T\rho)}\), where it equals \(T\rho + 2\sqrt{T\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\).


For comparison, take the same \(T\) Gaussian steps with \(\Delta_2 f = 1\), so that \(T\rho = T/(2\sigma^2)\). Advanced composition first needs a guarantee per step. The Gaussian mechanism of the approximate DP chapter gives \(\varepsilon_0\) with \(\sigma = \sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta_0) + \varepsilon_0}/\varepsilon_0\), so \(\varepsilon_0\) is about \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta_0)}/\sigma\). Then it gives \(\varepsilon \approx \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2T\ln(1/\delta)}\), which is \(2\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta_0)\ln(1/\delta)}/\sigma\). The corollary gives \(\sqrt{2T\ln(1/\delta)}/\sigma\) plus a lower-order term. That is smaller by a factor of about \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta_0)}\), with no failure probability \(T\delta_0\) to pay.
DP-SGD adds Poisson sampling to each step, and its log-moments come from a one-dimensional pair of distributions. By Lemma 14.1, after a division by \(C\), a step compares the noise distribution \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) with the mixture \((1-q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). In the mixture, the extra record is sampled with probability \(q\).

Theorem 14.3 (Log-moments of the sampled Gaussian) For every integer \(\lambda \ge 1\), one step of DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma\) has, under add/remove neighbours,
\[
\kappa(\lambda) \le \ln A_{\lambda+1}, \qquad A_{a} = \sum_{k=0}^{a}\binom{a}{k}(1-q)^{a-k}q^k\exp\left(\frac{k^2 - k}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\tag{14.14}\]


The proof is Section 3.3 of Mironov, Talwar and Zhang (2019). It expands the \(a\)-th power of the density ratio between the mixture and \(\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\) with the binomial theorem, which gives \(A_a\). Each term is then a Gaussian integral, \(\mathbb E[e^{k\xi/\sigma^2}] = e^{k^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) for \(\xi \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\). The hard part of the proof is to show that this pair, in this order, is the worst case over all neighbours and over the reverse order. For \(\sigma \ge 1\), small \(q\) and moderate \(\lambda\), the bound is \(q^2\lambda(\lambda+1)/((1-q)\sigma^2) + O(q^3\lambda^3/\sigma^3)\), which gives Theorem 14.1.
These pieces together give the moments accountant. It computes the log-moment of one step for every \(\lambda\), multiplies by \(T\) by Lemma 14.2, and converts with Theorem 14.2 at the best \(\lambda\):
\[
\varepsilon(\delta) = \min_{\lambda \ge 1}\ \frac{T\ln A_{\lambda+1} + \ln(1/\delta)}{\lambda}.
\tag{14.15}\]
The computation depends only on \(q\), \(\sigma\), \(T\) and \(\delta\), never on the data. So you can fix the privacy cost of a training run before you touch the data, and set the noise or the number of steps to meet a target. Figure 14.1 compares the accountant with the composition route on a typical setting.






Figure 14.1: Privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of DP-SGD with sampling rate \(q = 0.01\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma = 4\), against the number of epochs of \(1/q\) steps. Dashed: each step is \((\varepsilon_0,\delta_0)\)-DP by Corollary 14.1 with \(T = 1\), Poisson sampling makes it \((\ln(1 + q(e^{\varepsilon_0}-1)), q\delta_0)\)-DP, and advanced composition combines the steps, with \(\delta\) split evenly. Solid: the moments accountant Equation 14.15.




Example 14.1 With \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 4\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), Figure 14.1 shows the two accountings of the same algorithm. After \(100\) epochs, or \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, the composition route certifies \(\varepsilon = 22.08\) and the moments accountant certifies \(\varepsilon = 1.26\). After \(400\) epochs the values are \(61.41\) and \(2.58\). The first is no guarantee at all, and the second is a reasonable one.

These analyses use add/remove neighbours, while this book uses replace-one. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition, so a guarantee for one relation converts to the other at the cost of about twice the \(\varepsilon\).

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
14.4 DP-SGD in practice
DP-SGD replaces SGD directly, but its behaviour differs in three ways.
Accuracy. On the handwritten-digit benchmark MNIST, a well-tuned DP-SGD reached \(98.1\%\) accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 2.93\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), against about \(99.8\%\) without privacy (Papernot and coauthors, 2020). On the harder image benchmark CIFAR-10, it reached only \(66.2\%\) at \(\varepsilon = 7.53\), which is weak in both accuracy and privacy.
Architecture. Bounded activations such as \(\tanh\) work better than the rectified linear unit under DP-SGD, and the size of the network matters too. In each step, the noise vector \(b_t\) has expected squared norm \(d\sigma^2C^2\), while the sum of the gradients clipped to norm \(C\) has norm at most \(qnC\). So the ratio of signal to noise is at most about \(qn/(\sigma\sqrt d)\), which falls as the number of parameters \(d\) grows. So a network must be large enough to fit the task and no larger.
Hyperparameters. Each training run on the private data that tunes the learning rate, lot size, clipping norm or number of epochs spends privacy budget. Results that tune on the private data and do not count this cost overstate the privacy of the final model. Private selection picks the best of many private runs at a small constant factor in \(\varepsilon\) (Liu and Talwar). Public data helps too, for tuning or for pretraining a network whose last layers alone are then trained privately, which makes \(d\) smaller.

title: 14  Private Deep Learning
text:
14.5 Private aggregation of teacher ensembles
DP-SGD changes the inside of one training algorithm. Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) instead treats the learner as a black box, so any improvement in non-private learning carries over. The price is a different model of the data. In addition to a sensitive labelled training set, PATE needs a supply of public unlabelled feature vectors.
PATE is an instance of sample and aggregate. It splits the data into disjoint parts, runs a non-private algorithm on each part, and combines the answers by a private aggregation. One record affects only one part, so the aggregation has low sensitivity. In PATE, the parts train \(m\) classifiers, the teachers, and the aggregation is a vote.
The simplest task is one private prediction for a public feature vector \(x\). Each teacher votes for a label, and \(c_k\) is the number of votes for label \(k\). The mode \(a\) is the label with the most votes, the smallest one in case of a tie. The gap \(\Gamma = c_a - \max_{k\ne a}c_k\) measures how far the vote is from a change of winner. The private mode releases the mode only when a noisy gap is above a threshold, because a large gap means that one changed record cannot change the winner.

Definition 14.5 (Private mode of the teachers) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0, 1/2)\). Split the dataset into \(m\) fixed disjoint parts by position, train one teacher on each, and collect their votes on \(x\). Let \(a\) be the mode of the votes and \(\Gamma\) its gap, as above. Draw \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon)\), Laplace noise with scale \(2/\varepsilon\). If
\[
\Gamma + Z > \tau, \qquad \tau = 2 + \frac{2}{\varepsilon}\ln\frac{1}{2\delta},
\tag{14.16}\]
output the mode \(a\). Otherwise output a symbol \(\bot\) for “no answer”, or a uniformly random label.

When the teachers agree, the mode is stable, and its exact release costs little privacy. This is the propose-test-release idea of the chapter on beyond global sensitivity. It tests privately that the data is far from a dataset with another answer, and if so, releases the answer without noise. The private mode is the stable mode of that chapter applied to the votes, with a lower threshold so that the failure probability is \(\delta\), not \(\delta/2\).

Theorem 14.4 The private mode is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP. The teachers’ training algorithm may be randomized, with coins independent of everything else.


Proof. 

Fix the teachers’ coins; a guarantee for every fixed choice of coins implies one for random coins. Neighbours differ in one record, which lies in one part, so at most one teacher’s vote changes. That moves one vote from one label to another, and changes each count by at most \(1\).
The gap has sensitivity \(2\). If the mode stays the same, both terms of \(\Gamma\) change by at most \(1\). If the mode changes from \(a\) on \(D\) to \(a' \ne a\) on \(D'\), then \(c_{a'} + 1 \ge c'_{a'} \ge c'_a \ge c_a - 1\), so \(\Gamma \le c_a - c_{a'} \le 2\), and likewise \(\Gamma' \le 2\). In both cases \(|\Gamma - \Gamma'| \le 2\). So, by the Laplace mechanism, the indicator that the test passes is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Same mode. The output is a function of the test indicator and of the common mode, so it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by post-processing.
Different modes. By step 2, \(\Gamma \le 2\). The test then passes on \(D\) with probability at most \(\Pr[Z > \tau - 2] = \tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon(\tau-2)/2} = \delta\). Outside that event the output is \(\bot\), so for every set \(S\) of outputs, \[
\Pr[M(D)\in S] \le \Pr[M(D) = \bot]\,\mathbf 1[\bot\in S] + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') = \bot]\,\mathbf 1[\bot\in S] + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D')\in S] + \delta,
\tag{14.17}\] where the middle step is the \(\varepsilon\)-DP of the test from step 2. Replacing \(\bot\) by a random label is post-processing.


The accuracy depends on how good the teachers are. If the records are independent draws from a distribution, then teachers trained on disjoint parts vote independently on a fixed \(x\).

Proposition 14.1 Let \(\beta \in (0,1)\) be a failure probability, and let \(\tau\) be the threshold of Definition 14.5. Suppose each teacher, independently, votes for the correct label \(y\) of \(x\) with probability at least \(3/4\). If
\[
m \ge \max\left(4\tau + \frac8\varepsilon\ln\frac1\beta,\ 32\ln\frac2\beta\right),
\tag{14.18}\]
then the private mode outputs \(y\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. 

Let \(V\) be the number of correct votes. Its mean is at least \(3m/4\), and Hoeffding’s inequality for independent indicators gives \(\Pr[V \le 5m/8] \le e^{-2m(1/8)^2} = e^{-m/32} \le \beta/2\).
If \(V > 5m/8\), then \(y\) has a majority, so it is the mode, and every other label has at most \(m - V\) votes. So \(\Gamma \ge 2V - m > m/4\).
The test then fails with probability \(\Pr[Z \le \tau - \Gamma] \le \tfrac12 e^{-\varepsilon(m/4 - \tau)/2}\), because \(m/4 > \tau\). The first lower bound on \(m\) makes this at most \(\beta/2\).
A union bound over the two failure events gives the claim.



Example 14.2 With \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and \(\beta = 0.01\), the threshold is \(\tau = 2 + 2\ln(50{,}000) = 23.64\). The two lower bounds are \(94.56 + 8\ln 100 = 131.4\) and \(32\ln 200 = 169.5\), so \(170\) teachers suffice. If a teacher needs \(n_0\) records to be right three times in four, the private prediction needs \(170\,n_0\).

The number of teachers grows like \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\). This is the general price of sample and aggregate, about \(1/\varepsilon\) times more data than the non-private algorithm. That is often more than the best private algorithm for a specific task needs.
To answer \(k\) queries with \(k\) runs of the private mode costs about \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\), by advanced composition. The sparse vector technique of the sparse vector chapter does better when most queries are stable, because it pays only for the queries whose answer is above a threshold. Here each query asks whether the gap on the next point is small. So the technique pays only for the unstable points, where it outputs a random label, and it answers the stable ones with the exact mode. Its privacy cost grows like the square root of the number of unstable queries, not of all \(k\) (Bassily, Thakkar and Thakurta).
The answers \((x_1,\hat y_1), \dots, (x_k,\hat y_k)\), with public features and private labels, form a labelled dataset that is safe to release. PATE trains a non-private learner, the student, on it. If the labelling is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP and the public features do not depend on the private data, the student is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP too, by post-processing. The student then answers any number of queries at no further cost. So PATE turns a bounded number of private predictions into a private model.
