title: Deployments
text:
The earlier parts built differential privacy (DP) with a trusted curator who holds the data and releases noisy answers. This part asks what changes when the definition meets real systems with millions of users, daily data collection and outside analysts. The first chapter removes the curator, so that each person randomizes their own data, and measures the price in error. The second finds a middle ground with a shuffler, then returns to the central model to see how large deployments select, compose and budget.



Table 1: The chapters of this part.





Chapter
Question it answers




Local differential privacy
What does it cost to trust no one, and how do large deployments live with that cost?


The shuffle model and central deployments
How much does an anonymizing shuffler recover, and how do central deployments select, compose and budget?

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.1 The local model
Almost every mechanism so far ran on a trusted curator who saw the raw data. This chapter drops that trust, so that each person randomizes their own record before it leaves their device. We define this local model and show that, with \(n\) people, it costs a factor of about \(\sqrt n\) in accuracy on the simplest task. No noninteractive protocol can escape that cost.
The rest of the chapter studies three large deployments of the local model, each of which solves a problem the textbook protocol ignores. Google’s protects people who answer the same question every day, Apple’s finds values that no one knew to ask about, and Microsoft’s sends numbers in a single bit and copes with values that drift.
In the central model of the first chapter on the definition, people send their data to a curator, and the trust barrier sits at the output of the curator. In the local model the barrier moves to each person. An adversary may see anything that leaves the device of a person, and the curator is now just an analyst who receives messages.
This is the definition of differential privacy (DP) applied to a dataset with one record. In the simplest protocol, everyone speaks once and at the same time.
Local privacy implies central privacy, because the view of the analyst is a vector of messages and only one of them depends on any one record.
Randomized response, with each person reporting their true bit with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\), is an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer. So the first private algorithm of this book was a local protocol.
Protocols can also interact. In a sequentially interactive protocol the analyst addresses people one at a time, and the randomizer of person \(i\) may depend on the messages before theirs, but each person speaks only once. In a fully interactive protocol the analyst may return to a person many times, and all the messages that person ever sends must together form an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer of their record. This chapter proves its bounds for noninteractive protocols only.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
Definition 17.1 (Local randomizer) Let \(\varepsilon \ge 0\). A randomized algorithm \(R\colon \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer if for all inputs \(x, x' \in \mathcal X\) and all events \(S \subseteq \mathcal Y\),
\[
\Pr[R(x) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[R(x') \in S].
\tag{17.1}\]



Definition 17.2 (Noninteractive local protocol) A noninteractive \(\varepsilon\)-local protocol gives each person \(i\) an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer \(R_i\). Person \(i\) sends \(Y_i = R_i(X_i)\), using randomness independent of everyone else’s, and the analyst outputs a function of the messages \((Y_1, \dots, Y_n)\).



Proposition 17.1 The messages \((Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\) of a noninteractive \(\varepsilon\)-local protocol, viewed as the output of a mechanism on \(D\), are \(\varepsilon\)-DP. So is any function of them that the analyst computes.


Proof. 

Let \(D \sim D'\) be neighbours, which differ by replacing entry \(j\), and take an event \(S\). Write \(y_{-j}\) for a value of all the messages except the \(j\)-th, and \(S_{y_{-j}} = \{y_j : (y_j, y_{-j}) \in S\}\) for the slice of \(S\) through it.
The other messages have the same distribution under \(D\) and \(D'\), because they depend only on the other records and on independent randomness. Conditioning on them gives

\[
\Pr_D[Y \in S] = \mathbb E_{Y_{-j}}\!\left[\Pr[R_j(X_j) \in S_{Y_{-j}}]\right] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\mathbb E_{Y_{-j}}\!\left[\Pr[R_j(X'_j) \in S_{Y_{-j}}]\right] = e^{\varepsilon}\Pr_{D'}[Y \in S],
\tag{17.2}\]
where the inequality applies Definition 17.1 to each slice. 3. The analyst’s output is a post-processing of the messages, so it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by the post-processing property of the Laplace mechanism chapter.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.2 Counting bits, central and local
The cost of moving the barrier shows on the simplest task, in which each person holds a bit \(X_i \in \{0,1\}\), and the analyst wants the mean \(\mu = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\). Write \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) for the Laplace distribution with density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\). The Laplace mechanism adds \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta f/\varepsilon)\) noise to a query \(f\) whose value changes by at most \(\Delta f\) between neighbours, and it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. So a central curator, who sees the bits, can add Laplace noise to their mean.

Proposition 17.2 For every \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\beta \in (0,1)\), the central estimate \(\hat\mu = \mu + \mathrm{Lap}(1/(\varepsilon n))\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and with probability at least \(1-\beta\),
\[
|\hat\mu - \mu| \le \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{\varepsilon n}.
\tag{17.3}\]


Proof. 

Changing one bit changes \(\mu\) by at most \(1/n\), so the Laplace mechanism with \(\Delta f = 1/n\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
The Laplace tail is \(\Pr[|\mathrm{Lap}(b)| > t] = 2\int_t^\infty \frac{1}{2b}e^{-z/b}\,dz = e^{-t/b}\). Setting \(b = 1/(\varepsilon n)\) and \(t = b\ln(1/\beta)\) makes the tail equal to \(\beta\).


In the local model each person runs randomized response and sends \(Y_i\), equal to \(X_i\) with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1+e^\varepsilon)\) and to \(1 - X_i\) otherwise. A report equals \(1\) with probability \((1 + (e^\varepsilon - 1)X_i)/(e^\varepsilon+1)\), which is linear in \(X_i\). Solving for \(X_i\) gives the unbiased estimate of the analyst,
\[
\hat\mu = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(e^\varepsilon+1)\,Y_i - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}.
\tag{17.4}\]
This is the debiased estimator of the randomized response chapter with bias \(2\kappa = (e^\varepsilon-1)/(e^\varepsilon+1)\), written in terms of \(\varepsilon\). That chapter proved that, with probability at least \(1-\beta\),
\[
|\hat\mu - \mu| \le \coth\!\left(\frac\varepsilon2\right)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}}, \qquad \coth\!\left(\frac\varepsilon2\right) \ge \frac2\varepsilon .
\tag{17.5}\]
The two bounds reach an error of \(\alpha\) at different sizes. The central bound does so once \(n \ge \ln(1/\beta)/(\varepsilon\alpha)\). The local bound does so once \(n \ge \coth^2(\varepsilon/2)\ln(2/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\), a threshold of at least \(2\ln(2/\beta)/(\varepsilon^2\alpha^2)\). So the local estimate needs quadratically more data in \(1/\alpha\) and in \(1/\varepsilon\), as Figure 17.1 shows.

Example 17.1 Take \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\alpha = 0.01\) and \(\beta = 0.05\). The central estimate needs \(n \ge \ln 20/0.01\), that is, \(300\) people. The local one needs \(n \ge \coth^2(0.5)\ln 40/(2 \times 10^{-4})\), that is, \(86{,}370\) people, about \(288\) times as many.







Figure 17.1: Error of the mean of \(n\) bits at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Solid lines are the 95th percentile of the error over 2,000 simulated runs with \(\mu = 0.3\), dashed lines the bounds of Proposition 17.2 and Equation 17.5 with \(\beta = 0.05\). The central error falls as \(1/n\) and the local one as \(1/\sqrt n\), so the gap widens with \(n\).



This gap is why only companies with hundreds of millions of users have deployed local privacy. With a few thousand users, a local protocol returns mostly noise.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.3 The price is unavoidable
The local estimator is not merely a poor choice, because no noninteractive local protocol can do better than error of order \(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\). The reason is that a local randomizer shrinks the difference between two input distributions by a factor that depends only on \(\varepsilon\), and \(n\) independent messages cannot recover more than \(n\) such shrunken differences.
Two distances between distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) on a countable set measure this. The total variation distance is \(\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) = \frac12\sum_y |P(y) - Q(y)|\), the largest gap \(P(S) - Q(S)\) over events \(S\). The chi-squared divergence is
\[
\chi^2(P \,\|\, Q) = \sum_{y} \frac{(P(y) - Q(y))^2}{Q(y)},
\tag{17.6}\]
where a term in which both \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\) are zero is dropped, and a term in which only \(Q(y)\) is zero makes the divergence infinite. The lower bound needs two facts about these two distances. Total variation is at most a constant times the square root of the chi-squared divergence, and the chi-squared divergence behaves simply on products, which is where the \(n\) independent messages enter.

Lemma 17.1 For distributions on a countable set,

\(\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) \le \frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P\,\|\,Q)}\);
for product distributions, \(1 + \chi^2(P_1 \times P_2 \,\|\, Q_1 \times Q_2) = \big(1 + \chi^2(P_1\,\|\,Q_1)\big)\big(1 + \chi^2(P_2\,\|\,Q_2)\big)\).



Proof. 

Write \(|P(y) - Q(y)| = \frac{|P(y)-Q(y)|}{\sqrt{Q(y)}}\sqrt{Q(y)}\) and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the sum. Since \(\sum_y Q(y) = 1\), this gives \(\sum_y |P(y) - Q(y)| \le \sqrt{\chi^2(P\,\|\,Q)}\).
Expanding the square shows \(1 + \chi^2(P\,\|\,Q) = \sum_y P(y)^2/Q(y)\). For a product, this sum factorizes as \(\sum_{y_1} P_1(y_1)^2/Q_1(y_1) \cdot \sum_{y_2} P_2(y_2)^2/Q_2(y_2)\).


The key step is a contraction. Feed a local randomizer an input drawn from \(P_0\) or from \(P_1\), and compare the two resulting distributions of its message.

Lemma 17.2 Let \(R\) be an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer with a countable message set, and let \(P_0, P_1\) be distributions on \(\mathcal X\). Write \(W_0\) and \(W_1\) for the distributions of the message \(R(x)\) when \(x\) is drawn from \(P_0\) and from \(P_1\). Then
\[
\chi^2(W_0\,\|\,W_1) \le (e^\varepsilon - 1)^2\,\mathrm{TV}(P_0,P_1)^2 .
\tag{17.7}\]


Proof. 

Fix a message \(y\) and write \(Q(y \mid x) = \Pr[R(x) = y]\) and \(c_y = \inf_x Q(y\mid x)\). By Definition 17.1, every \(Q(y \mid x)\) lies in \([c_y, e^\varepsilon c_y]\). If \(c_y = 0\), then \(Q(y\mid x) = 0\) for every \(x\), and \(y\) contributes nothing.
Since \(\sum_x (P_0(x) - P_1(x)) = 0\), subtracting the midpoint \(m_y = (1+e^\varepsilon)c_y/2\) changes nothing:

\[
W_0(y) - W_1(y) = \sum_x \big(Q(y\mid x) - m_y\big)\big(P_0(x) - P_1(x)\big).
\tag{17.8}\]

Each factor \(|Q(y\mid x) - m_y|\) is at most \((e^\varepsilon - 1)c_y/2\), and \(\sum_x |P_0(x) - P_1(x)| = 2\,\mathrm{TV}(P_0,P_1)\). So \(|W_0(y) - W_1(y)| \le (e^\varepsilon - 1)c_y\,\mathrm{TV}(P_0,P_1)\).
The denominator satisfies \(W_1(y) \ge c_y\). Hence each term of \(\chi^2\) is at most \((e^\varepsilon-1)^2 c_y\,\mathrm{TV}(P_0,P_1)^2\).
Summing over \(y\) and using \(\sum_y c_y \le \sum_y Q(y \mid x) = 1\) for any fixed \(x\) gives the bound.


Now let the data be random. If each \(X_i\) is drawn independently from \(\mathrm{Bern}(p)\), the Bernoulli distribution with mean \(p\), then an accurate estimate of the mean must tell \(p = \frac12 - \alpha\) from \(p = \frac12 + \alpha\).

Theorem 17.1 (Lower bound for local counting) Let \(\alpha \in (0, \frac12]\), and let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent draws from \(\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12 + \alpha)\) or from \(\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12 - \alpha)\). Write \(P_+\) and \(P_-\) for the two distributions of the messages of a noninteractive \(\varepsilon\)-local protocol with countable message sets. Then
\[
\mathrm{TV}(P_+, P_-) \le \frac12\sqrt{\exp\!\big(4n(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\alpha^2\big) - 1}.
\tag{17.9}\]
Consequently, if an estimate \(\tilde\mu\) computed from the messages satisfies \(|\tilde\mu - p| < \alpha\) with probability at least \(3/4\) in both cases, then
\[
n \ge \frac{\ln 2}{4(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\alpha^2}, \qquad\text{and for } \varepsilon \le 1,\quad n \ge \frac{1}{18\,\varepsilon^2\alpha^2}.
\tag{17.10}\]


Proof. 

The two input distributions have \(\mathrm{TV}(\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12+\alpha), \mathrm{Bern}(\frac12-\alpha)) = 2\alpha\). By Lemma 17.2, each person’s message satisfies \(\chi^2 \le 4(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\alpha^2\) between the two cases.
The messages are independent, because the records and the coins are. By the product rule of Lemma 17.1 and \(1 + z \le e^z\), we get \(1 + \chi^2(P_+\,\|\,P_-) \le \exp(4n(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\alpha^2)\). The first part of the same lemma gives the bound on \(\mathrm{TV}\).
Take the test that answers “\(p = \frac12+\alpha\)” when \(\tilde\mu \ge \frac12\). In each case it errs only if \(|\tilde\mu - p| \ge \alpha\), so each error probability is at most \(\frac14\) and the two add up to at most \(\frac12\). For any test, the error probabilities add up to at least \(1 - \mathrm{TV}(P_+,P_-)\), because the chance of answering “\(+\)” differs between the cases by at most \(\mathrm{TV}\). So \(\mathrm{TV}(P_+, P_-) \ge \frac12\).
Combining steps 2 and 3 gives \(\exp(4n(e^\varepsilon-1)^2\alpha^2) \ge 2\), which is the first bound on \(n\).
For \(\varepsilon \le 1\), convexity of \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \le (e-1)\varepsilon\), and \(\ln 2/(4(e-1)^2) = 0.0587 > 1/18\).


The theorem is about data drawn at random, but it also constrains estimates of the empirical mean on fixed data. Suppose a protocol is within \(\alpha/2\) of the empirical mean with probability at least \(7/8\) on every dataset. When \(n \ge 2\ln(16)/\alpha^2\), Hoeffding’s inequality puts the empirical mean strictly within \(\alpha/2\) of \(p\) with probability at least \(7/8\). So the protocol is strictly within \(\alpha\) of \(p\) with probability at least \(3/4\), and the theorem applies to it. This reduction says nothing about smaller \(n\), and Chan, Shi and Song (2012) give a direct argument for fixed data.
For \(\varepsilon \le 1\), comparing the theorem with Equation 17.5 shows that randomized response is optimal up to a constant factor. The central estimate, which needs only about \(1/(\varepsilon\alpha)\) people, is out of reach of every noninteractive local protocol.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.4 Repeated questions: RAPPOR
Google’s first large deployment, RAPPOR, collected statistics from the Chrome browser. It met a problem that a one-off survey never has. The same question goes to the same person every day, and fresh randomness each day leaks the answer.

Example 17.2 (Averaging attack) Take \(\varepsilon = \ln 4\), so that randomized response tells the truth with probability \(4/5\). A single “yes” from a person whose answer is “no” happens with probability \(1/5\), which leaves good deniability. Now ask the same question on \(50\) days with fresh coins, and suppose \(40\) reports say “yes”. If the answer is “no”, this happens with probability \(\binom{50}{40}(1/5)^{40}(4/5)^{10} = 1.21 \times 10^{-19}\). If it is “yes”, it happens with probability \(0.140\). The likelihood ratio is \(4^{30} \approx 1.15 \times 10^{18}\), and the deniability is gone.

The attack is composition at work. Basic composition, from the Laplace mechanism chapter, says that \(k\) answers with fresh coins are \(k\varepsilon\)-DP, which here is \(50\ln 4 = 69.3\). The attack meets this bound exactly, because the all-“yes” outcome has likelihood ratio \(4^{50}\). So the fix is to randomize once and repeat.

Definition 17.3 (Memoization) A person who is asked a question for the first time runs their randomizer and stores the result. When asked the same question again, they send the stored result.

Memoization keeps the privacy cost of a single answer, however often the question comes.

Proposition 17.3 If the stored result comes from an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer, then any number of memoized answers to the same question is \(\varepsilon\)-locally private.


Proof. The sequence of answers is a function of the single stored result, so the claim follows from post-processing.

Memoization protects honest repetition, not repetition by an adversarial analyst. For example, an analyst can ask for “your PIN” and then for “your PIN reversed”, two questions with the same information that each get a fresh randomization.
RAPPOR handles values from any finite domain, not just bits, so it first encodes a value as a bit vector.

Definition 17.4 (Bloom filter) Fix a length \(K\) and \(h\) hash functions \(H_1, \dots, H_h\colon \mathcal X \to \{1,\dots,K\}\). The Bloom filter of a value \(v\) is the vector \(B \in \{0,1\}^K\) with \(B_j = 1\) exactly when \(H_l(v) = j\) for some \(l\).

With \(h = 1\) and no collisions the Bloom filter is a one-hot encoding of \(v\). In general, \(B\) has at most \(h\) ones. RAPPOR then applies two layers of randomized response, bit by bit.

Definition 17.5 (RAPPOR) Fix \(\nu \in (0,1)\), the noise level of the permanent layer, and probabilities \(p_0 < p_1\) in \((0,1)\), the chances of reporting a one in the instantaneous layer. A person with value \(v\) and Bloom filter \(B\) of length \(K\), from Definition 17.4, does the following.

Permanent randomized response. Once, they draw \(B' \in \{0,1\}^K\) with independent coordinates, where \(B'_j\) is \(1\) with probability \(\nu/2\), \(0\) with probability \(\nu/2\), and \(B_j\) otherwise. They memoize \(B'\).
Instantaneous randomized response. Each time they report, they send a fresh \(Y \in \{0,1\}^K\) with independent coordinates, where \(Y_j = 1\) with probability \(p_1\) if \(B'_j = 1\) and with probability \(p_0\) if \(B'_j = 0\).


The permanent layer carries the long-term guarantee. It holds against an analyst who sees every report the person ever sends, because all of them come from the one memoized vector.

Theorem 17.2 Run RAPPOR with \(h\) hash functions and permanent noise level \(\nu\). As a function of the value \(v\), the memoized vector \(B'\) is an \(\varepsilon_\infty\)-local randomizer with
\[
\varepsilon_\infty = 2h\ln\frac{1 - \nu/2}{\nu/2}.
\tag{17.11}\]
So is the whole sequence of reports \(Y\), however long.


Proof. 

Let \(v, v'\) have Bloom filters \(B, \tilde B\). Each has at most \(h\) ones, so they differ in at most \(2h\) coordinates.
Fix an outcome \(b \in \{0,1\}^K\). Coordinates are independent, so \(\Pr[B' = b]\) is a product over \(j\). The factors at coordinates where \(B_j = \tilde B_j\) are equal for \(v\) and \(v'\) and cancel in the ratio.
Each remaining factor is \(1 - \nu/2\) or \(\nu/2\), so each ratio is at most \((1-\nu/2)/(\nu/2)\), and there are at most \(2h\) of them. By the pointwise lemma of the randomized response chapter, this bound on single outcomes gives \(\varepsilon_\infty\)-privacy.
The reports depend on \(v\) only through \(B'\), so they are a post-processing of it.


The instantaneous layer gives a stronger guarantee for an analyst who sees one report. With both layers, a reported bit is \(1\) with probability \(p_1^* = (1-\frac \nu2)p_1 + \frac \nu2 p_0\) when \(B_j = 1\) and \(p_0^* = \frac \nu2 p_1 + (1-\frac \nu2)p_0\) when \(B_j = 0\). Then \(p_1^* > p_0^*\), because \(p_1^* - p_0^* = (1-\nu)(p_1-p_0)\).

Theorem 17.3 Run RAPPOR with \(h\) hash functions, and let \(p_1^*\) and \(p_0^*\) be the combined probabilities above. A single report \(Y\), as a function of \(v\), is an \(\varepsilon_1\)-local randomizer with
\[
\varepsilon_1 = h\ln\frac{p_1^*(1-p_0^*)}{p_0^*(1-p_1^*)} .
\tag{17.12}\]


Proof. 

Given \(B\), the coordinates of \(Y\) are independent, with \(\Pr[Y_j = 1] = p_1^*\) or \(p_0^*\) according to \(B_j\). As before, coordinates where \(B_j = \tilde B_j\) cancel.
Let \(A\) be the set of coordinates with \(B_j = 1\) and \(\tilde B_j = 0\), and \(A'\) the set with the reverse. Both have at most \(h\) elements, since each lies inside the ones of one filter.
On \(A\) the ratio is \(p_1^*/p_0^* > 1\) if \(y_j = 1\) and \((1-p_1^*)/(1-p_0^*) < 1\) if \(y_j = 0\), so it is at most \(p_1^*/p_0^*\). On \(A'\) it is at most \((1-p_0^*)/(1-p_1^*)\) by the same reasoning.
Multiplying, the ratio is at most \(\big(p_1^*(1-p_0^*)/(p_0^*(1-p_1^*))\big)^h\), and the pointwise lemma finishes the proof.


Typical parameters show how far apart the two guarantees can be.

Example 17.3 With \(h = 2\), \(\nu = 1/2\), \(p_0 = 1/2\) and \(p_1 = 3/4\), the long-term guarantee is \(\varepsilon_\infty = 4\ln 3 = 4.39\). The combined probabilities are \(p_1^* = 0.6875\) and \(p_0^* = 0.5625\), so a single report has \(\varepsilon_1 = 1.07\).

The second layer has one more purpose, which local privacy does not capture. A memoized \(B'\) of a few hundred bits is almost surely unique, so two reports that both reveal it link to the same person, as a cookie would. Fresh noise on each report breaks that link for an analyst who sees few reports. An analyst who sees many reports can average the noise away and recover \(B'\), but then still faces the \(\varepsilon_\infty\) guarantee of Theorem 17.2.
The analyst decodes the reports by debiasing the bit counts and fitting candidate values against them, in the spirit of Equation 17.4. Memoization fails when the value drifts. For example, a person’s age in days changes daily, each new value needs a new \(B'\), and \(k\) distinct values cost \(k\,\varepsilon_\infty\) by composition.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.5 Values no one knew: Apple
Apple deployed local privacy on its phones and computers. Around the randomizers it put measures outside the model of DP, for example it discards network addresses and limits the number of reports per day. Independent researchers later measured from the software of macOS that each report had \(\varepsilon\) of \(1\) or \(2\), but that a day could spend up to \(16\).
Most of Apple’s protocols build on a private count mean sketch, a hashed table that estimates frequencies. A device hashes its value into a short table with one of several hash functions, and randomizes the table before it sends it. A variant with the Hadamard transform lets each device send a single bit. That matters on a phone, where a report must cost a few bytes at most.
The new problem Apple solved is discovery. A hash maps a value to its encoding, but the encoding cannot be inverted. So to estimate how often a word is typed, the analyst must already have the word in its dictionary and test its encoding against the reports. Slang and new words are exactly the values that no dictionary holds, and a search of all strings is hopeless, since there are \(26^8 \approx 2.1 \times 10^{11}\) strings of eight letters.
The sequence fragment puzzle breaks a word into pieces short enough to enumerate. Take, for illustration, eight-letter words and fragments of two letters, and fix an eight-bit hash function \(H\) from words to \(\{0, \dots, 255\}\). A person with an eight-letter word \(w\) picks one of the starting positions \(j \in \{1, 3, 5, 7\}\) uniformly at random. They send \(j\) together with a private report of the puzzle piece \((w_j w_{j+1}, H(w))\), the two letters at position \(j\) and the hash of the whole word. The pieces come from a set of \(26^2 \times 256 = 173{,}056\) candidates, small enough for the analyst to estimate the frequency of every one at each position.
The position needs no protection, because the person chooses it at random, independently of the word, as the next result shows.

Proposition 17.4 If the private report of the pair is an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer, then the whole message \((j, \text{report})\) is \(\varepsilon\)-locally private.


Proof. The position \(j\) is drawn independently of \(w\). Conditional on \(j\), the message is an \(\varepsilon\)-local randomizer of \(w\). For an event \(S\), write \(S_j\) for the set of reports \(r\) with \((j, r) \in S\). Then \(\Pr[(j, \text{report}) \in S \mid w] = \sum_{j} \frac14 \Pr[\text{report} \in S_j \mid w, j]\) is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times the same sum for any other word.

An example shows how the analyst puts the pieces back together.

Example 17.4 Suppose many people type “snowfall”, and \(H(\text{snowfall}) = 117\). Their messages are spread over \((1, \text{sn}, 117)\), \((3, \text{ow}, 117)\), \((5, \text{fa}, 117)\) and \((7, \text{ll}, 117)\). Each of the four pairs is frequent at its position. Pieces that share the hash \(117\) are joined in order of position, giving the candidate “snowfall”. A second round of ordinary frequency estimation over the discovered words then counts it, and it removes candidates that a hash collision assembled from different words.

With this method Apple found abbreviations and slang that no dictionary held, and measured the frequency of each emoji, which differed between English and French keyboards.

title: 17  Local Differential Privacy
text:
17.6 Numbers in one bit: Microsoft
Microsoft collects usage telemetry from Windows, such as how long people spend in each application. These values are numbers in a range \([0, m]\), and the analyst wants their mean \(\mu\). The Laplace mechanism works locally. Person \(i\) sends \(Y_i = X_i + \mathrm{Lap}(m/\varepsilon)\), which is \(\varepsilon\)-local because the identity map on \([0,m]\) changes by at most \(m\). The mean of the reports then has standard deviation exactly \(\sqrt2\,m/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\), which is optimal for local protocols by Theorem 17.1 applied to values in \(\{0, m\}\). But each report is a real number of size about \(m/\varepsilon\), so it costs many bits, while a single bit sent with a probability that grows linearly with the value suffices.

Definition 17.6 (One-bit mean protocol) Person \(i\), with \(X_i \in [0,m]\), sends a bit \(Y_i\) with
\[
\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon+1} + \frac{X_i}{m}\cdot\frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}.
\tag{17.13}\]
The analyst outputs
\[
\hat\mu = \frac{m}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(e^\varepsilon+1)\,Y_i - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}.
\tag{17.14}\]

At \(X_i = 0\) and \(X_i = m\) this is randomized response, and between them it interpolates linearly. The estimate of the analyst inverts that linear relation, as Equation 17.4 did for bits, and it keeps the privacy and the accuracy of randomized response.

Theorem 17.4 The one-bit protocol is \(\varepsilon\)-locally private, and \(\hat\mu\) is unbiased. With probability at least \(1-\beta\),
\[
|\hat\mu - \mu| \le m\coth\!\left(\frac\varepsilon2\right)\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\beta)}{2n}},
\tag{17.15}\]
and the standard deviation of \(\hat\mu\) is at most \(m\coth(\varepsilon/2)/(2\sqrt n)\).


Proof. 

Privacy. For every \(x \in [0,m]\), \(\Pr[Y = 1]\) lies between \(1/(e^\varepsilon+1)\) and \(e^\varepsilon/(e^\varepsilon+1)\), and so does \(\Pr[Y = 0] = 1 - \Pr[Y=1]\). The ratio of two numbers in that interval is at most \(e^\varepsilon\), and the pointwise lemma applies.
Unbiasedness. Substituting \(\mathbb E[Y_i] = \Pr[Y_i = 1]\) gives \((e^\varepsilon+1)\mathbb E[Y_i] - 1 = (X_i/m)(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), so each term of the sum has mean \(X_i/m\), and \(\mathbb E[\hat\mu] = \mu\).
Error. Each term \(Z_i = m\big((e^\varepsilon+1)Y_i - 1\big)/(e^\varepsilon-1)\) takes the two values \(-m/(e^\varepsilon-1)\) and \(m e^\varepsilon/(e^\varepsilon-1)\), an interval of length \(m(e^\varepsilon+1)/(e^\varepsilon-1) = m\coth(\varepsilon/2)\). The \(Z_i\) are independent, and Hoeffding’s inequality for their average gives the bound, as in the randomized response chapter.
Variance. A bit has variance at most \(1/4\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_i) \le m^2\coth^2(\varepsilon/2)/4\), and the average of \(n\) independent terms has variance at most \(m^2\coth^2(\varepsilon/2)/(4n)\).


Since \(\coth(\varepsilon/2)/2 \approx 1/\varepsilon\) for small \(\varepsilon\), one bit loses nothing against the \(\sqrt 2/\varepsilon\) of the Laplace protocol. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the one-bit standard deviation is at most \(0.765\) times the Laplace one.

17.6.1 Memoization with drifting values
Daily usage is never exactly the same two days running, so the memoization of RAPPOR does not apply. And rounding to bins before memoizing poses a dilemma. Narrow bins change often and force new randomizations, while wide bins make each report wrong by up to half a bin. Randomized rounding solves the second problem. It rounds each value to \(0\) or to \(m\) at random, with probabilities chosen so that the rounded value is right on average, so two bins suffice without bias.

Definition 17.7 (Memoized one-bit protocol) Before any data arrive, person \(i\) does three things, independently of their data and of each other.

They run the one-bit protocol on the input \(0\) and store the bit \(A_i(0)\).
They run it on the input \(m\) and store the bit \(A_i(m)\).
They draw an offset \(u_i\) uniformly from \([0, m)\).

On a day when their value is \(x \in [0,m]\), they round it to \(r_i(x) = m\) if \(x + u_i \ge m\) and to \(r_i(x) = 0\) otherwise, and they send \(A_i(r_i(x))\).

The random offset is what makes the rounding right on average.

Lemma 17.3 For every \(x \in [0,m]\), \(\Pr[r_i(x) = m] = x/m\), so \(\mathbb E[r_i(x)] = x\).


Proof. The offset is uniform on \([0,m)\), so \(\Pr[u_i \ge m - x] = \big(m - (m-x)\big)/m = x/m\).

Unbiased rounding, together with stored bits that are themselves outputs of the one-bit protocol, makes the bit of each day look like a fresh run of that protocol.

Theorem 17.5 On each day, the bit sent by the memoized protocol has exactly the distribution of the one-bit protocol run on that day’s value \(x\). So each day’s bit is \(\varepsilon\)-locally private, and the estimator of Definition 17.6, applied to one day’s bits, is unbiased with the error bound of Theorem 17.4.


Proof. The offset and the two stored bits are independent. By Lemma 17.3,
\[
\Pr[\text{bit} = 1] = \frac xm\cdot\frac{e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon+1} + \Big(1 - \frac xm\Big)\frac{1}{e^\varepsilon+1} = \frac{1}{e^\varepsilon+1} + \frac xm\cdot\frac{e^\varepsilon-1}{e^\varepsilon+1},
\tag{17.16}\]
which is the probability in Definition 17.6. Different people use independent coins, so the bits of one day are independent, as the error bound requires.

Over many days, the bits depend on the data only through the sequence of rounded values. While the value of a person stays on one side of their threshold \(m - u_i\), they repeat one stored bit, and the analyst learns nothing new. A crossing shows in the reports only if the two stored bits differ, which happens with probability \((1 + e^{2\varepsilon})/(1+e^\varepsilon)^2\), or \(0.607\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Then the analyst learns the day on which the value crossed a threshold drawn uniformly at random. No \(\varepsilon\)-local guarantee for arbitrary sequences of values covers this leak, so the deployed protocol adds a further layer of randomness to the sent bits to blur the crossing points.

title: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments
text:
18.1 Encode, shuffle, analyze
The local model of the previous chapter trusts no one, and pays with an error \(\sqrt n\) times larger than the central model’s. This chapter first studies a middle ground for differential privacy (DP), the shuffle model, in which a party that only mixes messages lets each person add far less noise. It then turns to the central model, where a company holds the data, and studies a query service for outside analysts and two public data releases.
Google’s Prochlo system started from a failure of local privacy. Its designers wanted to count which of a thousand applications call which of a hundred system interfaces, \(10^5\) pairs in all. By their estimate, a local protocol such as RAPPOR would need reports from about a trillion people to count them usefully, more people than exist.
Their architecture has three stages, encode, shuffle, analyze. Each person encodes their data on their own device, for example with a local randomizer. A shuffler collects the encoded messages, removes their metadata such as arrival times and network addresses, and sends them on in a uniformly random order. The analyst sees only the shuffled batch and decodes statistics from it. So the shuffler has one job, which is to break the link between a message and its sender.
The users must trust the shuffler not to reveal the order. Prochlo runs it inside trusted hardware, an Intel SGX enclave, so trust rests on the hardware vendor. Side-channel attacks such as Spectre have shown that such hardware can leak. Another choice is a mix network of several servers, each of which shuffles and re-encrypts the batch. Then the order stays hidden unless all of them collude.
crumbs: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments

title: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments
text:
18.2 The shuffle model
Prochlo led to a formal model between the local and central ones. In it, the adversary sees the shuffled messages but not who sent which.

Definition 18.1 (Shuffle model) A protocol in the shuffle model gives each person the same randomizer \(R\colon \mathcal X \to \mathcal Y\). Person \(i\) sends \(Y_i = R(X_i)\), using randomness independent of everyone else’s, and the shuffler outputs \((Y_{\pi(1)}, \dots, Y_{\pi(n)})\) for a permutation \(\pi\) drawn uniformly at random. The protocol is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in the shuffle model if this shuffled output, as a mechanism on the dataset \(D\), is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP in the central sense.

The uniform order adds no information, so the shuffled output carries the same information as the multiset of messages. A local protocol is also a shuffle protocol with the same guarantee, because the shuffled output is a post-processing of the messages. The interesting protocols are those whose messages are not private one by one but become private once mixed.
The benchmark task is again a sum of bits. In the central model, a count plus Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) has error of order \(1/\varepsilon\). In the local model each person adds noise of that size, so the \(n\) independent noises add up to a standard deviation of order \(\sqrt n/\varepsilon\), and by the previous chapter’s lower bound no local protocol does better. The question is how close the shuffle model can get to \(1/\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments

title: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments
text:
18.3 Amplification by shuffling
The first answer holds for any local randomizer, because shuffling makes it more private, just as subsampling did in an earlier chapter. In the form first proved, a message that is \(\varepsilon_0\)-private on its own gives a shuffled batch whose parameter is smaller by a factor of order \(\sqrt n\).

Theorem 18.1 (Amplification by shuffling) Let \(n \ge 1000\), \(\delta \in (0, \frac1{100})\), and let \(R\) be an \(\varepsilon_0\)-local randomizer with \(0 < \varepsilon_0 < \frac12\). Then the shuffled output of \(R(X_1), \dots, R(X_n)\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon = 12\,\varepsilon_0\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{n}} .
\tag{18.1}\]


The proof is in Erlingsson and coauthors (2019, Theorem 7 and Corollary 9). When everyone uses the same randomizer, shuffling the records before randomizing them gives the same output distribution, and the proof works in that form. It moves the one differing record to the front, swaps it into a uniformly random position, and then bounds how much each later message reveals about that position.
The theorem applies only to randomizers that are already very private, but few deployments want \(\varepsilon_0 \le \frac12\), because local accuracy is worst there. Feldman, McMillan and Talwar (2021) cover the useful regime, \(\varepsilon_0\) of order \(\ln n\), where \(\varepsilon\) is still a constant. For every \(\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\big(n/(16\ln(2/\delta))\big)\), they give \(\varepsilon = O\big((1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0})\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(1/\delta)/n}\big)\). In their proof, the message of each other person is, with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), a “clone” of what the differing person might have sent, and the count of clones hides that person. The next section carries out this idea in full for one simple randomizer.

title: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments
section: 18.4 Counting bits in the shuffle model
text:
18.4 Counting bits in the shuffle model
For a sum of bits, a direct protocol reaches error of order \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon\), which does not depend on \(n\). Its randomizer is randomized response in which almost everyone tells the truth.

Definition 18.2 (Shuffled randomized response) Fix a coin probability \(\nu \in (0,1]\). Person \(i\), with bit \(X_i\), sends \(Y_i = X_i\) with probability \(1 - \nu\), and otherwise sends a fresh fair coin. The analyst sees the shuffled reports, counts their ones as \(Z = \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\), and estimates the count \(c = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) by
\[
\tilde c = \frac{Z - n\nu/2}{1 - \nu}.
\tag{18.2}\]

In the local model \(\nu\) would be a constant. Here it is of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\varepsilon^2 n)\), so only about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\) people in total send coins. These coins hide each single person, as the clones did above. Two lemmas prepare the proof, and both use \(\tau = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), the number for which \((1+\tau)/(1-\tau) = e^\varepsilon\). The first says that, when \(s\) is large, the number of ones among \(s\) fair coins hides whether one more bit, of any distribution, is added to it.

Lemma 18.1 Let \(\varepsilon > 0\), let \(\tau = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), and let \(s \ge 2/\tau\) be an integer. Let \(N\) be binomial with \(s\) trials and success probability \(\frac12\), and let \(B\) and \(B'\) be Bernoulli variables independent of \(N\), with any parameters. Then for every set \(S\) of integers,
\[
\Pr[N + B \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[N + B' \in S] + 2e^{-s\tau^2/8}.
\tag{18.3}\]


Proof. 

Write \(P(k) = \Pr[N = k] = \binom sk 2^{-s}\). For \(1 \le k \le s\), the ratio of consecutive probabilities is \(P(k-1)/P(k) = k/(s+1-k)\).
Let \(K\) be the set of integers \(k\) with \(|k - \frac{s+1}2| \le \frac{s+1}2\tau\). Writing \(k = \frac{s+1}2(1+v)\) with \(|v| \le \tau\), the ratio becomes \((1+v)/(1-v)\), which lies in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^{\varepsilon}]\). Since \(\tau < 1\), every \(k \in K\) satisfies \(1 \le k \le s\).
For \(k \in K\) and any Bernoulli parameter \(b\), \(\Pr[N + B = k] = (1-b)P(k) + bP(k-1)\) is at most \(\max(P(k), P(k-1))\). By step 2 this is at most \(e^\varepsilon\min(P(k), P(k-1))\), which is at most \(e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[N + B' = k]\).
Outside \(K\), use \(|N + B - \frac{s+1}2| \le |N - \frac s2| + \frac12\). So \(N + B \notin K\) requires \(|N - \frac s2| > \frac{(s+1)\tau - 1}{2}\), and this threshold is at least \(s\tau/4\) because \(s\tau \ge 2\). Hoeffding’s inequality for \(s\) fair coins gives \(\Pr[N + B\notin K] \le 2\exp(-2(s\tau/4)^2/s) = 2e^{-s\tau^2/8}\).
Split \(S\) into \(S \cap K\), bounded by step 3, and the rest, bounded by step 4.


The second lemma makes sure that enough people send coins. It is a lower tail bound for the binomial distribution, sharper than Hoeffding’s inequality when the mean is small.

Lemma 18.2 Let \(N\) be binomial with mean \(\mu\). Then
\[
\Pr\!\left[N \le \frac\mu2\right] \le \exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\ln 2)\,\mu}{2}\right).
\tag{18.4}\]


Proof. 

Let \(N\) have \(m\) trials with success probability \(p\), so \(\mu = mp\). For \(\lambda > 0\), Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{-\lambda N}\) gives \(\Pr[N \le a] \le e^{\lambda a}\,\mathbb E[e^{-\lambda N}]\).
The trials are independent, so \(\mathbb E[e^{-\lambda N}] = (1 - p + pe^{-\lambda})^m\). Using \(1 + z \le e^z\), this is at most \(\exp\big(\mu(e^{-\lambda} - 1)\big)\).
Take \(a = \mu/2\) and \(\lambda = \ln 2\). The exponent becomes \(\mu\ln 2/2 - \mu/2\).


The privacy theorem chooses \(\nu\) so that, by Lemma 18.2, enough people send coins with high probability. By Lemma 18.1, those coins then hide the one person in question.

Theorem 18.2 (Privacy of shuffled randomized response) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\delta \in (0,1)\), \(\tau = \tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) and \(n \ge 1 + 16\ln(4/\delta)/\tau^2\), and set
\[
\nu = \frac{16\ln(4/\delta)}{\tau^2(n-1)} .
\tag{18.5}\]
Then shuffled randomized response is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP in the shuffle model.


Proof. 

Reduce to the count. Given the count \(Z\), every arrangement of the shuffled bits with \(Z\) ones is equally likely. So the shuffled output and \(Z\) are functions of each other, up to independent randomness, and it suffices to prove that \(Z\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP.
Isolate one person. The count does not depend on the order of the people, so we may take neighbours \(D \sim D'\) that differ by replacing the record of person \(1\). Let \(J\) be the set of persons \(i \ge 2\) who send coins. Its law does not depend on the data, and given \(J\),

\[
Z = C_J + N + Y_1, \qquad C_J = \sum_{i \ge 2,\ i \notin J} X_i,
\tag{18.6}\]
where \(N\) counts the ones among the \(|J|\) fair coins. Both \(C_J\) and the law of \(N\) are the same under \(D\) and \(D'\), and only the Bernoulli variable \(Y_1\) changes. 3. Enough coins. Let \(s_0 = 8\ln(4/\delta)/\tau^2\). The size \(|J|\) is binomial with mean \((n-1)\nu = 2s_0\). By Lemma 18.2, \(\Pr[|J| < s_0] \le \exp(-(1-\ln 2)\,8\ln(4/\delta)/\tau^2)\). Since \(8(1-\ln 2) > 2\) and \(\tau < 1\), this is at most \((\delta/4)^2 \le \delta/4\). 4. Each large \(J\) is private. If \(|J| \ge s_0\), then \(|J|\tau \ge 8\ln 4/\tau > 2\), so Lemma 18.1 applies. Its error term is \(2e^{-|J|\tau^2/8} \le 2e^{-\ln(4/\delta)} = \delta/2\). Shifting by the constant \(C_J\) preserves the inequality, so for every event \(S\), \(\Pr_D[Z \in S \mid J] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr_{D'}[Z\in S \mid J] + \delta/2\). 5. Average over \(J\). Summing over sets with \(|J| \ge s_0\) and adding the probability of the others,
\[
\Pr_D[Z \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr_{D'}[Z \in S] + \frac\delta2 + \frac\delta4 \le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr_{D'}[Z \in S] + \delta.
\tag{18.7}\]

The coins also add error to the count. But only about \(n\nu\) people send them, so the error depends on \(n\nu\), which Equation 18.5 keeps independent of \(n\).

Theorem 18.3 (Accuracy of shuffled randomized response) For every dataset, \(\tilde c\) is an unbiased estimate of \(c\) with variance at most \(n\nu/(2(1-\nu)^2)\). With \(\nu\) as in Equation 18.5 and \(\beta \in (0,1)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\),
\[
|\tilde c - c| \le \frac{1}{1-\nu}\sqrt{\frac{n\nu}{2\beta}} \le \frac{4}{(1-\nu)\,\tau}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{\beta}} .
\tag{18.8}\]
For \(\varepsilon \le 1\) and \(\nu \le \frac12\), the right-hand side is at most \(18\sqrt{\ln(4/\delta)/\beta}\,/\varepsilon\).


Proof. 

Each report is \(1\) with probability \((1-\nu)X_i + \nu/2\), so \(\mathbb E[Z] = (1-\nu)c + n\nu/2\), and \(\tilde c\) is unbiased.
Each report is a Bernoulli variable with parameter \(\nu/2\) or \(1 - \nu/2\), so its variance is \(\frac \nu2(1 - \frac \nu2) \le \frac \nu2\). The reports are independent, so \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) \le n\nu/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde c) \le n\nu/(2(1-\nu)^2)\).
Chebyshev’s inequality gives the first bound. For the second, \(n\nu = 16\ln(4/\delta)\,n/(\tau^2(n-1)) \le 32\ln(4/\delta)/\tau^2\) when \(n \ge 2\).
The function \(\tanh\) is concave on \([0,\infty)\), so \(\tau \ge \tanh(\frac12)\,\varepsilon = 0.462\,\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon \le 1\). With \(1/(1-\nu) \le 2\), the constant is \(8/0.462 < 18\).


So the shuffled count has error \(O(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon)\), which does not grow with \(n\). That is within a factor \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\) of the central model and far from the local model’s \(\sqrt n/\varepsilon\), as Figure 18.1 shows over \(n\) and the example below shows at one setting.

Example 18.1 Take \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(n = 10^6\). Then \(\tau = 0.4621\), and Equation 18.5 gives \(\nu = 0.001139\), so about \(1{,}139\) people send coins. The standard deviation of \(\tilde c\) is at most \(23.9\). Local randomized response at the same \(\varepsilon\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt n\,e^{1/2}/(e - 1) = 959.5\), and central Laplace noise has \(\sqrt 2 = 1.414\).







Figure 18.1: Error of three private counts of \(n\) bits at \(\varepsilon = 1\), as the 95th percentile of the absolute error over 2,000 simulated runs on data with half the bits equal to one. The local error grows as \(\sqrt n\). The shuffled error, with \(\nu\) from Equation 18.5 and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), stays near 47, and the central Laplace error stays near 3.



The price is trust in the shuffler. Each message on its own is randomized response that keeps the true bit with probability \(1 - \nu/2\), so it is only \(\varepsilon_0\)-locally private with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln((2-\nu)/\nu) = 7.47\) in the example. So a shuffler that leaked the order would expose almost every bit. This \(\varepsilon_0\) is below \(\ln\big(n/(16\ln(2/\delta))\big) = 8.37\), so the protocol lies in the range that the clone analysis of the previous section covers.

title: 18  The Shuffle Model and Central Deployments
text:
18.5 A query service: LinkedIn
LinkedIn’s audience engagements service lets advertisers ask how members in a target audience engage with content, such as which articles or topics they click on most. It runs in the central model, so LinkedIn holds the data and answers each query with a private mechanism. This section covers two results of the research for it, a sharper analysis of the exponential mechanism and a fast way to run it.

18.5.1 Bounded range
Recall the exponential mechanism. It takes a score \(u(D, r)\) for each candidate \(r\) in a countable set, whose value changes by at most \(\Delta u\) between neighbours. It outputs \(r\) with probability proportional to \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta u))\), and it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Write
\[
L(y) = \ln\frac{\Pr[M(D) = y]}{\Pr[M(D') = y]}
\tag{18.9}\]
for the privacy loss of output \(y\) between neighbours \(D\) and \(D'\). Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP says that \(|L(y)| \le \varepsilon\), so the losses lie in an interval of width \(2\varepsilon\). The exponential mechanism satisfies a stronger condition.

Definition 18.3 (Bounded range) A mechanism \(M\) with a countable output set is \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range if for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all outputs \(y, y'\),
\[
\Pr[M(D) = y]\,\Pr[M(D') = y'] \le e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[M(D') = y]\,\Pr[M(D) = y'] .
\tag{18.10}\]

When the outputs have positive probability, the definition says that \(L(y) - L(y') \le \varepsilon\). So the privacy losses lie in an interval of width \(\varepsilon\), which need not be centred at zero. The next result shows that the two notions are within a factor of two of each other.

Proposition 18.1 An \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism with a countable output set is \(2\varepsilon\)-bounded range.


Proof. 

Same support. Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range. Suppose some output \(y\) has \(\Pr[M(D) = y] > 0\) but \(\Pr[M(D') = y] = 0\). With this \(y\), the right-hand side of the definition is zero for every \(y'\), and the left-hand side is \(\Pr[M(D) = y]\) times \(\Pr[M(D') = y']\). So the definition forces \(\Pr[M(D') = y'] = 0\) for every \(y'\), which is impossible. So \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) give positive probability to the same outputs, and \(L\) is finite on them.
Both signs occur. Both distributions sum to one over the common support, so some output \(y_+\) has \(L(y_+) \ge 0\) and some output \(y_-\) has \(L(y_-) \le 0\).
Width \(\varepsilon\) around zero. For every \(y\), bounded range gives \(L(y) \le L(y_-) + \varepsilon \le \varepsilon\) and \(L(y) \ge L(y_+) - \varepsilon \ge -\varepsilon\). The pointwise lemma of the randomized response chapter turns \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) into \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Converse. If \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) everywhere, then \(L(y) - L(y') \le 2\varepsilon\).


The general conversion loses a factor of two, but the exponential mechanism does not, because its privacy losses already lie in an interval of width \(\varepsilon\).

Proposition 18.2 The exponential mechanism with parameter \(\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range.


Proof. 

Write \(Z_D = \sum_r \exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta u))\) for the normalizing constant. Then \(L(r) = \frac{\varepsilon}{2\Delta u}\big(u(D,r) - u(D',r)\big) + \ln(Z_{D'}/Z_D)\).
The constant cancels in a difference: \(L(r) - L(r') = \frac{\varepsilon}{2\Delta u}\big[(u(D,r) - u(D',r)) - (u(D,r') - u(D',r'))\big]\).
Each bracketed difference is at most \(\Delta u\) in absolute value, so \(L(r) - L(r') \le \varepsilon\).


The factor of two matters when many selections are composed, and two lemmas make the composition precise. The first turns a tail bound on the privacy loss into a privacy guarantee. It holds for any output space, with \(L\) the logarithm of the ratio of mass functions or of densities.

Lemma 18.3 Let \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0,1]\). If for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) the loss satisfies \(\Pr_{y \sim M(D)}[L(y) > \varepsilon'] \le \delta\), then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. Fix an event \(S\) and let \(G = \{y : L(y) \le \varepsilon'\}\). On \(S \cap G\) the probability under \(D\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) times that under \(D'\), so \(\Pr[M(D) \in S\cap G] \le e^{\varepsilon'}\Pr[M(D')\in S]\). The rest of \(S\) has probability at most \(\Pr[M(D) \notin G] \le \delta\) under \(D\).

The second lemma bounds the mean loss. It uses Hoeffding’s lemma, the key step in the proof of Hoeffding’s inequality: a random variable \(W\) in an interval of length \(\ell\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda(W - \mathbb E W)}] \le e^{\lambda^2\ell^2/8}\) for every real \(\lambda\).

Lemma 18.4 If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range and \(D \sim D'\), then \(\mathbb E_{y\sim M(D)}[L(y)] \le \varepsilon^2/8\).


Proof. 

Under \(y \sim M(D)\), the variable \(W = -L(y)\) lies in an interval of length \(\varepsilon\), and \(\mathbb E[e^{W}] = \sum_y \Pr[M(D) = y]\,\frac{\Pr[M(D')=y]}{\Pr[M(D)=y]} = 1\).
Hoeffding’s lemma with \(\lambda = 1\) gives \(1 = \mathbb E[e^W] \le e^{\mathbb E W + \varepsilon^2/8}\), so \(\mathbb E[L] = -\mathbb E[W] \le \varepsilon^2/8\).


The two lemmas combine into a composition theorem. The total privacy loss of \(k\) steps is a sum of \(k\) losses, each with mean at most \(\varepsilon^2/8\) and a range of width \(\varepsilon\). So the sum concentrates around \(k\varepsilon^2/8\), and Lemma 18.3 turns that concentration into a guarantee.

Theorem 18.4 (Composition of bounded-range mechanisms) Run \(k\) mechanisms in sequence on the same dataset, where the \(j\)-th may be chosen as a function of the outputs of the first \(j-1\), and each is \(\varepsilon\)-bounded range whatever those outputs are. For every \(\delta \in (0,1)\), the sequence of outputs is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with
\[
\varepsilon' = \frac{k\varepsilon^2}{8} + \varepsilon\sqrt{\frac{k\ln(1/\delta)}{2}} .
\tag{18.11}\]


Proof. 

The probability of an output sequence is the product of the conditional probabilities of its terms, so the loss is a sum \(L = \sum_{j=1}^k L_j\), where \(L_j\) is the loss of the \(j\)-th output given the earlier ones.
Given the earlier outputs, \(L_j\) lies in an interval of length \(\varepsilon\), by bounded range, and its conditional mean is at most \(\varepsilon^2/8\), by Lemma 18.4. Let \(V_j\) be \(L_j\) minus its conditional mean, so \(L \le \sum_j V_j + k\varepsilon^2/8\).
For \(\lambda > 0\), Hoeffding’s lemma applied conditionally gives \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda V_j} \mid \text{earlier outputs}] \le e^{\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/8}\). Taking conditional expectations from the last term to the first gives \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda\sum_j V_j}] \le e^{k\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/8}\).
By Markov’s inequality, \(\Pr[\sum_j V_j \ge t] \le e^{-\lambda t + k\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/8}\). Choosing \(\lambda = 4t/(k\varepsilon^2)\) makes this \(e^{-2t^2/(k\varepsilon^2)}\), which equals \(\delta\) at \(t = \varepsilon\sqrt{k\ln(1/\delta)/2}\).
So \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon'] \le \delta\) for every pair of neighbours, and Lemma 18.3 finishes the proof.


Advanced composition gives \(\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) for \(k\) mechanisms that are known only to be \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The square-root term of Theorem 18.4 is half as large. Its linear term \(k\varepsilon^2/8\) is also about a quarter of \(k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \approx k\varepsilon^2/2\) for small \(\varepsilon\).

Example 18.2 Compose \(k = 100\) exponential mechanisms, each with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Basic composition gives \(10.00\), advanced composition \(5.76\), and Theorem 18.4 gives \(2.75\).



18.5.2 Top-\(k\) selection with Gumbel noise
An advertiser usually wants the few most popular items in a histogram, such as the top topics among an audience, not every count. LinkedIn’s algorithms depend on two things. The domain of items is known in advance or not. And a person’s contribution is \(m\)-restricted when each person adds one to at most \(m\) counts, and unrestricted otherwise. For example, hires are \(1\)-restricted, because a hire adds one to one employer, but skills are not, because one person can list many.
With \(m\)-restricted contributions, replacing one person changes the vector of counts by at most \(2m\) in \(\ell_1\) norm. So Laplace noise of scale \(2m/\varepsilon\) on every count, followed by taking the top \(k\), is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, but its noise grows with \(m\). For unrestricted contributions it is better to select with the exponential mechanism, with the count of an item as its score. A count changes by at most one between neighbours, whatever the number of counts that a person touches. Peeling selects the top item, removes it, and repeats \(k\) times. Each round is the exponential mechanism, so by Proposition 18.2 and Theorem 18.4 its cost depends on \(k\) and not on \(m\).
Sampling from the exponential mechanism needs its normalizing constant, and peeling needs it \(k\) times. Adding noise of the right shape and taking a maximum avoids both, and the right shape is the Gumbel distribution.

Definition 18.4 (Gumbel distribution) The Gumbel distribution with scale \(b > 0\) has cumulative distribution function \(\Pr[G \le g] = \exp(-e^{-g/b})\) for real \(g\).

Adding independent Gumbel noise to each score and taking the largest gives exactly the distribution of the exponential mechanism, and taking the \(k\) largest gives exactly peeling.

Theorem 18.5 (Gumbel-max trick) Let \(u_1, \dots, u_d\) be scores, let \(G_1, \dots, G_d\) be independent Gumbel variables with scale \(b\), and write \(w_i = e^{u_i/b}\). Then

the index of the largest noisy score \(u_i + G_i\) is \(i\) with probability \(w_i/\sum_{j} w_j\);
the indices of the \(k\) largest noisy scores, in decreasing order, have the distribution of \(k\) rounds of peeling, where each round picks a remaining item \(i\) with probability proportional to \(w_i\).



Proof. 

Exponential race. Let \(E_i = e^{-(u_i + G_i)/b}\). Then \(\Pr[E_i > t] = \Pr[G_i < -b\ln t - u_i] = \exp(-w_i t)\) for \(t > 0\). So the \(E_i\) are independent exponential variables with rates \(w_i\), and the noisy scores in decreasing order are the \(E_i\) in increasing order.
The first finisher. With \(W = \sum_j w_j\), the chance that \(E_i\) is the smallest is

\[
\int_0^\infty w_i e^{-w_i t}\prod_{j \ne i} e^{-w_j t}\,dt = \frac{w_i}{W}.
\tag{18.12}\]
This proves the first claim. 3. Memorylessness. Condition on \(E_i\) being smallest, with value \(t\). This is the event that \(E_j > t\) for every \(j \ne i\), and given it, the excesses \(E_j - t\) are independent exponential variables with the original rates \(w_j\), because \(\Pr[E_j > t + s \mid E_j > t] = e^{-w_j s}\). 4. Induction. By step 3, the order of the remaining \(E_j\) is a fresh exponential race among the remaining items. Step 2 applied to it shows that the next item is chosen with probability proportional to its \(w_j\), and repeating gives the second claim.

Counts change by at most one between neighbours, so take \(b = 2/\varepsilon_0\). Then \(w_i = e^{\varepsilon_0 u_i/2}\), and the first claim is the exponential mechanism with parameter \(\varepsilon_0\). By the second claim, adding Gumbel noise once and reporting the \(k\) largest noisy counts is peeling, so it has the guarantee of peeling from Theorem 18.4. It draws \(d\) noise values and selects the top \(k\) once, in time of order \(d\) plus the time of that selection. Peeling takes time of order \(kd\).


18.5.3 Queries from outside
Here, unlike in the previous chapter, outside analysts choose the queries, and they can be careless or malicious. Each advertiser has a privacy budget for its own queries. Two advertisers with budget \(\varepsilon\) each can combine their answers, and then basic composition gives only \(2\varepsilon\) about the members. Many advertisers together would erase the guarantee. The mechanisms cannot rule this out, so LinkedIn relies on vetting and on agreements not to share results. It also chooses \(\varepsilon\) and the monthly number of queries so that the attacks it models fail.

18.6 Data releases
The last two deployments do not answer queries. Each publishes a fixed dataset once, computed in the central model.

18.6.1 Mobility reports
During the Covid-19 pandemic, Google published community mobility reports from the location history of users who opted in. For each region and day, they gave the change in visits to places such as parks, workplaces and residences, relative to a baseline from before the pandemic. The counts of visits get Laplace noise after a bound on what each person adds. A person counts at most once per category and place, and in at most four such pairs per day, kept at random. So the contributions are \(m\)-restricted, as in the counts of LinkedIn. The reports drop metrics whose noisy count of people is below \(100\), and changes that the noise makes too uncertain.


18.6.2 A URL dataset with zero-concentrated privacy
Facebook and the academic organization Social Science One released a dataset on how users interact with web links shared on Facebook. It covers more than 38 million URLs, and researchers get access through a proposal process. The raw data are events, such as “a woman aged 35 to 44 in Germany shared this URL on this date”. The release aggregates them by URL, month, country, age and gender, and publishes noisy counts of views, clicks, shares, likes and other reactions.
The noise is Gaussian, and the guarantee is zero-concentrated differential privacy, a variant of DP that suits Gaussian noise. It uses the Rényi divergence. For an order \(\alpha > 1\) and two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\), write \(p\) and \(q\) for their densities, or their mass functions on a countable set. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is
\[
D_\alpha(P\,\|\,Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p(y)^\alpha q(y)^{1-\alpha}\,dy ,
\tag{18.13}\]
with a sum in place of the integral on a countable set. It is zero when \(P = Q\) and grows as they move apart. Zero-concentrated privacy asks that the divergence between the outputs on neighbours grow at most linearly in the order \(\alpha\).

Definition 18.5 (Zero-concentrated differential privacy) Let \(\rho \ge 0\). A mechanism \(M\) is \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated differentially private if for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and all \(\alpha > 1\),
\[
D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \rho\,\alpha .
\tag{18.14}\]

It has one parameter, like pure DP, but composes like advanced composition, as the next three results show. It lies between the two, because an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zero-concentrated, and the converse holds with a \(\delta\).
The first two results follow from private deep learning, where Definition 14.4 defines the log-moment \(\kappa_M(\lambda)\). It is the worst case over neighbours of the logarithm of the average \(\lambda\)-th power of the density ratio \(p/q\) under \(p\). For one pair of neighbours and \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\), that logarithm is a multiple of the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\), by its definition:
\[
\ln\int p^{\alpha}q^{1-\alpha}\,dy = (\alpha - 1)\,D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big).
\tag{18.15}\]
So a mechanism is \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated exactly when \(\kappa_M(\lambda) \le \rho\lambda(\lambda+1)\) for every \(\lambda > 0\).

Lemma 18.5 Let \(M_1\) be \(\rho_1\)-zero-concentrated, and let \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) be a mechanism chosen as a function of the output \(y_1\) of \(M_1\), which is \(\rho_2\)-zero-concentrated for every \(y_1\). Then the mechanism that outputs \((y_1, y_2)\) is \((\rho_1 + \rho_2)\)-zero-concentrated. In particular, this holds for two mechanisms run with independent coins.


Proof. By the equivalence above, \(\kappa_{M_1}(\lambda) \le \rho_1\lambda(\lambda+1)\) and \(\kappa_{M_2(\cdot;y_1)}(\lambda) \le \rho_2\lambda(\lambda+1)\) for every \(y_1\) and every \(\lambda > 0\). Lemma 14.2 adds the two bounds, so \(\kappa_M(\lambda) \le (\rho_1 + \rho_2)\lambda(\lambda+1)\), which is the claim.

The second result gives the guarantee of the Gaussian mechanism, which is why the release uses it.

Proposition 18.3 (Gaussian mechanism) Let \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) change by at most \(\Delta_2 f\) in Euclidean norm between neighbours. Then \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\), with \(Z\) a vector of \(d\) independent normal variables of mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), is \((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\)-zero-concentrated.


Proof. Lemma 14.3 gives \(\kappa_M(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda+1)(\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) for every \(\lambda > 0\), which by the equivalence above is \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated privacy with \(\rho = (\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\).

The third result converts a zero-concentrated guarantee into an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee, the form in which a release usually states its budget.

Proposition 18.4 A \(\rho\)-zero-concentrated mechanism is \((\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta \in (0,1)\).


Proof. 

If \(\rho = 0\), every Rényi divergence is \(0\), so \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) have the same distribution and the claim holds. Otherwise let \(y \sim M(D)\), with density \(p\), and let \(L = \ln(p(y)/q(y))\), where \(q\) is the density of \(M(D')\). For \(\alpha > 1\), \(\mathbb E[e^{(\alpha-1)L}] = \int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha} \le e^{(\alpha-1)\alpha\rho}\).
Markov’s inequality gives \(\Pr[L > t] \le e^{(\alpha-1)(\alpha\rho - t)}\).
Take \(t = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) and \(\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\). Writing \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\), the exponent is \(\sqrt{\ell/\rho}\,\big(\rho + \sqrt{\rho\ell} - \rho - 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\big) = -\ell\), so \(\Pr[L > t] \le \delta\).
Lemma 18.3 finishes the proof.


The budget of the release raises a question that recurs in deployments: what is a neighbour? User-level privacy hides everything one person did, and action-level privacy hides one action, such as one click. User-level privacy is the goal, but a few users act thousands of times, and hiding them would drown every count in noise. So the release protects each action strongly enough that a user with at most a high percentile of the activity distribution gets a stated user-level guarantee. Heavier users still have the action-level one.

Example 18.3 Suppose each action adds one to a single cell, and the actions of one user fall in different cells. Replacing one action changes two counts by one each, a Euclidean change of \(\sqrt 2\). Replacing all \(k\) actions of a user changes at most \(2k\) counts, a change of at most \(\sqrt{2k}\). Then by Proposition 18.3, \(k\) actions cost \(k\) times the action-level \(\rho\). To give users with at most \(20\) actions \((0.5, 10^{-6})\)-DP, solve \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln 10^6} = 0.5\) for \(\rho = 0.00444\) at the user level. The action level is then \(\rho = 0.000222\), which Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt2/\sqrt{2\rho} = 67.1\) achieves. A single action alone is protected at \((0.111, 10^{-6})\)-DP.

The largest deployment, the US Census Bureau’s use of DP for the 2020 census, is complex enough to need a separate treatment.
